en: Now begins the fourth chapter.
[In this chapter on the fruits [of yoga], the first quarter treats the definition of liberation while living (jīvanmukti).
Now begins the fourth chapter.

That supreme Brahman, through the knowledge of which liberation is attained while living—liberation devoid of departure from the body or transition to another state—that am I, the fearless one named Rāma. //1//
Topic 1.1.1:
Repetition. Sūtras 1–2:
Repetition [of meditation] is required because of the repeated instruction. (BS 4.1.1)

In the third chapter, the investigation concerning the means (*sādhana*) based on the higher and lower knowledges has for the most part been completed. Now, here in the fourth chapter, the investigation concerning the results (*phala*) will follow;
and certain other matters arising incidentally will also be considered.
First, by means of several topical discussions (*adhikaraṇa*), we shall follow up on the remainder of the investigation into the locus of the means of knowledge.
[The scriptures state: "Verily, the Self, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.21);
"Having known that very [Self], the wise man should practice wisdom" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.6).

Regarding such scriptural passages as, "That [Self] is to be sought, that is to be desired to be known" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1), a doubt arises: should the cognition be performed once, or should it be repeated?
What, then, is the prima facie view? It should be performed once, like the *prayāja* offerings and so forth.
For by that much alone, the purpose of the treatise is fulfilled;
if it were performed while [the injunction] is not being heard, it would result in something that is not the meaning of the treatise.
But surely, repeated instructions have been cited, such as "it should be heard, it should be reflected upon, it should be meditated upon," and so forth?
Even so, as long as one repeats the word [of the scripture]—namely, that there is hearing once, reflection once, and meditative concentration once—it is not excessive.
However, in cases where instruction is given only once, such as "one should meditate" (*upāsīta*) and similar passages, there is no repetition.
This being the position reached, we reply: repetition of the mental realization (*pratyaya*) must be performed.
Why? Because of the repeated instruction.
For such repeated instructions as "It is to be heard, it is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon" indicate the repetition of the mental state (*pratyaya*).
But was it not said that one should repeat only as much as the words [of the text] prescribe, and nothing more? No.
There is no fault, because [the practice] culminates in vision (*darśana*).
For hearing and the other [limbs of yoga], when repeated, culminate in vision and thus have a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*),
just as threshing and so forth culminate in the production of rice and the like.
Moreover, both *upāsana* (worship) and *nididhyāsana* (meditative reflection) denote actions in which the quality of repetition (*āvṛtti*) is inherently included.
For instance, in common usage, one who follows a teacher or a king with total devotion is said to "worship" (*upāste*) them;
likewise, a woman whose husband is away who remembers him incessantly out of longing is said to "meditate" (*dhyāyati*) upon her husband.
Furthermore, the use of the terms *vid* (to know) and *upāsti* (to meditate upon) is observed in the Vedāntas without distinction;

in some places, having begun with *vid*, one concludes with *upāsti*, as for example: "He who knows what he knows—him I have told this" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.1.4), and here [the student says], "O Venerable Sir, instruct me further regarding that deity whom you meditate upon" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.2.2).

And in some cases, having begun with "one should meditate" (*upāsīta*), he concludes with "one who knows thus," as for example: "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.18.1), and here [he concludes]:
"He who knows thus shines and glows with fame, glory, and the splendor of sacred knowledge" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.18.3).
Therefore, even when the instruction is given only once, the necessity of repetition is established.
"But the repeated instruction indicates repetition. (Sūtra 1) / "Oṃ.
Repetition [of meditation] is required because of the repeated instruction.

Having described the means (*sādhana*), the fruit (*phala*) is now being described; thus he states the connection between the two chapters as the relationship of cause and effect: "In the third [chapter]," etc.
He says "by way of the discussion of the fruit" (*prasaṅgena*) because the departure [of the soul] and the path beginning with light (*arcirādimārga*) are now being investigated.
Previously, the means such as renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), which were explicitly stated by the Śruti, were considered;
now, however, until the section on "non-clinging" (*adyāśleṣādhikaraṇa*), matters such as repetition (*āvṛtti*)—which are understood through the logical necessity of the result—are being considered.

From that point onward, the first quarter [of the second chapter] treats liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*); then, in the second quarter, the departure of the soul (*utkrānti*); in the third, the determination of the path beginning with light (*arcirādi*) and the destination; and in the fourth, the determination of the fruits of knowledge (*jñāna*) and meditation (*upāsana*). Such is the analysis of the subject matter of the quarters.

Regarding the first topical section (*adhikaraṇa*), having restated the subject matter—the means such as hearing (*śravaṇa*)—he states the doubt arising from the observation of two types of practice: "Or rather, the Self...

Since all the topical sections consist of an inquiry into the means and fruits of the knowledge of the Self derived from the Śruti, the connections to the Śruti, the scripture (*śāstra*), the book (*adhyāya*), and the quarter (*pāda*) have been stated.
The connection between each respective section follows from the relationship between their respective subject matters.

With the intermediate connection characterized by the analogy that just as there is no distinction in liberation, there is likewise no distinction in repetition regarding hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "What, then, [is the case]?
In this prima facie view, since hearing and so forth have an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) like the *prayāja* offerings, the result is their performance only once.

In the Siddhānta, however, the distinction is that, like the act of threshing (*avaghāta*), there is repetition for as long as the result persists, because it has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*). One might object: "But surely, since repeated instruction would otherwise be inexplicable, the intention of the scripture lies in the repetition of the means. To this he replies: "Even so," meaning that since the repeated mention is justified by the need to establish the combination (*samuccaya*) of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and the other means, it does not intend to enjoin repetition.
He states that even regarding the means for the direct realization of the qualified [Brahman], there is no need for repetition, using the word "once" (*sakṛt*).
Although the instruction given more than once might be otherwise accounted for as indicating either repetition or a combination [of methods],

nevertheless, since it is improper to postulate a mere unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) when a visible result is possible, the fruit of direct realization resulting from hearing and so forth occurs through the door of repetition.

Because it has been observed in the case of the *ṣaḍja* note and others, the repeated mention indicates a return [to the same practice], according to the principle that "what is seen serves a purpose. Thus he says: "not because it culminates in mere observation. However, regarding meditation (*dhyāna*), since its repetition is explicitly heard in the scriptural word "one should meditate" (*upāsīta*), it is not merely implied by the sense of the matter; thus he says: "Moreover... (*api ca*).

Although the word *upāsti* (meditation) signifies repetition, one might ask: "How is repetition established in the cases of the *ahaṃgrahas* (identifications with the Self), which are designated by the word *veda* (knows)? To this, he says: "And [the rule] regarding *vid* and *upāsti*.
He provides an example of the two words having the same meaning: "In some places...

When it is said that whatever Raikva knows—that reality of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—and whatever anyone other than Raikva knows, all that is included within its fruit, then in this way he spoke of Raikva as being superior.
Thus was the speech of one swan to another;
having heard it, Jānaśruti went to Raikva and said,
"O Venerable One,"
"Teach me this deity known to Raikva"—the meaning is "instruct me.

Thus, the repetition of meditation, which is the means for the direct realization of both the qualified (saguṇa) and the unqualified (nirguṇa) Brahman, is both scripturally enjoined and established by the nature of the case, because it serves a visible purpose;
however, the distinction is that for hearing (śravaṇa) and reflection (manana), repetition is established solely by the nature of the case, as they are taught more than once. //1//
And because of the indicative mark. BBs_4,1.2.
The indicative mark (*liṅga*) also indicates the repetition of the meditation;

for, having introduced the knowledge of the *udgītha* with "The sun is the *udgītha*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.5.1), that [view] is set aside on account of the defect of having only one son, and it is said: "He should turn back toward the rays" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.5.2).
Thus, by establishing the cognition of the multiplicity of rays for the sake of having many sons, [the author] demonstrates the repetition of the practice as something established.
Therefore, by analogy with that, the establishment of repetition applies to all practices.
To this, he says: "Granted that there may be repetition in the case of practices whose fruits are yet to be accomplished."
Since excellence through repetition is possible in those [meditations], one might ask:

"What is the purpose of repetition in that case where the cognition has the Supreme Brahman as its object—that Supreme Brahman which, being of the very nature of eternally pure, enlightened, and liberated, presents itself as the Self?
If it is argued that repetition must be accepted because the realization of Brahman as the Self is impossible from hearing it only once, we say: No.
Even in the case of repetition, that [result] would be untenable;

for if a sentence such as "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7), when heard but once, were not to produce the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self, then what hope could there be that the very same sentence, when repeated, would produce it?

Now, it might be argued that a sentence alone cannot directly bring about the realization of any object; therefore, a sentence, depending upon reasoning (*yukti*), will cause one to experience the identity of Brahman and the Self.
Even so, repetition remains entirely purposeless;
for that reasoning, once set in motion even a single time, will itself cause its own object to be experienced.
Furthermore, it might be argued that through speech and verbal expression, a cognition is produced only with respect to a general object and not a particular one.

For example, from the statement "I have a pain in my heart" and from such signs as the trembling of the limbs, another person perceives only the general existence of the pain, but does not experience its particularity in the way that the sufferer himself does.
If it is argued that specific experience is what removes ignorance, and therefore there must be repetition for that purpose, we say no.
For even when that much [instruction] is performed repeatedly, the arising of specific knowledge is impossible.
Indeed, a distinction that is not apprehended by scripture and reasoning when applied once cannot be apprehended even if those two are applied a hundred times.

Therefore, whether a specific distinction or even a mere generality is established through scripture and reasoning, in either case, those two perform their own function as soon as they have operated once; thus, repetition is useless.
Furthermore, it cannot be maintained that scripture and reasoning, when applied once, fail to produce an experience for anyone, because the intelligence of those who understand is diverse.

Moreover, in the case of worldly objects which possess multiple parts and consist of both general and particular features, it may be that one perceives one part with one act of attention and another part with another, such that practice is useful— as in the case of learning long recitations and the like. However, it is not logical to require practice for the arising of valid cognition regarding Brahman, which is devoid of distinctions, free from general and particular features, and consists solely of pure consciousness.

To this it is replied: Repetition would be purposeless for one who is able to realize the identity of Brahman and the self (*brahmātmatva*) immediately upon the statement "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) being uttered once;
however, for one who is not so able, repetition is indeed useful.
For instance, in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*: "That thou art, O Śvetaketu" (Chā. 6.8.7).

Having thus instructed him with the words, "May the Blessed One inform me further," [Nārada] being urged again, [the teacher] dispels each respective ground for doubt and teaches "That thou art" repeatedly.
And thus it has been shown in such passages as, "It is to be heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.6).

Now, an objection is raised: if the sentence "That thou art," when heard only once, is unable to bring about the experience of its own meaning, then even if it is repeated, it will certainly not be able to do so.
This is not a fault;
for indeed, there is nothing that is impossible regarding what is observed.
Indeed, we see those who, having grasped the meaning of a sentence with difficulty upon hearing it only once, repeat it and correctly comprehend it by setting aside various fallacious appearances.
Moreover, this sentence "That thou art" (tattvamasi) teaches that the referent of the word "thou" (tvam-padārtha) possesses the nature of the referent of the word "that" (tat-padārtha).

By the word "that," the already-mentioned Brahman— the existent, the seer, and the cause of the origin and so forth of the world— is denoted, as in "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1) and "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.28).
"The unseen seer" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.11);
"the unknown knower" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.11);
"unborn, undecaying, immortal, neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8).
This and more is well-known from the scriptures.
In that context, by words such as "unborn" (*ajā*), the modifications of being such as birth and so forth are excluded;
and by words such as "not gross" (*asthūla*), the properties of substance such as grossness and so forth are excluded.

Furthermore, by terms such as "consciousness" (vijñāna) and so forth, its nature as the light of pure sentience is expressed. This entity, which is free from all the attributes of transmigratory existence, whose essence is experience, and which is designated as Brahman, is well-known among those proficient in the Vedānta as the referent of that term.
Likewise, the referent of the term *tvaṃ* (you), which is the inner self (*pratyagātman*) as the listener, is conceived as being within the body and determined to extend up to pure consciousness.

In this regard, for those whose knowledge of these two word-referents is obstructed by ignorance, doubt, or misconception, the sentence "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) is unable to produce valid knowledge regarding its own meaning, because the meaning of a sentence is preceded by the knowledge of its word-referents.

Therefore, for this reason, one must apply oneself to the study of the scriptures and the practice of reasoning, which have as their purpose the discrimination of the categories of existence (*padārtha-viveka*).

And although the Self (*ātman*) to be realized is partless (*niraṃśa*), nevertheless, many parts characterized by the body, senses, mind, intellect, objects, and sensations have been superimposed upon it; therein, by means of a single point of attention, one [part] is [grasped].
It is logical that there is a sequential realization in the sense that "one [cognition] removes another";
however, that [sequential process] is merely the preliminary form of the realization of the self.
But for those of subtle intellect, there is no obstruction regarding the objects of things characterized by ignorance, doubt, or error.
If it is held that they are capable of experiencing the meaning of the sentence "That thou art" as soon as it is stated once, then the futility of repetition is indeed accepted;
for the realization of the Self, having arisen just once, removes ignorance, and thus no sequence whatsoever is admitted here.
This would indeed be logical if anyone were to have such a realization;
for the realization of one's own suffering and so forth is powerful.
Therefore, if it is argued that no one realizes the non-existence of suffering and so forth, we say: no.
For it is established that the conceit of being subject to suffering and so forth is a false conceit, just like the conceit [of identity] regarding the body and its adjuncts.
Indeed, it is observed as a false conceit when, while the body is being cut or burned, one perceives, "I am being cut; I am being burned.
Likewise, even with respect to those more external than oneself, such as sons and friends, when they are suffering, an imposition is observed such as, "I myself am suffering," and so forth.
Likewise, there would also be the conceit of being a sufferer and so forth;
for suffering and the like are perceived as external to consciousness, just like the body and other such things, and they do not persist during states such as deep sleep.

On the contrary, they declare that consciousness persists even in deep sleep, in passages such as: "Verily, when there he does not see, yet seeing indeed he does not see" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23).
Therefore, this experience of the Self is "I am," consisting of a single consciousness, entirely liberated from all suffering.
For one who experiences the Self in this manner, no further duty remains.
Thus says the Śruti: "What shall we do with offspring, we for whom this Self is this world? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).
Thus, it is shown that for the knower of the Self there is nothing further to be done.
Smṛti also says: "But for that person who rejoices only in the Self, who is satisfied with the Self, and who is content in the Self alone, no duty remains" (Gītā 3.17).
However, for one in whom this experience does not arise immediately, repetition is accepted for the sake of that very experience.
Even in that case, one should not cause such a person to engage in repetition by diverting them from the meaning of the sentence "That thou art";
for they do not marry off a bride in order to kill the groom.

Furthermore, for one who has been appointed to this [task], the thought arises: "I am authorized; I am the agent; this was done poorly by me due to a lack of intelligence. From that cognition of Brahman, a contrary cognition arises.

However, for one who is himself dull-witted and would wish to abandon that meaning of the sentence due to a lack of intelligence, the stabilization of that very meaning of the sentence through repetition and so forth is accepted as a logical method of speech.
Therefore, even regarding the cognition whose object is the Supreme Brahman, the establishment of repetition is proven in the instructions on its means. // 2 //
Because one performs meditation by identifying the Sun alone with the *udgītha*, Kauṣītaki said to his son, "You are my only son";
therefore, you must not act in that way, but rather "revolve around many rays and the Sun"—that is, revolve around them separately. The elision of the *t* (in *paryāvartayatāt*) is a Vedic archaism.

Here, by the word "paryāvṛtti" (repetition), the repetition of the meditation on the *udgītha* is stated as an established fact; then, by the mark (*liṅga*) of the commonality of being meditations or the commonality of culminating in a fruit, he states that repetition is established for hearing, reflection, and meditation everywhere—saying, "and because of the mark.

Thus, repetition has been stated regarding the means for the direct realization of both the qualified (*saguṇa*) and the unqualified (*nirguṇa* [Brahman]). In this regard, having accepted the repetition of the meditation on the qualified and so forth, he raises an objection concerning the repetition of hearing and so forth regarding the unqualified, starting with the words "here it is said":
is [the scripture] capable of producing the direct realization of the unqualified, or not?
Having stated that repetition is useless because direct realization is accomplished from a sentence heard only once in the first case, he raises the second objection with the words "once" (*sakṛt*).
He says "no" (*na*) to the point that even for one who is incapable, the result would not be achieved despite repetition.
The phrase "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*) means that even if there is capability through the addition of reasoning for one who is inherently incapable.

He raises an objection, saying "But it might be so," [suggesting] that even though indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) has arisen through both verbal testimony and reasoning, repetition (*āvṛtti*) is required for the sake of direct realization (*aparokṣajñāna*).

He refutes this, saying "Not even by repetition," because those two [means], by their very nature, have the capacity to produce only indirect knowledge; therefore, even with repetition, direct intuition would not occur.

He concludes, saying "Therefore," [asserting] that whether those two possess the power to produce direct intuition or the power to produce indirect knowledge, in either case, they do not depend upon repetition.
He says "nor" (*na ca*) because there is no fixed rule regarding repetition due to the diversity of knowers (*pramātṛ*).
He says "moreover" (*api ca*) because it is likewise so due to the partlessness (*anaṃśatva*) of the object of knowledge (*prameya*).

For there would be two kinds of qualified persons (*adhikārī*): one whose obstacles such as all forms of doubt (*asaṃbhāvanā*) have been dispelled through practice in previous births, and another who still possesses such obstacles.

Regarding this, he provides the resolution: "To this it is said. He states that the first [repetition] is accepted as being purposeless, whereas for the second, there is a dependence on it for the sake of removing obstacles;
thus he says, "For instance," providing the evidence (*liṅga*) for the fact that repetition serves to remove obstacles.

Just as the auditory organ, though capable of directly perceiving the distinctions between musical notes such as *ṣaḍja* and others, requires repeated practice, so too the sentence—though capable of bringing about the direct realization of Brahman as the Self—requires that [practice]. Relying on this experience, he says: "For there is nothing impossible in what is observed. Since the referent indicated by the words *tat* and *tvam* is difficult to understand, there is the possibility of obstacles such as doubt caused by ignorance; therefore, repetition must be accepted for the destruction of those obstacles. With these considerations in mind, preceded by a distinction between the expressed meaning and the indicated meaning, he says "Moreover" (*api ca*), and so forth.
Regarding the statement that repetition is useless because the object of knowledge is partless,
he says "even though" (yadyapi).
The meaning is that repetition in the form of "I am not the body, I am not the senses" is appropriate for the purpose of dispelling superimposed parts.
If the meaning of the sentence has already been known, how can there be a rule for practice?

For it is argued that since a cognition produced by a means of valid knowledge cannot be subject to practice, and since one who already possesses such knowledge cannot be bound by rules such as hearing (śravaṇa) and so forth, [the author] says "tat tu" (but that).
The meaning is that the restriction of the activities of hearing and so forth is indeed performed prior to the arising of that knowledge.
He restates what was said regarding the further doubt with the words "of those who...
He expresses the further doubt with the words "it is true...
The meaning is that, because it contradicts the direct perception of being subject to suffering, the cognition of oneness does not arise from the statement.
He states "no," etc., because there is no contradiction since perception is erroneous.
The meaning is: suffering and so forth are not attributes of the self (ātman) because they are visible, like the body and so on;
nor are they the very nature of the self, because they do not persist even when the self exists, like consciousness (caitanya) by way of their exclusion [from the self].

He says "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) to show that the experience of the meaning of the sentence is not contradicted, because cognitions such as suffering are erroneous with respect to the Self, which is consciousness and free from suffering.
To the question, "Even when such experience has arisen, why should one not continue to perform practices such as repetition (*āvṛtti*)?", he says "And not thus" (*na caivam*).

*Rati* is desire; satisfaction through the desire for the Self (*ātmakāmatā*) is the cessation of thirst for sense objects; the distinction is that contentment (*saṃtoṣaḥ*) consists in the experience of the bliss of the Self.

[Objection: Surely, in the case of repetition, activity must be said to proceed from an injunction; and thus, due to the cognition of being enjoined, there would be no realization of the self as a non-agent. To this, he says: "In that case also.

The meaning is that even if repetition is accepted, neither the teacher nor anyone else would cause [the student] to engage in it through an injunction by displacing him from the experience "I am a non-agent," because of the aforementioned defect.
If so, how then does activity occur? To this, he says: "But he who..."
The meaning is: "due to lack of eloquence, lack of conviction, and so forth.

The meaning is that, in accordance with the student's intellect, one should employ repetition and other methods through words such as "it should be recited" for the sake of establishing the primary goal. //2//
Section on the Meditation on the Self (Ātmatva-upāsanā-adhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 3. 2. [The section concerning the meditation on the nature of the Self. Sūtra 3.
However, people accept [the existence of] a self and cause others to grasp it.
One considers whether that Supreme Self, characterized as described in the scriptures, is to be grasped as "I" or as "other than me.
But how can there be doubt when the word "self," which refers to the inner self (*pratyagātman*), is being heard?

It is said: this word "Self" (ātman) can be accepted in its primary sense if the non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) is possible; otherwise, however, it must be accepted as secondary (gauṇa). What, then, is the initial position? It should not be grasped as "I am [the Self]," for one whose qualities are the opposite cannot be grasped as having qualities such as freedom from sin (apahatapāpmatva), nor can one who has qualities such as freedom from sin be grasped as having opposite qualities.
Furthermore, the Supreme Lord possesses qualities such as being free from evil, whereas the embodied soul possesses qualities contrary to those.
If the transmigrating soul were identical with the Lord, it would follow that the Lord does not exist;
consequently, the scripture would be rendered purposeless.
Even if transmigrating beings were identical with the Lord, the scriptures would be rendered useless due to the absence of any [eligible] candidate for instruction,
and there would also be a contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge.

If it is argued that even if they are distinct, one must cultivate the vision of identity based on scripture— just as one views Viṣṇu and others in images and the like— we grant that this may indeed be so.
But it must not be concluded by us that the Lord is not the primary Self of the transmigrating soul.
This being the position, we reply: the Supreme Lord alone is to be understood as the Self.
For, within the context of the Supreme Lord, the Jābālas approach Him precisely as the Self, saying: "I am indeed You, O Venerable Lord; You indeed are I, O Venerable Lord."
Thus, other acknowledgments of selfhood, such as "I am Brahman" and so forth, are also to be understood in this way.
Furthermore, the Vedānta texts cause one to grasp the Lord precisely as the Self, as in: "This is your Self, which is within all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.1).
"This is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.3);
"That is the Truth, that is the Self, That art thou" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7)— such passages as these [are the source].

As for the claim that this is a meditation on a symbol (*pratīka-darśana*) according to the principle of the Viṣṇu-image, that is incorrect, because it would entail a figurative sense (*gauṇatva*) and because of the disparity between the statements. For where a meditation on a symbol is intended, the statement occurs only once, as in: "The mind is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.18.1).
In passages such as "The sun is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.19.1), [the relationship is that of a symbol].
Here, however, he says, "I am you and you are I";
therefore, because of this difference from the scriptural texts on symbols, there is the realization of non-difference.
And because of the deprecation of the view of difference;

for it is said: "Now, he who worships another deity, thinking 'He is one and I am another,' does not know" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10); and "He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.7).
Thus, abundant scriptural passages such as these refute the perception of difference.
As for what was said— that two things with contradictory qualities cannot arise from one another’s self—
this is not a fault.
Because falsity is logically established through the presence of contradictory qualities.
Furthermore, as for what was said regarding the undesirable consequence of the non-existence of God—
that is incorrect.

This is because of the authority of the scriptures and because [the opponent] does not accept [our position]. For we do not admit that the transmigrating self is established as being identical with God; rather, what is intended to be established is that the transmigrating self, through the removal of its state of transmigration, has God as its true nature.
This being the case, it is established that the non-dual God possesses qualities such as freedom from sin, while the contrary qualities belonging to the other [the transmigrator] are false.
As for what was also said— that there is an absence of a qualified candidate for liberation and that there is contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge—
that too is incorrect,
because transmigratory existence is admitted prior to awakening.
Furthermore, because linguistic usage such as perception and so forth has that [duality] as its object;

for by such passages as, "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14), [the text] demonstrates the absence of perception and so forth upon awakening.

If it is argued that in the absence of perception and the other means of knowledge, there would follow the non-existence of scripture as well, we say no; for this is accepted [by us], as it is said: "In this state, the father becomes no longer a father" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.22).
Having begun thus, because of the statement "The Vedas are non-Vedas" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.22), we indeed accept the non-existence of even the Śruti upon awakening.
If it is asked, "Whose is this lack of awakening?"—
To that which you ask, we say "that is yours.
Now, have I not been declared by the Śruti to be the Lord himself? If you are thus awakened, there is no lack of awakening for anyone.

Furthermore, the objection raised by some—that because ignorance (avidyā) belongs to the Self, the existence of non-duality (advaita) is untenable due to the Self having a second entity—is also refuted by this very [explanation].
Therefore, one should fix the mind on the Lord as being simply the Self. // 3 //
However, people accept [the self] as "I" and grasp it as such.

Since the repetition of meditation and so forth was mentioned previously, depending on that, he states the doubt—arising from the two views of identity and difference—regarding what should be meditated upon during the time of repeating meditation for the sake of the knowledge of reality: "Is it 'I am Brahman,' or 'The Lord is my master'? This is expressed by the word "yaḥ" (who/that).

In the passage beginning with "He is known from the word alone," [the author] raises a doubt by questioning how there can be a determination of identity through such scriptural texts on non-difference as "This Self is Brahman.

He states, "It is said," indicating that the doubt arises by relying on the superiority of perception and other means of knowledge regarding difference, which are supported by scriptural texts on difference.
Regarding both cases—the figurative and the primary senses of the non-difference scriptures—there is a specific result.

Although this resolution of contradictions with perception and other means of knowledge belongs properly to the second chapter, it is nonetheless relevant here because the certainty that the scriptural teaching of unity is not contradicted is an internal factor for meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
He states, "Not I," [implying] that the perception of unity between two contradictory things is unestablished.

Furthermore, having raised the alternatives—whether unity consists in the Lord being merely the individual soul (*jīva*), or the individual soul being merely the Lord—he refutes them in succession, beginning with the words "And of the Lord... and so forth.
He raises an objection, saying "even though there is difference," [suggesting] that one should practice meditation on unity for the sake of the authority of the scriptural texts concerning oneness.
He replies, saying "certainly," [meaning]: meditation on oneness is indeed what we ourselves accept;
however, actual oneness does not exist.

Since it is impossible for the non-difference scriptures to be figurative when they have as their purport the unprecedented (apūrva) result [of liberation], and since the difference scriptures merely restate an imagined difference—given that even perception and other means of knowledge have that [imagined difference] as their object, and that contradictory attributes are false like those of a reflection and its original—the primary oneness is established; thus he concludes with the words beginning "In this way" (*evam*).
It is not the Lord’s state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*) that is to be taught, such that the Lord would cease to exist, but rather the living soul’s state of being the Lord (*īśvaratva*).

Nor is there an absence of qualified candidates [for liberation] in this way, because we accept a distinction among qualified candidates prior to the awakening to oneness; thus he says, "As for what was stated," and so forth.
One who has faith in the truth of the Veda raises an objection: "Because of the absence of perception and other means of knowledge."

Since sequential order and accentuation do not exist in the phonemes themselves, one must admit that they are superimposed upon the sounds as perceived; and thus, the falsity of the Veda—which consists of phonemes qualified by superimposed sequence and accent—is unavoidable.
As for the disputants' insistence on its truth, that is merely a manifestation of ignorance (avidyā). Therefore, he says "No," [meaning] the absence of the Veda's truth is not a defect.
He challenges this ignorance with the question: "Of what? (kasya).

He says, "You who... because the question and so forth are rooted in ignorance; thus, since her realization is established in you alone, it is illogical for there to be an implication (*ākṣepa*) of you [as being ignorant].
He raises an objection, "But surely...": how can there be ignorance in me, who am non-different from the Omniscient One?

Prior to the knowledge of non-difference, you yourself—being pure consciousness (cinmātra)—are the locus of ignorance, because it is impossible to deny ignorance that is established by experience. However, upon the arising of knowledge, since that indeterminable (anirvācya) ignorance is sublated, there is no requirement for a locus; thus he says, "If this is so. Furthermore, by its indeterminability, other defects are also refuted; thus he says, "As for that which... //3//

"Not in a symbol, for he is not that.
[Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.18.1: "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman with respect to the self; then, with respect to the divine, 'Space is Brahman.
Likewise, 'The sun is Brahman' is an instruction. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.19.1)
Regarding such meditations on symbols as "He who meditates on Name as Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.5), a doubt arises: should the grasping of the Self be performed in these cases as well, or not?
What, then, is the prima facie position?
Even in those cases, it is more reasonable to maintain the apprehension of a self.
Why?

Because Brahman is well-known in the scriptures as the Self, and because the symbols (pratīkas) are modifications of Brahman; therefore, since they possess the nature of Brahman, it is logical that they possess the nature of the Self as well.
This being the case, we reply: one should not fix the notion of the Self upon the symbols (pratīka).
For that worshiper would not conceive of the symbols as separate entities in their own right as being the Self.
As for the argument that because the symbols are modifications (vikāra) of Brahman they possess the nature of Brahman, and therefore the nature of the Self—that is not so.
That is incorrect,
because it would entail the absence of the representative symbol (pratīka).
For, by the sublation of the nature of the modification, the name and so forth, which have arisen, come to be based solely upon Brahman.
Furthermore, if their own nature were sublated, how could name and the rest be considered symbols (*pratīka*), or how could there be the apprehension of them as the Self?
Nor can the view of the Self be inferred from the instructions on the contemplation of Brahman simply because Brahman is the Self;
for [in those cases] agency and other such attributes have not been negated.
For the teaching that Brahman is the Self is intended to eliminate attributes such as agency and the like, which belong to the transmigratory state (saṃsāra) and are subject to dissolution;
whereas the injunction for meditation is given without eliminating those [attributes].
Consequently, because the meditator is equated with the symbols (pratīka), the apprehension of them as the Self is not tenable.

For there is no mutual identity between a necklace and a svastika; rather, as we have stated, if they were one through the nature of gold—or through the nature of Brahman—it would follow that the symbols (pratīkas) would cease to exist. Therefore, the vision of the Self is not to be applied to the symbols. // 4 //
"Not in the symbol, for he [is not there]"—there is doubt because meditation can occur in both ways.

Just as "seizing by the I" (ahaṅgraha) was prescribed regarding Brahman because of the existence of non-difference, so too regarding symbols: since they are modifications of Brahman, they are non-different from Brahman, and thus, because the existence of non-difference from the individual soul (jīva) is present, "seizing by the I" should be performed.
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is established by means of an illustration;
here, there is no distinction between meditations on symbols (*pratīkopāsti*) and meditations involving the grasping of the self (*ahaṅgrahopāsti*).
However, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the result is the establishment of a distinction.
The connection of these three sections (*adhikaraṇa*) with the current chapter (*pāda*) is incidental;
the distinction is that they have arisen in connection with the meditation on the identity of Brahman.

Is the identification with the "I" (*ahaṅgraha*) in the case of symbols (*pratīka*) due to the force of experiencing them as the Self, or because there exists an actual non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman?
He says "not today" and explains: "for he does not," meaning that he does not experience it.
He refutes the second [position] as well by way of its non-establishment, saying: "as for what again..."

The meaning is that since identity of nature between a modification (*vikāra*) and Brahman is impossible, their identity must be stated as being through sublation (*bādha*); however, if the symbol (*pratīka*) were subject to sublation, the injunction for meditation upon it would not be possible.
Furthermore, the operation of the injunction for meditation must be stated to occur without the sublation of agency and so forth, because such an injunction is untenable if there is sublation.

Thus, it is not logical to conceive of the meditation on symbols through the superimposition of the "I" (*ahaṅgraha-upāsti*), by making the knowledge of identity with Brahman—which is rooted in sublation—the mediating instrument.
He states that [the view is] contradicted by sublation: "And not of Brahman.

Therefore, since there is a difference in essential nature between the individual soul (jīva) and the symbol (pratīka), and because no injunction for the practice of identification (ahaṅgraha) is heard regarding them, he concludes the result: "And therefore," etc.

Just as there is no mutual identity between a necklace (rucaka) and a svastika despite their unity in the nature of gold, so too there is an equal distinction between the individual soul and the symbol despite their unity in the nature of Brahman.

And if, because of the certainty that those two do not exist apart from the substratum (dharmin), there were an identity of substance, then it would mean that meditation (upāsanā) has been declared to be abolished; such is the meaning. //4//

The Section Concerning the Vision of Brahman (Brahmadṛṣṭyadhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 5.
The view of Brahman [is to be superimposed] because of superiority.
Regarding those very examples, another doubt arises: should the views of the sun and so forth be superimposed upon Brahman, or should the view of Brahman be superimposed upon the sun and so forth?
Whence does this doubt arise? From the fact that the cause for determining the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is not yet ascertained.
For here, the word *brahman* is observed to be in grammatical apposition with words such as *āditya*,
as seen in expressions like "The sun is Brahman, the breath is Brahman, lightning is Brahman," due to the use of identical case endings.
And yet, a direct apposition in this context is not possible.
Because the words "Brahman," "Āditya," and so forth, denote different objects;
for there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) such as "cow" and "horse.

[Objection: But surely, because of the relationship of material cause and effect (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) between Brahman and the Ādityas, there would be coreferentiality, just as in the case of clay and a bowl.
It is said: "No.
For in this way, there would be a dissolution of the modification due to its grammatical coreferentiality with the material cause;
and we have already stated that this leads to the undesirable consequence of the absence of the *pratīka*.
Furthermore, this would then be a statement concerning the Supreme Self, and consequently, the qualification for meditative worship (*upāsana*) would be sublated;
moreover, the assumption of a limited modification as the material cause would be rendered purposeless.

Therefore, since there is the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the vision of one thing upon another—as in the case of "The Brāhmaṇa is Agni Vaiśvānara"—the doubt arises as to which vision should be superimposed upon what.
In this regard, the initial position reached is that there is no restriction, because there is no scriptural injunction to impose one.
Alternatively, the position reached is that the meditations on the sun and so forth are indeed to be applied to Brahman;
for it is the established rule of scripture that Brahman is thus worshipped through the meditations on the sun and so forth, and that the worship of Brahman is productive of fruit.
Therefore, the view of Brahman does not apply to the sun and so forth.
This being the position reached, we reply: the view of Brahman alone should indeed be applied to the sun and so forth.
Why?
Because of elevation:
in this way, the sun and other celestial bodies are perceived as elevated due to the superimposition upon them of the perception of elevation.
And thus, the worldly principle is followed:
for it is a worldly principle that a superior vision should be superimposed upon an inferior object,
just as the vision of a king is [superimposed] upon a charioteer.
And that [view] must be followed,
because in its absence there would be the consequence of transgression;
for a king who is embraced by the vision of a charioteer, even when being led to degradation, cannot lead to his own welfare.

[Objection: "Surely, because the scripture is authoritative, the possibility of sin (pratyavāya) in this matter should not be suspected; nor is it proper to restrict a scriptural perspective by means of worldly logic.
[Reply: To this it is said: This would be so once the meaning of the scripture has been definitively determined.
However, when that meaning is doubtful, there is no contradiction in resorting even to worldly logic for the sake of reaching a decision.
And thus, it follows that one who, while superimposing the vision of the superior upon the meaning of the scripture being determined, were to superimpose the vision of the inferior, would incur sin.

Furthermore, because they appear first and there is no contradiction, the words "Āditya" and so forth must be understood in their primary sense. Since the word "Brahman," which arrives later, cannot be in grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with them through its primary function once the intellect has been occupied by those [words] functioning in their own primary senses, it must be for the purpose of enjoining the meditation on Brahman [upon them].
Thus it remains;
because of the presence of the particle *iti*, this alone is the proper meaning of the word *brahman*.

For instance, in all such passages as "the instruction is *brahman*," "one should meditate on [it] as *brahman*," and "one worships [it] as *brahman*," the word *brahman* is uttered followed by *iti*, whereas the words for Āditya and others are uttered in their pure form.

And thus, just as in the case where one perceives mother-of-pearl as "silver," the word *śuktikā* (mother-of-pearl) denotes the mother-of-pearl itself, whereas the word "silver" is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇārtha*) to denote the perception of silver—
for one merely perceives "silver" and there is no silver there—
so too here it is understood that one should perceive the sun and so forth as Brahman.

Moreover, the remainder of the passage itself shows, by means of the accusative case-ending, that it is Āditya and the others who are pervaded by the act of meditation: "He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon Āditya as Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.19.4);
"He who meditates upon speech as Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.2.2);
and "He who meditates upon volition as Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.4.3).
As for the claim that Brahman alone is to be meditated upon here in order to obtain the fruit,
that is incorrect; for,
according to the reasoning already stated, it is understood that the sun and the other deities themselves are the objects of meditation.

As for the fruit, however—just as in the case of meditations on Āditya and so forth, even in the meditation on the Sun and others, Brahman alone will bestow it because He is the presiding lord of all.

And this has been explained in the sūtra: "The fruit [comes] from Him, because that is logical" (Brahma-sūtra 3.2.38). Furthermore, Brahman’s status as the object of meditation here consists in the superimposition of the vision of Him upon the symbols (pratīkas), just as Viṣṇu and others are superimposed upon images and the like. // 5 //
The view of Brahman [is mentioned] because of its superiority.
The connection [between the two views] consists in their having the same object.
He states the seed of doubt by means of the question "Why? and so forth.

The grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) that is heard in the scripture is not primary, because a non-difference between Brahman and its modification is impossible, just as it is between a cow and a horse.
Nor is it based on the relationship of material cause and effect (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*).
Because the sentence would then result in having Brahman as its primary purport through the modification and sublation [of the literal meaning],
and this is not an acceptable consequence,
as it would contradict the injunctive scripture stating, "One should meditate on Name as Brahman."
Furthermore, because it would follow that the mention of specific names would be purposeless;
for if [the passage] were intended to refer to Brahman, one would have to say "everything is Brahman.

Therefore, by process of elimination, superimposition (adhyāsa) alone is the cause of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), and since there is no restrictive factor regarding superimposition, the meaning is that doubt arises.

Regarding the principle that "even the inferior among the superior and the inferior should be meditated upon because it yields fruit," [the author] says "Or rather" (*athavā*) out of dissatisfaction with that view. Here, the result is the accomplishment of the meditation on Brahman through the perception of it as a modification (*vikāra*).

However, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), since the status of Brahman as an object of meditation through the perception of it as a modification would lead to its degradation and thus the attainment of fruit would not be established, the result is that the modifications themselves are to be meditated upon by perceiving them as the superior Brahman.
Furthermore, when a meaning that is not contradicted by worldly logic is possible, a contradictory meaning should not be accepted, as it would entail the risk of sin (pratyavāya).
Moreover, since the words "Āditya" and so forth are heard first, it is logical to accept them in their primary sense because no contradiction has yet arisen;
whereas in the case of the word "Brahman," one must accept the figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) of a meditative vision (dṛṣṭi).
And thus, he states that the meaning of the sentence is precisely that the sun and so forth are to be meditated upon through the vision of Brahman, by saying "and because of being first.
He provides another reason for the word *brahman* alone having the sense of "vision" by saying "because of its being followed by the particle *iti*.
The meaning is that it is well known in common usage that a word preceded by the particle *iti* indicates the action with which it is syntactically connected.
He states that by virtue of the mention of "the second" (*dvitīyāśruteḥ*), only Āditya and the others are the objects of worship—this is expressed in the words, "The remainder of the passage also...
He reiterates the principle already stated—that only the superior [deity] is to be worshipped—in the words, "As for what was said...

He then states that this established principle is set aside by the two mentions of "the second," by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), and by worldly logic (*nyāya*)—this is expressed in the words, "That..."
If Brahman is not the object of worship, how can it be the bestower of the fruit?
To this he says: "But the fruit...

Furthermore, even though that Brahman—by whose vision the modification attains excellence—is a qualifier [of the object], its status as the object of worship does not cease; thus he says: "And such... //5//
Topic: [The meditation] on the Āditya and others. Sūtra 6. *ādityādimatyadhikaraṇam* (The section concerning the meditation on the Āditya and others). Sūtra 6.
And the meditations on the limbs [of the sacrifice] as the sun and so forth are appropriate, because it is logical; for example:
"One should meditate upon him who shines yonder as the Udgītha" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.3.1), and "One should meditate on the fivefold Sāman in the worlds" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.2.1).

Regarding such meditations connected with the constituent parts [of the sacrifice], as in "One should meditate on the sevenfold Sāman in speech" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.8.1) and "This earth is indeed the Ṛc, fire is the Sāman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.1), a doubt arises: are the views of the Udgītha and so forth enjoined upon the sun and so forth, or are the views of the sun and so forth enjoined upon the Udgītha and so forth?

In this regard, it follows that there is no restriction, because there is no cause for restriction. For here, unlike in the case of Brahman, no specific excellence of any [other deity] is determined; indeed, because Brahman is the cause of the entire world and possesses qualities such as being free from sin, it can be determined as superior to Āditya and the others.
But there is no reason for determining any specific distinction of excellence among the sun, the *udgītha*, and so forth, since they are equally modifications;
or rather, why should the cognitions of the *udgītha* and so forth be superimposed upon the sun and so forth as a rule?
For what reason?

Because the *udgītha* and other such elements are of the nature of ritual action (*karma*), and because it is well known that ritual action results in the attainment of fruits, the Sun and other deities—when worshipped through the meditative identifications (*matibhiḥ*) with the *udgītha* and so forth—will become causes of the fruit while being of the nature of ritual action.
And thus [it is said]: "This [earth] itself is the *ṛc*, fire is the *sāman*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.1).

Thus, in this context, by the statement "This very Sāman is superimposed upon this Ṛc" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.1), the word *ṛc* refers to the earth and the word *sāman* refers to fire; and this is appropriate if one intends to effect the meditation (*dṛṣṭi*) of the Ṛc and Sāman upon the earth and fire, but not if one intends to effect the meditation of the earth and fire upon the Ṛc and Sāman.
For the word "king" is applied figuratively to the steward because he performs the functions of a king, but the word "steward" is not applied to the king.

Furthermore, from the mention of the locative case in the passage, "One should meditate on the fivefold Sāman in the worlds" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.2.1), it is understood that the Sāman is to be superimposed upon the worlds.

And the passage, "This Gāyatra is woven upon the vital breaths" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.11.1), shows this very same thing. Furthermore, in cases such as "The sun is Brahman— this is the instruction" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.19.1), where the sun and so forth are mentioned first, Brahman is superimposed as that which is mentioned last.

Furthermore, in Vedic texts such as "The earth is the *hiṅkāra*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.2.1), those mentioned first, such as the earth, are identified with those mentioned last, such as the *hiṅkāra*. Therefore,
this is a superimposition of a subordinate part (*aṅga*) upon non-subordinate parts (*anaṅga*), such as the sun and so forth.

This being the case, we reply: the meditations on the Sun and so forth are indeed to be applied to the subordinate parts of the sacrifice, such as the *udgītha* and others. Why? Because it is logical (*upapatti*).

For in this way, through proximity to the unseen potency (*apūrva*), the success of the ritual action is logically established when the *udgītha* and other elements are consecrated by the meditations on the Sun and so forth.

And the passage, "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the secret doctrine (upaniṣad), that alone becomes more powerful" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.10), shows that knowledge is a cause for the success of ritual action.
Let it be so regarding those results which consist in the success of ritual action; however—

But how is it in the case of those meditations on the Sāman that have independent fruits, such as "He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in the worlds" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.2.3)?

Even in those cases, since there is an authorized person qualified for the rite, it is proper to assume a fruit through its proximity to the primary apūrva (transcendental result), just like the rule regarding the *godohana* vessel and so forth.

Furthermore, because the sun and other deities are of the nature of the fruit, their superiority over the *udgītha* and other elements—which are of the nature of ritual action—is logically established; for in the scriptures, the fruit of ritual action is taught to consist in the attainment of the sun and other such states.

Moreover, having introduced the *udgītha* itself as the object of meditation in the passages, "One should meditate upon this syllable 'Om' as the *udgītha*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.1) and "This indeed is the further explanation of that very syllable" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.10), [the text] prescribes the meditations on the Sun and so forth.
As for what was said— that the Sun and others, when meditated upon through the notions of the *udgītha* and so forth, will become subordinate to ritual action and produce a fruit—
that is incorrect; for it is logical that the meditation itself, being an action, possesses its own fruit.
Furthermore, because the Udgītha and other elements, even when perceived as the Sun and so forth, do not lose their nature as constituent parts of ritual action;
whereas the application of the words "Ṛc" and "Sāman" to the earth and fire in the passage, "This Sāman is supported upon this Ṛc" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.1), is merely figurative.
And secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) operates through a connection with its own primary meaning, whether that connection be proximate or remote.

In this regard, although the application of the terms *ṛk* and *sāman* to the earth and fire occurs precisely because of their proximity, it is nevertheless determined that this usage arises from a connection with the words *ṛk* and *sāman*.
For even the word *kṣattṛ*, when applied to a king for some particular reason, cannot be prevented [from being used in that sense].
And the statement, "This [earth] is indeed the Ṛg-verse" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.1), determines that the earth is the Ṛg-verse itself according to the arrangement of the syllables;
for if the earth were being determined as the Ṛg-verse, the arrangement of the syllables would have been "This is indeed the earth."

And by the statement, "He who, knowing thus, sings the Sāman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.7.7), it concludes that the knowledge rests solely upon the subordinate members [of the sacrifice], not upon the earth and so forth.
Likewise: "One should meditate on the fivefold Sāman in the worlds" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.2.1).

Thus, although the worlds are indicated by the locative case, they should nevertheless be superimposed upon the *sāman* itself; for it is understood from the accusative indication that the *sāman* is the object of meditation.
For when the worlds are superimposed upon the *sāman*, the *sāman* comes to be meditated upon as having the worlds as its self.
Otherwise, however, the worlds would be meditated upon as having the *sāman* as their self.
By this, passages such as "This Gāyatra is woven upon the vital breaths" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.11.1) are explained;
for even there, the second designation is similar: "Now, indeed, one should meditate upon yonder sun as the sevenfold Sāman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.9.1).
Thus, even there [in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad], it is said: "Indeed, the meditation on the entire Sāman is good" (Chā.
2.8.1), as well as "of the fivefold [Sāman]" (Chā.
2.7.2) and "now, of the sevenfold [Sāman]" (Chā. 2.8.1).
And since the meditation on the *sāman* itself is introduced at the outset, the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of Āditya and so forth occurs upon that very *sāman*.

Precisely because the *sāman* is understood to be the object of meditation, even though there is a reversal in the specific designation— such as "The earth is the *hiṅkāra*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.2.1)— the perception of the earth and so forth must be applied to the *hiṅkāra* and the other parts of the chant.

Therefore, it is established that the conceptions of the Āditya and so forth, which do not have those [deities] as their primary referents, should be superimposed upon the constituent parts of the sacrifice, such as the Udgītha and others. // 6 //
The Sāman has five parts— namely the *hiṅkāra*, *prastāva*, *udgītha*, *pratīhāra*, and *nidhana*— in the worlds known as Earth, Fire, Atmosphere, Sun, and Heaven, beginning with Āditya.
The distinction is that [the Sāman] consists of seven parts by means of two additional divisions: namely, "taireva" as the *ādi* (beginning) and "upadrava.
Therefore, because this specific detail is not known, there is doubt.

By way of a counter-example—arguing that, as in the previous case, there is no fixed rule due to the lack of determination regarding superiority—the opponent states the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "tatra."

He states the primary prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) by means of an illustration: "Or rather," [meaning] that because the Udgītha and other ritual forms are superior due to their proximity to the fruit—unlike Siddhārtha Āditya and others who are already established entities—there is a rule regarding their being qualifiers, just as in the case of Brahman.
It should be understood that the very establishment of each respective position constitutes the result of the preceding and following arguments.

Furthermore, regarding the point that the perception of the limbs (aṅga) occurs only in what are not actually limbs, he provides the indicative mark (liṅga) for the use of words denoting "limbs" in reference to them: "And thus, this very [text]," etc.
This means that this Sāman called "Agni" is "superimposed" (adhyūḍham)—that is, situated above—upon this Ṛc which has the form of the earth.
Just as the Sāman is perceived upon the Ṛc, Agni is perceived upon the earth;
therefore, because of this similarity, the meditation is enjoined that the earth itself is the Ṛc and Agni is the Sāman.

In this regard, if there were a perception of the earth and fire as being the *ṛk* and *sāman*—which are themselves auxiliary parts of the ritual (*karmāṅga*)—then the application of the terms *ṛk* and *sāman* to the earth and fire would not be possible; to illustrate this point, he says: "as [the term] 'charioteer' [is applied to a kṣatriya].
Therefore, the meaning is that because the usage [of those terms] would otherwise be inexplicable, there is a perception of the earth and fire as the *ṛk* and *sāman*.
And he says "also" (api ca) to show that it is exactly so by means of the locative of object (*viṣayasaptamī*).
[The word] *sāma* refers to the chant known as the *gāyatra*.
Furthermore, he says "first" (*prathama*) to show that it is also so by the principle of the established conclusion (*siddhāntanyāya*) of the preceding section.
He establishes the conclusion that the limbs [of the sacrifice] are to be meditated upon as being bodiless, with the words "Thus.

For it is heard in scripture that the fruit of these meditations is the successful completion of the ritual action (*karmasamṛddhi*); and that is possible when the limbs are being refined by those meditations.
The meaning is that [the limbs] generate an *apūrva* (unseen potency) from the primary ritual action (*prakṛta-karma*) which is conducive to their own perfection.

Now, one might object: where the fruit of meditations (*upāsti*) is heard as being dependent on the limbs of the primary ritual action through the medium of the *apūrva*, let it be granted that those limbs are the objects of meditation (*upāsya*) for the sake of the attainment of that fruit; however, in those meditations whose fruits are independent of that—such as the worlds (*loka*) and so forth—how can there be a distinction regarding the object of meditation?
Thus he raises an objection with the words "Let it be so.

Just as the *godohana* vessel, although its fruit is independent [of the main rite], is accepted as having a fruit only by way of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the main action, so too in the case of meditations (*upāsanā*) whose fruits are the worlds and so forth, the postulation of a fruit occurs only by way of the auxiliary character of the unseen potency (*apūrva*) of the ritual act; for only one who is qualified for the ritual act has the qualification for meditations based on those auxiliaries.
Therefore, he provides the resolution that the limbs themselves are indeed the objects of meditation with the words "even in those" (*teṣv api*).
He refutes the previously stated argument that there is no fixed rule because no superiority can be determined by saying "the nature of the fruit" (*phalātma*).
Furthermore, he states that the limb is the object of meditation on the strength of the opening statement (*upakrama*) with the words "moreover" (*api ca*).
The meaning is that there should be an addition [to the list] of qualities such as being the "most flavorful" (*rasatama*).
He refutes the second prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words beginning "as for what was said," etc.;
the meaning is "having attained the state of being action (*karmabhūya*), that is, having attained the nature of action."

[The opponent argues: "If actions are viewed as having the nature of the perfected Sun and so forth, their status as actions would be lost. To this, [the author] says: "in the form of the Sun and so forth. Just as the perception of fire in a boy is figurative, the cognitions of the Sun and so forth regarding the *udgītha* and other parts are figurative; therefore, they do not sublate the status of being an action. The intention is that the cognition of the non-limbs [of the sacrifice] in the limbs is not contradictory. He dispels the previously stated impossibility of practical application with the words: "This very [point]."
He states the connection regarding the seed of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with the words "and indication.
In the case of "a hamlet on the Ganges," indication of the bank is observed through a direct relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*);
in the case of "the boy is fire," indication is observed through an indirect relation (*paramparā-sambandha*) consisting in the possession of qualities such as purity residing in the fire.

And thus, in this case, even in the view that the *Ṛk* and *Sāman* are to be seen as the earth and fire, it is logical that the words *Ṛk* and *Sāman* indicate the earth and fire through a secondary relationship (paramparā-sambandha) consisting in being the object of vision with respect to their own primary denotations; this is the meaning. Now, one might object: "It is not proper for a word expressing a symbol (*pratīka*) to have an indicative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) toward the object of meditation, because the word 'charioteer' (*kṣattṛ*) is used to denote a Kṣatriya. To this, he raises the doubt: "In that regard, although... (*tatra yadyapi*).

Nevertheless, because of the connection between the *ṛc* and the *sāman*, it was stated separately regarding the primary pair—earth and fire—that "the *sāman* is mounted upon this *ṛc*. If, in the phrase "this [fire] upon this [earth]," those two were again taken as the primary subjects, there would be a redundancy. Therefore, the meaning is that the terms for the symbols (earth and fire) are used here in proximity to their symbols through the perception of non-difference from the prototypes, in order to strengthen that identity.
If one objects, "In that case, the word *kṣattṛ* (charioteer/minister) would also apply to the king," he says: "The *kṣattri*... [and so forth].

The meaning is that for the application [of a term] based on its established usage (*sthitaprayoga*), some specific cause (*nimitta*) must be stated; it is not the case that the application is to be established merely because a cause exists.

*Kṣattṛ* means a charioteer (*sūta*); when he performs the duties of the charioteer, such as driving the chariot, like a king, then the word *kṣattṛ* applies to the king as well—this is the literal meaning of the words.
Regarding the point that the visualization of earth and so forth should be applied to the *Ṛk* and other Vedas themselves, he states another reason: "This [world]," etc.
He refutes the notion that the worlds are the objects of meditation by means of the locative case in the phrase "likewise in the worlds" (*tathā lokeṣu*). The meaning is:

rather than you having to violate both the accusative and the locative cases in the injunction "one should meditate on the worlds as the Sāman," it is better to meditate on the Sāman as the worlds, which involves violating the locative case alone.

The meaning is that by this—namely, by the parsimony of breaking down the single case-ending—it has been explained that the *Gāyatra* Sāman is to be meditated upon as having the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as its self.
Now, one might ask: "If there is equality of case-endings, how is the decision made? To this he says: "Even where...

Having begun with "The meditation on the Sāman is good," and having described the meditation on the five-limbed Sāman—starting with the syllable *hiṅkāra* as the earth and so forth—and having concluded with "Thus is the meditation on the fivefold [Sāman],"...
The word "atha" (now) introduces the meditation on the sevenfold Sāman; therefore, the meaning is that the Sāman alone is the object of meditation.
As for the argument that the earth and so forth should be meditated upon because they come first, he replies to that with the words: "Precisely from this."

The meaning is that although, with respect to the injunction of "earth-ness" directed toward the *hiṅkāra*, the subject of the injunction ought to be mentioned first, nevertheless, by the force of the stated reasoning, the reversal [of order] is to be accepted. //6//
Section on Sitting (Āsīna-adhikaraṇa), Sūtras 7–10. 6. [The discussion concerning] one who is seated.
"Because of the possibility [of sitting], he is seated.

(BBs 4.1.7) First, regarding those meditations connected with the constituent parts of ritual action (*karma*), there is no consideration of sitting and so forth because they are dependent on the ritual action itself. Nor is there such consideration in the case of perfect knowledge (*samyagdarśana*), because cognition is dependent on the reality of the object. However, regarding the other meditations, one considers whether one may proceed without restriction—standing, sitting, or lying down—or whether there is a restriction that one must proceed only while sitting.
In this regard, since meditation is mental in nature, there is no restriction regarding the posture of the body.
This being the position reached, the author says: "One should meditate while sitting.
Why? Because it is possible.

What is called *upāsana* (meditative worship) is the production of a continuous flow of identical cognitions; and that is not possible for one who is walking or running, because movement and such activities distract the mind.
Even for one who is standing, the mind is occupied with supporting the body and thus is incapable of investigating a subtle object.
Even for one who is lying down, he might suddenly be overcome by sleep.
However, for one who is seated, such a great fault is easily avoided; thus, meditation by him is possible. // 7 //
"Because it is possible for one who is seated":

since we observe the performance of ritual acts in various ways—whether by one who has risen from [the seat] or by one who remains seated—a doubt arises. The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) argues that, just as the mode of performing meditations based on the constituent parts (*aṅga*) of rituals was described as not requiring a restriction regarding the seat, so too there is no such restriction for meditations not based on those constituent parts; thus he says, "In that case."
In this [system], there is no necessity for the practice of postures (āsana);

however, in the Siddhānta, although the mind and the body are distinct, it is established by experience that when the body is restless, the mind remains unsteady. Therefore, since meditations (upāsanas) involve mental operations, there is a requirement for the regulation of posture (āsana-niyama) for the sake of bodily steadiness—this is the difference in result.
Whether standing or rising. //7//
And from meditative absorption as well. BBs_4,1.8.
Moreover, he meditates on that object which consists in producing a continuous flow of similar cognitions.

And the verb "to meditate" (*dhyāyati*) is observed to be used in reference to those whose bodily movements are relaxed, whose gaze is fixed, and whose minds are concentrated on a single object; as in the expressions, "The crane meditates," "He who has lost his kinsman meditates," and "He sits without exertion."
Therefore, meditation is also an action to be performed while seated. // 8 //
Furthermore, meditators should remain seated, because they possess the fitness for the meaning of the word "meditates," like the crane and others; thus he says: "And because of meditation" (8).
And also with reference to immovability. BBs_4,1.9 /

Moreover, in the passage "The earth, as it were, meditates" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.6.1), the expression "meditates" regarding the earth and other elements occurs only with reference to their immobility; and that is an indicative mark for the fact that meditation is an activity performed while seated. // 9 //
Right here, he states a scriptural illustration: "And immovability," thus [verse 9].
And they record this in their tradition. (BBs 4.1.10)
Moreover, the learned also remember that posture is an ancillary to meditation, as in the passage beginning, "Having established a firm seat for oneself in a clean place" (Gītā 6.11).
For this very reason, specific postures such as the lotus posture (padmaka) and others are taught in the Yoga Śāstra. // 10 //
He states that there is a restrictive rule (niyama) because of the recollection of Brahmā, Śārīra, and Āsana, saying: "And they remember... (sūtra 10).
Section 7:
One-Pointedness of Mind. Sūtra 11.
Where there is one-pointedness, there is no distinction [of direction, etc. (BBs 4.1.11).
A doubt arises regarding direction, place, and time: is there some restrictive rule or not?

Since a restriction of direction and so forth is generally observed in Vedic undertakings, for one who thinks that there might be some such rule here as well, he says in response: regarding direction, place, and time, the restriction is solely determined by the purpose (*arthalakṣaṇa*).

In whichever direction, place, or time one’s mind attains single-minded concentration with ease, there alone one should practice meditation. This is because no specific rule is heard regarding the eastward direction, the forenoon, or a site sloping toward the east;
for the desired state of single-mindedness is the same everywhere.
Now, some indeed prescribe a specific rule: "On level ground, pure, free from gravel, fire, and sand, and devoid of noise, water-sources, and the like..."
"Just as [it is said]: 'One should practice in a place agreeable to the mind, not one that pains the eyes, taking refuge in a cave or a windless spot' (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.10).
To this it is replied: True, there is indeed a rule of this kind.
But since this [concentration] exists, the Teacher, acting as a friend, declares that there is a restriction regarding the specific objects for those who have attained it:
"favorable to the mind" (manonukūle)—this scriptural statement shows precisely that it must be where one-pointedness occurs. // 11 //
Where there is one-pointedness, there is no distinction.

Regarding those meditations (*upāsanā*) that do not depend on specific limbs [of the ritual], a doubt arises as to whether there is a restriction concerning the east and other directions, sacred sites (*tīrtha*), and so forth, as well as times such as dusk and so forth, or whether there is none; for both possibilities are conceivable.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that because these meditations have a single object and are enjoined like sacrifices and other rites, there must be a restriction regarding direction and the rest. This constitutes the connection [between the topics].
In this context, there is emphasis on direction and so forth in the preliminary stage (*pūrvapakṣa*), whereas in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) there is no such emphasis.

The distinction is that because one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgrya*) regarding the object of meditation is primary, it is appropriate to include the location and other factors as implied by that primary factor. Thus, it is characterized solely by its purpose.
The meaning is that [the scripture] has as its mark only the fruit of one-pointedness (*aikāgrya*).

The sense is that, just as it is prescribed that "one should perform the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice on ground sloping toward the east" (*prācīnapravaṇe*), no specific direction or other such detail is heard here; therefore, inference is not applicable.
He raises the objection that the non-hearing of a specific detail is unestablished: "But surely there is also a specific detail... and so forth.
Gravel refers to fine pebbles.
The avoidance of bodies of water is for the sake of warding off cold.
A "maśaka" is a mosquito that causes pain to the eyes.

Accepting the scriptural injunction regarding the rules for place and so forth, the author of the Sūtras instructs out of friendship that there should be no regard for those requirements of place and so on—such as facing the east—which are incompatible with one-pointedness of mind.
[For] if one insists on such places and so forth, distraction of the mind would occur, leading to the destruction of meditative absorption; let this not happen. //11//
