For it is observed even there until the point of departure.
It was established in the first section (*adhikaraṇa*) that a repetition must be observed in all meditations (*upāsana*).

Among those, as for the meditations intended for the sake of perfect knowledge (*samyak-darśana*), their measure of repetition is already known, because—like the threshing of grain—they terminate with the accomplishment of their effect.
For once the task of right vision has been accomplished, no further effort can be enjoined;
this is because the scripture has no jurisdiction over one who has realized the identity with Brahman, which is beyond all injunctions.

However, regarding those [practices] whose fruit is worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), there arises this consideration: should one desist after repeating the means for some time, or should one repeat them as long as one lives?
What, then, is the prima facie view?

One should abandon the meditative practice after practicing the mental representation for some time, because the purpose of the term "meditation" (upāsana)—which is characterized by repetition—has been fulfilled.
This being the position, we reply: one should repeat the mental representation until the moment of death.
Because of the power of the final cognition, one attains the unseen fruit (*adṛṣṭaphala*).
For even the karmas, when initiating a fruit to be experienced in another birth, project at the time of death a corresponding consciousness through cultivation (*bhāvanā-vijñāna*), as it is said:
"He becomes possessed of consciousness; he enters [the womb] with consciousness itself," and "With whatever mind he comes to the vital breath (*prāṇa*)."
"Prāṇa, joined with heat (tejas) and together with the self (ātman), leads [the person] to the world as it has been conceived"— from such scriptural passages as these,
and from the illustration of the caterpillar (tṛṇajalūkā),

it follows that these mental impressions (pratyayāḥ) would require nothing other than the persistence of their own nature, apart from the cognition consisting of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā-vijñāna) occurring at the time of death.
Therefore, since those meditative states (*pratyaya*) which consist in the cultivation of the fruit to be attained do not cease until death, there must be repetition [of their practice].

Thus, scripture (*śruti*) shows the persistence of these meditative states even at the time of death: "Whatever his resolve (*kratu*) may be, with that he departs from this world. Smṛti also says: "Whichever state of being one remembers while casting off the body at the end..."
"Whatever [state] one constantly contemplates, O son of Kuntī, that alone one attains" (Gītā 8.6), and "at the time of departure with an unshaken mind" (Gītā 8.10);
furthermore, by stating "at the final hour he should take recourse to this triad," the scripture declares that there remains a duty to be performed even at the moment of death. // 12 //
"Until the final departure.
He states its connection with the [preceding] separated term: "repetition.
The meaning is: of that wise person who has realized his identity with Brahman, which is not subject to injunction.
He states the doubt, beginning with "But those which," because the practice of meditations on the Self (ahaṅgrahopāsana) is seen to be performed in both ways.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that, just as there is no regard for rules regarding direction and so forth because they are not prescribed, likewise there is no rule regarding repetition because there is no prescription for repeating the meditation until death.
He establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the repetition continues until death, beginning with "Thus."

He states the authority for the fact that meditations (*upāsana*) and ritual acts (*karman*) serve as causes for the fruit by means of the manifestation of the fruit to be attained at the time of death: "With consciousness" (*savijñāna*).
Consciousness consists of the manifestation of the fruit produced by mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*); "with consciousness" means accompanied by that.

"One whose mind is fixed on which world" (*yaccitta*) refers to one whose intention (*saṃkalpa*) is directed toward that world; the meaning is that after the manifestation of the fruit, the mind dissolves into the vital breath (*prāṇa*) together with that intended world.
The vital breath (*udāna*) is *tejas*;
the self (*ātman*) is the living soul (*jīva*).
And by the scriptural mention of the analogy of the leech, the meaning is that there is a manifestation of the future fruit.

Let it be granted that this final cognition [of the Self] is like the result of ritual action (*karman*), which operates through the medium of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*); however, from where does the non-return [to transmigratory existence] until death arise? To this, he says: "But the cognitions...
Because the cognitions of meditation (*upāsti*) proceed in a continuous stream (*dhārāvāhikatayā*), the final cognition is simply the non-cessation of their own nature;

no other factor mediated by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is required. This is because all entities, by their very nature, do not depend on anything of their own kind, and thus it is impossible for cognitions to require another cognition [as a mediating cause].
The point is that since it is impossible for actions to have the final cognition as their fruit through a visible means, one must assume an invisible (adṛṣṭa) means.
"Kratu" means meditation.
The meditator [recites] this triad: "Thou art imperishable."
The meaning is that one should remember these three mantras—‘acyutamasi’, ‘prāṇasaṃśitamasi’, and [the third] even at the time of death. //12//
The Section on the Attainment of That. Sūtra 13.
Upon the attainment of that [knowledge], there is the non-clinging and destruction of subsequent and prior sins, because of the designation thereof.
The third section on what remains is concluded.
Now, the consideration regarding the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman is commenced.
When Brahman is realized, there arises the doubt as to whether that evil which has the opposite result [of liberation] is destroyed or not destroyed.
What, then, is the prima facie position? Since action exists for the sake of its fruit, its destruction is not possible without having given its fruit.
For its power to bestow a fruit is established by scripture;

if the fruit were to be experienced and the [karmic] debt discharged even without that [power], the scripture would be rendered meaningless. Furthermore, they record in the Smṛti: "Indeed, action is not exhausted."
But if this is so, does it not follow that the instruction regarding expiation (*prāyaścitta*) becomes purposeless?
This is not a fault,
because expiations are established as being contingent upon specific conditions (*naimittika*), just like the *iṣṭi* sacrifice performed when a house has caught fire and so forth.

Moreover, since expiations are prescribed in connection with faults, they may indeed serve the purpose of exhausting those faults; however, there is no such injunction regarding the knowledge of Brahman.
[Objection: But if the destruction of karma is not admitted for the knower of Brahman, then because the fruit of that karma must necessarily be experienced, there would be no liberation. [Reply:
This is not so, it is said.
"Liberation will depend upon place, time, and cause, just like the fruit of ritual action;
therefore, there is no cessation of evil upon the realization of Brahman.

This being the position reached, we reply: upon that realization—that is, when there is realization of Brahman—there occurs the non-clinging and destruction of future and past evils respectively: the non-clinging of the future and the destruction of the past.
Why?
Because of that designation.
For thus, in the context of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), there is the non-connection with future evil that might otherwise be expected to be connected [to the knower].
He declares for the wise man: "Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows this" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.14.3).
Likewise, he declares the destruction of previously accumulated sin: "Just as the tuft of a reed-stalk thrown into a fire is consumed, even so all his evils are consumed" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.24.3).
5.24.3) Thus it is said.

This is another designation for the exhaustion of karma: "The knot of the heart is broken, all doubts are severed, and one's karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8).
As for what was said— that if one postulates the destruction of karma whose fruit has not yet been experienced, the scripture would be rendered meaningless—
this is not a fault; for we do not deny that karma possesses a power that yields its fruit.
We maintain that it indeed exists, but it is obstructed by other causes such as ignorance (avidyā) and the like;
moreover, the scripture is concerned solely with the existence of the capacity itself, and not with its obstruction or non-obstruction.
As for the traditional teaching that "karma is not exhausted," this too is a general rule; namely, that karma is not exhausted except through experience, because that is its purpose.

However, its exhaustion through expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) and the like is indeed accepted, as in such passages as "He overcomes all evil" and "He who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice, or he who speaks thus, overcomes even the murder of a Brahmin. As for what was said—that these will be merely occasional expiations—[that is not so].
That is incorrect;
for when these [acts] are enjoined with the connection of a fault, since the result consisting of the destruction of that fault is possible, it is illogical to postulate another result.

Furthermore, as for what was said—that there is no injunction of knowledge with the aim of the destruction of faults as there is in the case of expiation (prāyaścitta)—[that is refuted by the following].
To this we reply: first of all, injunctions certainly exist for those meditations that possess qualities (*saguṇavidyā*).
And in the supplementary passages (*vākyaśeṣa*) of those [meditations], the attainment of sovereignty and the cessation of evil are stated to belong to the one who possesses that knowledge.
Since there is no reason to disregard these two, it is therefore determined that the fruit of those [meditations] is the attainment of sovereignty preceded by the abandonment of evil.

In the case of the knowledge of the attributeless (nirguṇa), although there is no injunction [to practice it], nevertheless, through the realization of the Self as a non-agent, the destruction of karma is established. Furthermore, by the term "non-attachment" (aśleṣa), it is shown that the knower of Brahman does not even assume the state of being an agent with respect to future actions.

As for past actions, although one may have—as it were—assumed the state of being an agent due to false knowledge, nevertheless, because false knowledge is removed by the power of knowledge, those actions also dissolve; thus he says "destruction" (vināśa).
Thus:

Brahman, whose nature is non-agency and non-enjoyment throughout all three periods of time—the opposite of the previously established agency and enjoyership—is "I am. Neither previously was I an agent or an enjoyer, nor am I now, nor shall I be in the future.
Thus the knower of Brahman understands;
and in this very way liberation is possible.
For otherwise, in the absence of the exhaustion of karmas that have been operating since beginningless time, there would be no liberation.
Furthermore, liberation cannot be like the fruit of action, dependent as it is on place, time, and instrumental causes;
for that would entail the consequence of impermanence,
and it is also because liberation is the fruit of knowledge, which cannot be something beyond perception.
Therefore, it is certain that upon the realization of Brahman, there is the destruction of evil. 13.

Just as there are duties to be performed for as long as life lasts by lay followers (upāsakas), such is not the case for those who have realized the Self; thus, he speaks of liberation while living (jīvanmukti), characterized by the exhaustion of karma, in the words "Upon the attainment of that" (tadadhigame).

Furthermore, although this is a chapter on results (phalādhyāya), an investigation into the means was conducted therein for the sake of showing the preeminence of the result among the means of knowledge;
now, he says "Having gone" (gate) to indicate that the consideration of the result belonging to this chapter on results is being undertaken.
A doubt arises from the scriptural teaching that actions terminate in their fruits and from the scriptural teaching that [karma] is destroyed by knowledge;

in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), even for the knower of truth, liberation occurs only after experiencing the accumulated sins, whereas in the established conclusion (siddhānta), because sin is destroyed simultaneously with knowledge, there is liberation while living (jīvanmukti). This is the result [of the inquiry].
By the scriptural prohibitions such as "one should not kill," it is understood that the unseen demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) possesses a power to bestow suffering;
and they also record in their Smṛtis that "karma is not exhausted until it has been experienced.
Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that sin persists until its fruit is reached and does not perish in the interim.
If it is objected: "In that case, there would be no injunction for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the purpose of destroying that [defect]," we say: No.

Just as when the occasion of a house fire occurs for one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), there is the injunction for a sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) stating, "One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Kṣāmavat," so too, when a defect exists merely as the occasion, the injunction for expiation does not establish the destruction of the defect as its purpose.
If it is objected: "This is an unequal analogy," [we reply:]...

It is appropriate that the house-burning, because it is already accomplished and because it is unfit [to be an end], serves merely as a causal occasion (*nimitta*) and thus lacks fruit; however, in the case of the rule "one who possesses a fault (*doṣavat*) shall perform penance" (*prāyaścitta*), it is inappropriate [to treat it as a mere occasion], because—as in the case of "one who is dirty shall bathe"—it is possible for the word *doṣa* (fault) to have as its primary meaning the attainment of a result by way of cessation, and because scripture declares the removal of sin through penance, as in: "He who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice overcomes the murder of a Brahmin."
To show that expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is merely occasional (*naimittika*), he says "Moreover" (*apica*).

The meaning is that there is no injunction for knowledge as being for the purpose of destroying defects, because such passages as "And his actions perish" are merely laudatory of knowledge. He says "It is not so stated" to show that liberation will occur at another place and time after the experience of the fruits of karma, on the authority of the scriptures.

He establishes the existence of that [destruction of karma] through the passage beginning with "In this way," on the grounds that the destruction of karma through knowledge is something unprecedented (*apūrva*) and because it contradicts other means of valid cognition; thus, it is impossible for numerous passages devoted to that [knowledge] to be merely commendatory.
"Non-clinging" (*aśleṣa*) is the non-production of a new unseen potency (*apūrva*) from sinful action.

Having stated the designation regarding the knowledge of Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa-brahmavidyā*), he states it regarding the attributeless [Brahman] (*nirguṇa*) with the words: "This is another."
He refutes the opponent's statement with the words "As for what was said," and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: the scriptures of injunction and prohibition—such as "What has not been experienced does not perish"—as well as the Smṛti, are authoritative proof regarding the capacity of karma to produce its fruit; therefore, if one were to admit the destruction of even such a potent [karma] due to some cause, there would be a contradiction with the scriptures.

He states that the knowledge of reality regarding the Self destroys all evil because it sublates the superimposition rooted in that [Self], just as waking consciousness sublates the superimposition of agency rooted in the evil of a dream; thus he says, "nevertheless, from the realization of the non-agent Self. He confirms the meaning of the scripture through reasoning with the words, "and 'non-attachment'": because the root superimposition does not arise, there is no attachment to sin.
The meaning is that through the destruction of that [ignorance], there is the destruction of that [superimposition].
He cites the experience of the wise regarding the absence of superimposition, beginning with the words "pūrva" (previous).
And he states that the exhaustion of karma is established through knowledge by the force of the scriptures on liberation, beginning with the words "evam eva" (just so).
The meaning is: "only when there is the destruction of karma through knowledge.
He refutes the claim that liberation is similar to the fruit of karma with the words "and not" (na ca). //12//

The Section on Non-Attachment (Itarāsaṃśleṣādhikaraṇa). Sūtra 14.
In the same way, there is no attachment for the other [merit] as well, upon falling away.

(BBs 4.1.14) In the preceding section, it was established on the basis of scriptural teaching that the non-attachment and destruction of natural sin—which is the cause of bondage—are brought about by knowledge.

However, raising the objection that merit, being based on scripture, is not in contradiction with scriptural knowledge, this present section extends the reasoning of the previous one in order to refute that view.
In the same way as [the non-performance of] sin, there is both non-attachment to and the destruction of other meritorious karma for one who possesses knowledge.
Why? Because that [merit], being a cause for its own fruit, would entail the consequence of obstructing the fruit of knowledge.
As it is said: "He indeed crosses over both of these" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).
This is because in such scriptural passages as these, the destruction of good deeds (*sukṛta*) is designated just like that of evil deeds (*duṣkṛta*);

and because the destruction of karma, which is caused by the realization of the Self as a non-agent, is equal for both good and evil deeds; and because of the scriptural statement without distinction: "And his actions are exhausted" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8).

Even where the word *pāpman* (evil) is seen used alone, it should be understood that by that very term merit (*puṇya*) is also included, because [merit] is an inferior fruit compared to the fruit of knowledge. Furthermore, the word *pāpman* is applied even to merit in the Śruti: "Day and night do not cross this bridge" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.4.1).

Thus, here, having enumerated both what is well-done and ill-done together, the word "evil" (*pāpman*) is used without distinction even for merit (*puṇya*) in the context of the statement, "all evils turn back from here.
However, in the phrase "at the falling away" (*pāte tu*), the word "but" (*tu*) is for the purpose of emphasis.

Thus, since the non-clinging and destruction of merit and demerit—the two causes of bondage—are established through the power of knowledge, it emphasizes that liberation for the knower is necessarily certain at the fall of the body. 14.
But for the other [the destruction of demerit] as well,

there is no need for considerations such as consistency (*saṃgati*), because it is an extended application (*atideśa*). Having stated the further doubt— namely, that "merit is destroyed by knowledge or not," following the previous pattern— that knowledge does not destroy merit because, like merit, it is scriptural (*śāstrīya*)— he explains the extended application with the words beginning "of dharma" (*dharmasya*).

The meaning is that the inference [that knowledge destroys merit] is sublated by scripture supported by logic, namely: "Knowledge destroys merit because it annihilates ignorance along with its root. Now, one might object: the general scriptural statement, "And they are exhausted," refers specifically to evil, since there is a specific scriptural statement, "He crosses over all evil. To this, he says: "Even where it is said 'only'... He states the result of the two preceding sections concerning the exhaustion of both evil and merit: "But at the fall... (14).
Section 11: The Topic of What Has Not Yet Begun (Anārabdha-adhikaraṇa). Sūtra 15.
"But only those whose effects have not yet begun [are destroyed], because that is the limit.

(BBs 4.1.15) In the two preceding sections, it was determined that the destruction of good and evil deeds caused by knowledge occurs; now it is considered whether this occurs without distinction for both deeds whose effects have already begun and those whose effects have not yet begun, or specifically only for those whose effects have not yet begun.

Since such scriptural passages as "In that state, he indeed transcends both of these" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upani�ṣad 4.4.22) are heard without qualification, it follows that there is destruction [of karma] without distinction.
This being the position reached, the author replies: "But only those whose effects have not yet begun."

Only those previously accumulated in other births whose fruits have not yet begun to manifest, as well as those accumulated in this very life prior to the arising of knowledge, are destroyed by the attainment of knowledge; however, those actions whose effects have already commenced and whose fruits have been partially experienced— by which this birth, the locus of the knowledge of Brahman, was produced— are not destroyed.

Whence is this [known]? From the scriptural passage, "For him there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be merged" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2), which establishes that the attainment of security occurs upon the fall of the body.
For otherwise, if all karma were destroyed by knowledge, there would be no cause for continued existence, and thus one would attain security immediately after the acquisition of knowledge.
In that regard, one should not say that [liberation] awaits the falling of the body.
For surely, by the very power of the reality itself, this realization of the non-agent self, while exhausting karmas, would exhaust some and yet neglect others.
Indeed, it cannot be maintained that when there is an equal contact of fire with seeds, the seed-potency of some is destroyed while that of others is not destroyed.
It is said: First of all, the arising of knowledge is not possible without depending upon the accumulation of karma (*karmāśaya*) whose effects have already begun.

And once that [accumulation] has been depended upon, just as in the case of a potter’s wheel, there can be no obstruction in the interim for that which has set its motion in progress; thus, there remains the maintenance until the exhaustion of the momentum.
For even the realization of the Self as a non-agent destroys karmas by subverting false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*).
However, even though it has been sublated, false cognition—like the cognition of two moons—continues for some time due to the force of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, one should not dispute here whether or not the body is maintained for some time by one who knows Brahman;
for how could another possibly refute both the realization of Brahman within one's own heart and the maintenance of the body by the same person?
And this very point is explained through the description of the characteristics of one whose wisdom is steady (*sthitaprajña*) in the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*.
Therefore, the conclusion is that only those good and evil deeds whose effects have not yet begun are destroyed by the power of knowledge (*vidyā*). // 15 //

"But only those whose effects have not yet begun," taking as their object the destruction of the aforementioned karma, they are destroyed; thus, based on the scriptural statement without qualification (*aviśeṣa-śruti*) and the scriptural statement "for him there is delay only so long" (*tasya tāvadeva ciram*), he states the doubt with the words "of the two former.
The result in both cases is the non-establishment or the establishment of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*).

When the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) arises according to the logic of the previously established doctrine, the author states the exception (apavāda) that the aforementioned general rule regarding the destruction of karma applies only to other karmas already set in motion (prārabdha), using the word "thus" (evam). The word *sāmi* signifies "halfway" or "partial. The meaning of the scripture is that the delay lasts only as long as one is not liberated from the karma already set in motion; upon liberation from that, one attains Brahman.

Because there are scriptural and traditional indications (*liṅga*) that those who know reality, such as Yājñavalkya and others, maintained their bodies until the fall of the body; and because the strength of *prārabdha* karma is established by its being a necessary support (*upajīvya*) for the knowledge of reality as its cause; and because the knowledge of reality obstructed by that [karma] destroys only the obscuring portion of ignorance (*avidyā*)—leaving aside the portion called the power of projection (*vikṣepa-śakti*) which is required for the maintenance of that [body]—it is said: "It is not so," and so forth.
The residual impression (*saṃskāra*) of that [state] is merely a trace of the ignorance that causes distraction.
Furthermore, regarding the liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), he states his own experience with respect to his disciples: "Moreover, not at all," etc. (verse 15).
Topic 12: The Agnihotra and other rites. Sūtras 16–17.

"But the Agnihotra and so forth are for that very purpose, because it is seen [in scripture]. Regarding the doubt that the principle of the non-clinging and destruction of merit—just as with demerit—is extended by analogy to all merit, the author replies: "But the Agnihotra and so forth. The word "but" (tu) dispels that doubt.
The meaning is that the Vedic obligatory rites, such as the Agnihotra and so forth, serve precisely that purpose which is the purpose of knowledge;

for [the scripture] says: "Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, and by charity" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22). Why? Because of this [scriptural statement].
This is because of such scriptural indications.
Now, one might object that since knowledge and action have distinct effects, their unity of effect is untenable.
This is not a fault.

Just as even curd and poison, when combined with molasses and mantras respectively, are observed to produce the effects of satisfaction and nourishment, so too it is logical that action (karman), when conjoined with knowledge, can have liberation as its effect.
[Objection: But liberation is not something to be produced; how then can it be said to be the effect of action?
This is not a fault,
because action assists from a distance;
for it is only knowledge that brings about attainment, and thus action is figuratively described as the cause of liberation through the medium of knowledge.
For this very reason, this declaration of oneness regarding the effect refers to that which has transcended its objective domain;

for one who knows Brahman, no future Agnihotra or similar rites are possible, because such a person has realized the identity with Brahman— which is not subject to injunction— and thus lies outside the scope of the scripture.
In the case of meditations possessing attributes (*saguṇavidyā*), however, since agency has not been transcended, future rites such as the *agnihotra* are possible.
Even for those, because they are performed without desire for rewards and thus lack any other effect, their connection with knowledge is logically established. // 16 //

Regarding the Agnihotra and other such rites— whether obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*)— there arises a doubt as to whether they are destroyed by knowledge or not. Anticipating the objection that they are destroyed because of the scriptural statement without qualification, "He crosses over both merit and demerit," the author establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) as an exception (*apavāda*) to the previously stated extension (*atideśa*) in the words beginning with "of merit" (*puṇyasya*),
asserting that this applies only to optional (*kāmya*) merit distinct from the obligatory and occasional.

In this regard, the distinction is as follows: according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the performance of obligatory rites and so forth for the sake of knowledge is not established, following the maxim of "washing away mud"; however, according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), since they serve the purpose of generating knowledge, their establishment is secured.

Here, in the commentary (*bhāṣya*), it should be understood that after stating—according to the opinion of others—that knowledge and action have a single direct result, the author's own view is stated: that they are causes of liberation both directly and indirectly.
"From this very [reason]" means that since there is an absence of karma subsequent to knowledge, it refers to prior karma.
The association of the knowledge of the attributeless (nirguṇa-vidyā) with ritual action was shown to be as useless for achieving satisfaction as a plow is for eating;
now, he states the appropriateness of the Sūtra by taking it to refer to the knowledge of the qualified (saguṇa-vidyā): "In the case of the qualified [knowledges]," etc. //16//

But with reference to what subject is this statement regarding non-attachment and destruction made? Or with reference to what subject is that statement of certain reciters of the Veda regarding the distribution [of deeds]: "His sons inherit his property; his friends [inherit] his good deeds"?
"Those who hate [the practitioner] perform evil deeds. To this, he recites the following: "For some, there is also another [result] for both. (BBs 4.1.17)

Therefore, apart from the obligatory rites such as the Agnihotra, there is indeed another "good deed" (sādhukṛtyā) which is performed with a view toward its fruit; regarding that, the application has been stated by some reciters of the Veda: "His friends take over his good deeds.
And this description of the non-clinging and destruction of that very [deed]—just like the evil—is likewise [to be understood as] the non-clinging of the other [type of deed] as well.

Thus, both teachers, Jaimini and Bādarāyaṇa, are in agreement regarding the fact that rites performed for the sake of desired results (kāmya-karma) of such a nature do not contribute toward knowledge (vidyā). 17.
He grasps the meaning of the subsequent sutra with the words beginning "What...

The sense is this: whatever meritorious or sinful action other than that which has already begun (prārabdha) is performed—whether out of desire or otherwise—that alone produces a corresponding karma for the wise man and his enemy respectively, while it itself is destroyed by knowledge. //17//
Topic 13: The Means for the Attainment of Knowledge (vidyājñānasādhana). Sūtra 18.
"By knowledge alone"—

this has indeed been established in the immediately preceding section: that the obligatory *agnihotra* and other rites, when performed by one seeking liberation with liberation as their intended purpose,
serve as a cause for the purification of the mind (*sattva*) by way of being the means for the destruction of previously accumulated sins.
Since it serves as the cause for attaining Brahman, which has liberation as its purpose, it shares a single goal with the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).
In this regard, there exists both karma such as the *agnihotra* that is conjoined with knowledge based on the ritual subsidiaries (*aṅga*), and that which is independent.

[This is seen in passages such as: "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices," "He who, knowing thus, offers oblations," "He who, knowing thus, recites," "He who, knowing thus, sings," and "Therefore, let him make one who knows thus the *brahmán* priest, and not one who does not know thus."

From such scriptural statements as "Life" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.17.10) and "Therefore both perform [the sacrifice]: he who knows this thus, and he who does not know" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.10), it follows that there is [action] conjoined with knowledge, and there is also action alone.

In this regard, the following is considered: Is it only the ritual action such as the Agnihotra when conjoined with knowledge that, for one seeking liberation, serves as a cause for knowledge by attaining a single purpose with it, and not the action alone? Or do both—the action conjoined with knowledge and the action alone—equally [serve as causes]? Whence arises this doubt? From the scriptural statement, "They desire to know this very Self through sacrifice," which declares that sacrifices and other rites are, without distinction, auxiliary means to the knowledge of the Self.

Furthermore, since it is understood that rites such as the *agnihotra* are no different when conjoined with knowledge (*vidyā*), what then is the prima facie position? It is that only the *agnihotra* and other rites conjoined with knowledge serve as auxiliaries to the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyā*), and not those devoid of knowledge;
for it is understood that [the rite] belonging to one endowed with knowledge is superior to that which is devoid of knowledge.

From such scriptural passages as, "On whatever day one offers [the oblation], on that very day one who knows thus conquers recurrent death," and from the *Bhagavad Gītā*: "The intellect with which, O Pārtha, you shall cast off the bond of action" (2.39),
and "For action is far inferior, O Dhanañjaya, to the yoga of wisdom" (2.49).
"And because of such Smṛti passages as these.
This being the position reached, the author replies: "For [it is said], 'Whatever [one does] by means of knowledge,'" etc.
This is true.
Action such as the Agnihotra joined with knowledge is superior to action devoid of knowledge, just as a learned Brāhmaṇa is superior to a Brāhmaṇa devoid of learning.
Nevertheless, action such as the Agnihotra is not entirely independent of knowledge;
why? Because it is heard in scripture, without distinction, that "they desire to know this very Self by means of sacrifice," thus establishing the Agnihotra and other rites as causes for knowledge.

Now, it might be argued that since it is understood that the Agnihotra and other rites conjoined with knowledge are superior to those devoid of knowledge, it is logical that the Agnihotra and so forth, when lacking knowledge, are entirely independent as causes for the knowledge of the Self.
This is not so;

because the Agnihotra and other rites, when accompanied by knowledge, possess a superior capacity due to their association with the cause of knowledge, they will have a certain excellence as a cause toward the realization of the Self, whereas this is not the case for those devoid of knowledge.
Thus it is reasonable to conclude this.

However, one cannot maintain that the Agnihotra and other rites—which are heard in the passage "They desire to know through sacrifice" (*yajñena vividiṣanti*) as being limbs of self-knowledge without distinction—are not limbs [of knowledge].
For so says the Śruti: "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the Upaniṣad, that alone becomes more powerful" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.10).

Thus, by stating that ritual action such as the *agnihotra* becomes more powerful (*vīryavattara*) when conjoined with knowledge, [the text] speaks of a certain excellence regarding its own result; it thereby demonstrates that even for one devoid of knowledge, that very same action possesses power toward that specific purpose.
And the "power" of an action is its capacity for forcefulness in accomplishing its own intended result.
Therefore, both the Agnihotra and other rites performed constantly— whether conjoined with knowledge or devoid of knowledge— by one desiring liberation, with the aim of liberation,

during this life or in another birth prior to the arising of knowledge, serve as a cause for the realization of Brahman by way of being the means for destroying accumulated sins that act as obstacles to the attainment of Brahman, according to their respective capacities.

It is established that the practice, depending upon internal causes such as hearing, reflection, faith, and single-minded devotion, becomes a single effect together with the knowledge of Brahman. // 18 //
"By means of knowledge alone," etc.

Having relied upon the subject matter previously stated in the passage beginning with "etad vai," and having formulated a doubt accompanied by its seed, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "Only that which is conjoined with knowledge [leads to the goal].
In this prima facie view, it is established that ritual action devoid of meditation on its constituent parts does not serve the purpose of knowledge.
The distinction is that, according to our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*), that [result] is accomplished [by action alone].
Let it be granted that, by the power of knowledge (*vidyā*), there is some excellence in ritual action qualified by knowledge, characterized as its being more rapid in producing knowledge;
yet this does not render mere [unqualified] action useless, because that would contradict the scriptural injunction regarding the desire to know (*vividiṣā-śruti*).
Furthermore, it is not appropriate to restrict the words "sacrifice" and so forth in that scriptural passage to refer only to actions accompanied by knowledge;
for the meaning of the Siddhānta section is that the scripture, "Whatever one does with knowledge," indicates that even [action] alone possesses power. //18//
Section 14:
The Refutation of the Other [Doctrine]. Sūtra 19.
"But having exhausted the others through experience, he then attains [Brahman].

It has been stated that the destruction of merit and demerit whose effects have not yet begun occurs through the power of knowledge; however, having exhausted through experience those other merits and demerits whose effects have already begun, one attains Brahman, according to the text: "For him there is delay only so long as he is not released from the body."
This is known from such scriptural passages as, "Then I shall attain [fulfillment]" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2), and "Being Brahman, he merges into Brahman.

Now, one might object: even when perfect realization has occurred, just as the perception of duality persists before the fall of the body according to the analogy of seeing two moons, so too would it persist after that point. No; it does not.
Because of the absence of a cause [for persistence].
For in that case, the cause for continued existence is the exhaustion of the remainder of experience, and there is nothing of that sort remaining.
[Objection: But will another latent impression of karma (karmāśaya) not initiate new experience? [Reply: No.
Because its seed has been burnt;
for it is only when supported by false knowledge that another karma initiates a subsequent experience after the fall of the body,
and that other karma, being supported by false knowledge, initiates yet another experience after the fall of the body, whereas that false knowledge [is abandoned] through right knowledge.
Because it has been burnt by knowledge, this is correct: upon the exhaustion of the commenced effects, liberation necessarily occurs for the wise one. // 19 //
Having exhausted the other [karmas] through experience, one attains [liberation].
Here, the knower of reality is the subject;

since there is doubt as to whether he transmigrates after the exhaustion of *prārabdha* (commenced karma) or not—based on the presence or absence of its cause—the author begins the final conclusion with the words "anārabdha" (not commenced).
When it is stated that uncommenced karma (*anārabdhakarman*) is destroyed, the question arises as to how commenced karma (*ārabdha*) is destroyed; this [next section] follows because of that inquiry.

The distinction is that, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), disembodied liberation (*videhakaivalya*) is not established, whereas according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is established.

The prima facie view is presented by means of the analogy from the *Anārabdhādhikaraṇa*: "Does the knower of reality (*tattvavid*) continue to transmigrate even after the fall of the body, since he possesses the fitness for transmigration just as before the fall of the body?"—thus [the author says], "Now, [is it not so]... (*nanu*).
Because there is an absence of karma that serves as the cause for enjoyment, the reason [you have provided] is unestablished.
As for whatever other accumulated karma exists, it is not the cause of the fruit,
because its root has been burnt away.
For ignorance and the other afflictions (kleśas) are the root of karma and its fruit.
As it is stated in the Yogaśāstra: "The latent deposit of karma has its root in the afflictions; as long as the root exists, there is its fruition.

Since that root has been consumed by the fire of knowledge, how can there be further transmigration? Therefore, it is established that upon the fall of the body, there is absolute liberation (kaivalya). //19//
Thus ends the first quarter of the fourth chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda, the disciple of the venerable Govindabhagavatpūjyapāda. // 1 //
Thus ends the first quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā*, composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya, the blessed Śrī Govindānanda Bhagavatpāda.
Thus ends the first quarter of the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Liberation while Living" (*jīvanmukti-nirūpaṇa*).
The Second Quarter of the Fourth Chapter START BsCom_4,2.1.1
The Second Quarter of the Fourth Chapter. In this quarter, there is an investigation into the departure and journey [of the soul]. 1. The Section concerning Speech (Vāk-adhikaraṇa). Sūtras 1–2.
"Speech [is merged] in mind, because it is so seen and because of the scriptural statement.

(BBs 4.2.1) Now, intending to introduce the path of the gods (*devayāna*) for the attainment of the fruit in other forms of knowledge, [the author] first explains the sequence of departure (*utkrānti*) according to the scriptures;
for he will state that the departure is the same for both the knower and the ignorant.

There is a scriptural text concerning the time of death: "Of this person, my dear, when he is departing, speech merges into the mind, the mind into the breath, the breath into heat, and the heat into the supreme deity" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.6).
Here there arises a doubt: is it said that speech itself, as a functional entity, merges into the mind, or rather that the function of speech [merges]?
In this regard, it follows that speech itself merges into the mind;
for in this way, the scriptural statement is supported.
Otherwise, there would be a figurative interpretation (*lakṣaṇā*).
And when there is no room for a secondary sense (*lakṣaṇā*), direct denotation (*śruti*) is more appropriate than a secondary sense;
therefore, this dissolution of speech itself occurs in the mind.
This being the position reached, we reply: since it has already been explained that "speech" refers to its function (*vṛtti*), the Teacher reads the text simply as "speech [dissolves] in the mind."
This is true;
however, he will state later on, "There is no division, because of the scriptural statement" (Brahma Sūtra 4.2.16).
Therefore, it is understood that in this context, what is intended is merely the cessation of the functioning [of the intellect].

If, however, one intended to speak of the dissolution of reality (*tattvapralaya*), then since there is equality of non-distinction everywhere, why would it be specified that "non-distinction" occurs only in the subsequent [stage]?
Therefore, in this context, the intention is to describe the withdrawal of the functions (*vṛttyupasaṃhāra*).
The meaning is that the function of speech is withdrawn first while the function of the mind remains present.
Why?
Because it is observed.
For it is indeed observed that the withdrawal of speech occurs prior to the activity of the mind, even while the mental activity is still present.
Now, it was argued that on the strength of the scriptural statement, this dissolution of speech alone in the mind is logical;
[the author] says "no," because the mind is not its material cause (*atatprakṛtitvāt*).
For it is logical that the dissolution of something occurs in that from which its origin arose, as in the case of a clay bowl dissolving into clay;
however, there is no means of valid cognition whatsoever to show that speech originates from the mind.
Furthermore, the emergence and suppression of functions are observed even when they do not rely upon the primary material cause.
For the activity of the fiery element, fire, arises from its fuel consisting of earthly substances and subsides in water.
How then, on this view, can it be said that "speech merges into the mind"? To this he says: "and from sound."

The word [in the sūtra] is also applicable to this position; the meaning is that it is due to the figurative treatment of the non-difference between the function (vṛtti) and that which possesses the function (vṛttimat). // 1 // [Note:
For one who is striving [to control the mind] at the time of death, because of the observation that speech merges into the mind, and because of the scriptural statement.]

Immediately after the statement regarding the fruit of knowledge (*jñāna*), the fruit of meditation (*upāsanā*)—which resides in the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*)—must be stated. That [fruit] is to be attained via the path beginning with light (*arcirādi-mārga*), and the attainment of that path is accomplished through the process of departure from the body (*utkrānti*). Therefore, this fourth section on departure (*utkrāntipāda*), which is implied by the fruit of meditation, has a logical connection (*saṅgati*) to the chapter. Furthermore, its immediate succession to the preceding section is appropriate because it is implied by the fruit of meditation, which must be stated immediately after the statement regarding the fruit of knowledge. Thus he says: "Now" (*atha*).
Since it might be thought that there is no departure (utkrānti) for the worshipper as there is for the man of knowledge, he says: "Equal" (samāna).
The wise one is the worshipper;
for him, there is departure just as for one who is not a worshipper.
The meaning is that it will be stated [later] "due to ignorance.
"Prayataḥ" means "of one who is dying.

Regarding the word *vāk*, there is a doubt because, through both its derivation as an instrument (*karaṇa*) and its derivation as a state of being (*bhāva*), there is the appearance of both the instrument and its function (*vṛtti*) merging [into the mind].
In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), because the instruments [of action] dissolve into their own essential nature, liberation occurs for one who has merely died;
however, in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the continuity of transmigratory existence is maintained.
The distinction is this: since speech cannot dissolve into its true essence within a mind that is not its material cause, there is only the cessation of its activity.
He raises the doubt as to how there can be the supply of supplementary words (*vṛttipadādhyāhāra*) in the Sūtra by asking, "How? The meaning of the resolution is as follows:

since the author of the Sūtras, the knower of reality, will later state the dissolution of the senses into their own essential nature (*svarūpalaya*), it is appropriate here to supply those words on that basis;
for otherwise, if the dissolution of the senses were the same for the ignorant person as well, it would be improper to state the specific distinction that is about to be explained.

He establishes the final conclusion—that even the Śruti does not teach the logically contradictory doctrine that "the modification dissolves back into its own material cause"—with the words, "Because it does not have that as its material cause" (*atatprakṛtitvāt*).

He states "and because of the word" (*śabdācca*) to indicate that while the logical principle (*nyāya*) is stronger due to being free from any alternative application (*niravakāśatva*), the verbal testimony (*śabda*) has scope for application either through etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*)—as in the case of the word *vāk* meaning "speech"—or through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). //1//
And for this very reason, all [the other faculties] follow [the mind]. 4.2.2.
"Therefore, with his vital heat stilled, [the soul] enters again into a new existence through the senses merging into the mind" (Praśna Upaniṣad 3.9).
Here, the merging of all the senses without distinction into the mind is heard in the scripture.

In this regard, for the very same reason as in the case of speech—since it is observed that the functions of the eyes and other organs also cease when the mind remains with its functions suspended, and since their dissolution into the essential element (tattva) is impossible and verbal testimony supports this—all the sense organs follow the mind solely by way of their functions.

Although there is no distinction in the withdrawal of all the instruments (karaṇas) into the mind, the separate mention of speech in the phrase "speech is merged into the mind" is for the sake of following the specific example given. 2.
He extends the principle stated for speech to the eyes and other senses with the words "these very [senses]":
the meaning of the scriptural passage is that one whose bodily heat has subsided attains rebirth after departing from that body.
This is because the word *indriya* found in the scripture can appropriately be understood as referring to their functions (*vṛtti*).

If the dissolution of the functions of all the senses is intended [to be the same as that of speech and mind], then for what purpose is there a separate sūtra stating "speech and mind"? To this he says: "Of all the instruments" (sarveṣāṃ karaṇānām). //2//
Section on the Mind. Sūtra 3. The mind is the instrument [of cognition]. Sūtra 3.
That [subtle] mind [merges] into the vital breath, according to the subsequent [scriptural passage].
It has been established that in the statement, "Speech merges into the mind" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.6), what is intended is the merging of the function (vṛtti).
Now, regarding the subsequent statement, "The mind [is merged] in breath" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.6),

when a doubt arises as to whether it is intended here that only the functions merge or that the possessor of the functions merges, the initial position is that it is indeed the merger of the possessor of the functions that is intended;
for this is supported by the direct scriptural statement and is logically consistent with the fact that the latter is the material cause of the former.

For instance: "The mind, my dear, consists of food; the vital breath consists of water" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.5.4). Thus, they declare that the mind has food as its source and the vital breath has water as its source. Furthermore, the Śruti states: "And the waters created food."
And as for the claim that the mind [merges] into the vital breath because of the non-difference between the material cause and its modification—this being the position reached, we reply:
it must be understood from the subsequent statement that even that mind, when its external sensory functions have ceased, merges into the vital breath solely by way of its own mental functions.

For it is observed that in one who is about to fall asleep or about to die, while the activity of the vital breath—which consists of pulsation—remains present, there is a cessation of the activities of the mind.
Furthermore, the merging of the mind's own nature into the vital breath (prāṇa) is not possible,
because the mind does not have that as its material cause (prakṛti). But was it not shown that the vital breath is the material cause of the mind?
This is not the essence;
for the mind cannot merge into the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by virtue of such a mere physical conduit.
For if that were so, the mind would merge into food, and food into water, and the vital breath would likewise merge into water alone.

For even on this view, there is no evidence whatsoever that the mind is born from water transformed into the state of vital breath; therefore, there is no merging of the mind’s own nature into the vital breath.

However, it has been shown that the scriptural statement is possible even with respect to the merging of its function (*vṛtti*), by means of the metaphorical identification of the function and the possessor of the function. // 3 //
That mind [is merged] in the vital breath (prāṇa), according to the subsequent [scriptural passage].
The sequence of the topics [of discussion] follows both the sequence of the sentences and the sequence of their meanings.

There was doubt based on both direct scriptural statement (śruti) and logical reasoning (nyāya); however, because it contradicted the stronger principle, the [prior] scriptural statement regarding speech was set aside.

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) conclusion—just as before—is that since air (*ab*) is the material cause (*prakṛti*) of breath (*prāṇa*) and food (*anna*) is the material cause of mind (*manas*), the scriptural statement regarding the mind is not contradicted by the principle that "an effect dissolves into its material cause. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: even if air and food stand in the relation of material cause and effect, their respective effects—breath and mind—do not thereby stand in that same relation. For if they did, it would follow absurdly that ice and a jar would also stand in the relation of material cause and effect. Therefore, because this contradicts the logical principle, the scriptural statement must be set aside as before;
such is the distinction.

The meaning is that the mind, whose functions of the external senses have been withdrawn by [the yogin], and whose own functions have become dissolved, likewise dissolves into the vital breath (prāṇa) precisely through the dissolution of its functions.
"Even so" means even in the view that the vital breath is a modification of water.
Therefore, because the vital breath (prāṇa) is the direct material cause of the mind, the word "mind" indicates its function; this is the meaning. //3//
END BsCom_4,2.2.3 START BsCom_4,2.3.4 3.
Section on Superintendents (adhyakṣa-adhikaraṇam) / Sūtras 4–6.
"That [subtle body] [merges] with the presiding [deity], because of its approaching that and so forth" (BBs 4.2.4).
It has been established that for whatever there is no origination from something, the dissolution of its function into that [source] does not mean the dissolution of its own nature.
Now, this is being considered regarding the statement: "The vital breath [merges] into heat" (prāṇas tejasi).

Is the withdrawal of the function of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) into heat (*tejas*) exactly as stated in the scripture, or rather into the individual soul (*jīva*), who is the presiding lord over the cage of the body and senses?
In this regard, since the scriptural statement is beyond doubt, the merging of the vital breath must occur into heat alone, as it is improper to assume what is not stated in scripture.
This being the position reached, the author of the Sūtras establishes the following: "It [merges] into the presiding lord."
That primary vital breath (prāṇa) abides in the cognitional self (vijñānātman), which is the presiding overseer characterized by the limiting adjuncts of ignorance, karma, and prior cognition;
the meaning is that the function of the vital breath becomes subordinate to that [self].
Why? Because of its approaching that [self] and so forth.

In the same way, at the time of death, all the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) gather around this self, as another scriptural passage shows: "When he becomes one who breathes upwards. Indeed, that other scripture demonstrates without distinction that all the vital breaths follow the presiding self; and it specifies this further: "As he departs, the vital breath departs after him" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2).
Thus, he demonstrates that the fivefold vital breath (*prāṇa*) follows its presiding overseer (*adhyakṣa*), and that the others follow it:
"As the principal breath departs, all the vital breaths depart after it" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2).

Furthermore, by showing that the overseer possesses internal consciousness through the statement "He becomes endowed with consciousness," it indicates that the vital breath, in which the entire collection of instruments has been absorbed, remains within him.
But is it not heard in scripture that "the vital breath [merges] into heat"? How then can the addition be made that "the vital breath [merges] into the presiding deity"?

This is not a fault, because the activity of departing and so forth—found even in other scriptural passages—is primarily concerned with the presiding deity, and because a specific detail must necessarily be taken into account. // 4 //
Regarding the passage "The vital breath [is merged] in heat" (Chāndogya Up.

6.8.6), having raised a doubt based on the scriptural statements concerning its departure and so forth, and relying on the dissolution of the functions of the vital breath— which is established by the logic already stated— the author presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words beginning "It is settled," asserting that the departure and other such phenomena are possible even without dissolution into the individual soul (*jīva*).

Considering that the word *tejas* (fire/heat) has its primary sense here, whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) it serves as an indicator (*lakṣaka*) for the individual soul (*jīva*) as conditioned by the elements, he applies the Sūtra with the words "He, the one under discussion," and so forth.
The meaning is: [the soul] having ignorance, karma, and latent impressions (*vāsanā*) as its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
The meaning of the reason is: "because of the scriptural statements regarding the approach, following, and abiding of the vital breaths (prāṇas) toward that individual soul (jīva).

Just as servants approach a king who intends to set out on a journey, even so all the vital breaths approach face-to-face the soul desiring to go to the next world; thus, "approach" is heard in scripture.
Furthermore, "following" is heard in the scripture [in the passage]: "As he departs... and so forth.
He states the scriptural testimony regarding the abiding of the vital breaths in the individual soul (jīva) with the words, "possessed of consciousness" (*savijñāna*).

For the meaning is that, through the scriptural mention of the accompaniment of consciousness so as to understand the fruit to be attained by the soul, the persistence of the organs together with the chief vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) within the soul is made manifest. //4//
How then is the scriptural statement "the vital breath [merges] into heat" to be understood? To this he says:
"Because of the scriptural statement regarding the elements.

(BBs 4.2.5) It should be understood that he—the presiding overseer conjoined with the vital breath—abides within the subtle elements which are the seeds of the body and are accompanied by fire (*tejas*), because of the scriptural statement: "The breath [is merged] in fire. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.6)
But surely this scriptural passage shows the abiding of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in heat (*tejas*), not that of the presiding self (*adhyakṣa*) conjoined with the vital breath?
This is not a fault,
because the presiding self is also included within the intermediate stage by the statement "that [is] the presiding self."
For even one who, having gone from Srughna to Mathurā, proceeds from Mathurā to Pāṭaliputra, can be said to "go from Srughna to Pāṭaliputra.

Therefore, the statement "the vital breath [merges] into heat" refers to the presiding self (adhyakṣa) conjoined with the vital breath, whose abiding is within the elements that accompany that heat. 5.

Although the dissolution of the vital breath (prāṇa) into heat (tejas) without any intervening medium is heard in scripture, nevertheless, for the sake of honoring both scriptural statements, the vital breath dissolves into the individual soul (jīva), and through the soul, into the elemental constituents such as heat that serve as its limiting adjuncts. To clarify the meaning of the scripture, he takes up the Sūtra with the words: "How then? Nor should it be argued that the scriptural mention of heat is primary because the departure toward the soul is possible even without dissolution.
The sense is that "merging" (laya) here refers simply to the state of the vital breath (prāṇa) remaining inactive after the individual soul (jīva) has returned [to the body].

Anticipating the objection—"Why is the soul's residence in the elements explained as being by force?"—he says, beginning with "nanu," that it is on the strength of the scriptural passage cited in the Sūtra, "He [merges] in the presiding deity.
He provides an illustration for how the vital breath reaches the elements through the medium of the soul, saying, "For even he who... etc.
Regarding the question, "How [is it] with respect to the elements that accompany fire? it is said: as far as only one thing is heard, namely, "the vital breath in fire."
Therefore, he says:
"For [the soul] does not abide in one [element], since [the scriptures] show [it to be so].
(BBs 4.2.6) The soul does not abide in the element of fire alone at the time of seeking another body, because it is observed that the body, which is the effect, is composed of multiple elements.
And this same point is demonstrated by the question and answer: "Water has the form of a person" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.3.3).
This was explained here [in the Brahma Sūtras] at 3.1.2: "But because it consists of three elements, on account of the predominance [of water].
Furthermore, both Śruti and Smṛti demonstrate this very point.

The Śruti says: "Consisting of earth, consisting of water, consisting of air, consisting of ether, consisting of fire," and so forth. The Smṛti also says: "The subtle, imperishable particles which are said to belong to the five elements—with them, all this comes into being in successive order," and so forth.

But is it not the case that, when the instruments such as speech have been withdrawn at the time of seeking another body, another Śruti—beginning with "Where then does this person become? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.13)—establishes that action is the substratum, stating: "What they spoke of was indeed action; what they praised was indeed action" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.13)?

To this it is replied: In that context, it was stated that action is the basis [of bondage], because the activity of the bond—consisting of the senses and their objects and designated as "grasping" (graha) and "over-grasping" (atigraha)—is impelled by action.
Here, however, it is stated that the production of another body arises from the appropriation of the elements (bhūta), and thus the elements are the basis.
Furthermore, even from the word of praise used there, only the preeminence of action is demonstrated, but other bases are not excluded.
Therefore, there is no contradiction. (6) [Note:
"Daśārdhānām" refers to the five gross elements; "aṇvyaḥ" means subtle.]
They are called *mātrās* because they are measured (*mīyante*).
It has been explained in the *Raṃhaty-adhikaraṇa* that the fivefold-combined elements (*pañcīkṛta-bhūtāni*) are necessary for the commencement of the gross body;
these [elements] are subtle (*aṇvyaḥ*), meaning minute.
They are called *mātrās* because they are measured (*mīyante*), being delimited; they are indestructible until liberation,
meaning they are the subtle portions of the five elements.

Raising the objection that the soul's being the substratum of the elements contradicts scriptural statements regarding its being the substratum of karma, [the author] replies with the words "But surely... and so forth, stating that there is no contradiction between both positions because karma is the substratum in the sense of being the cause, whereas the elements are the substratum in the sense of being the material cause of the body.
The statement of the scripture is that what Yājñavalkya and Ārtabhāga spoke of as the support of the soul was indeed karma. //6//
Section on the Commencement of the Course of Transmigration (Āsṛtyupakramādhikaraṇa), Sūtra 7.
4. The section concerning the commencement of the course of transmigration (āsṛtyupakrama). Sūtra 7.
"And [this departure] is common until the commencement of the path, and immortality is attained without having burned away [the body].

Regarding this departure, for those who are in doubt as to whether it is the same for both the knower and the ignorant, or whether it possesses specific distinctions, the initial position reached is that it possesses specific distinctions;
for this departure is characterized by its dependence on the elements.
Furthermore, living beings depend upon [the senses] for rebirth;
however, rebirth does not occur for the wise man.
For it is an established principle that "the wise man attains immortality."
Therefore, this departure belongs only to the ignorant.
[Objection: But surely, because it is mentioned in the context of knowledge (vidyā), it must belong only to the knower. [Reply: No;
for it is a mere restatement of what is already established, just like the state of deep sleep and so forth.

For instance, in the passages, "When this person is said to sleep," "when he is said to feel hunger," and "when he is said to feel thirst" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.3, 5), sleep and so forth— which are common to all living beings— are merely mentioned even within the context of knowledge (*vidyā*), for the purpose of establishing the reality intended to be taught; they are not intended to be prescribed as specific attributes of the knower.

Thus, this departure (*utkrānti*) is described only with reference to the common people, in order to establish that "That which a person striving for perfection attains as his light when he reaches the Supreme Deity—that Self is the Reality; Thou art That" (*tat tvam asi*).
Furthermore, this departure is denied for the knower in the passage: "His vital breaths do not depart" (*na tasya prāṇā utkrāmanti*, Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6).
Therefore, this [departure] belongs only to the ignorant.

This being the position reached, we reply: this departure—beginning with "Speech merges into the mind," and so forth—is common to both the knower and the ignorant until the commencement of the path (āsṛti), because there is no scriptural statement to the contrary.

Impelled by karma, [the soul] transmigrates, depending upon the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma) which are non-contradictory and constitute the seed of the body, in order to experience the assumption of a body;
the knower, however, resorts to the door of the vein of liberation illuminated by knowledge.
This very point has been stated [in the sūtra] as "from the beginning of the stream" (āsṛti-upakramāt).

[Objection: Surely immortality is what must be attained by the knower, and that is not dependent upon another place; so why, in that case, would there be a resort to the elements or the commencement of a path? [Reply:

To this it is said: "Without having burned this"—that is, without having utterly consumed the afflictions such as ignorance through the power of lower knowledge (aparavidyā)—one who seeks relative immortality may indeed have a resort to the elements and a commencement of a path.
For the movement of life-breaths that are without a support is not possible;
therefore, there is no fault. // 7 //

Thus, because the external senses first attain dissolution of their functions into the mind, the function of the mind then dissolves into the vital breath (prāṇa), and the function of the vital breath dissolves into the individual soul (jīva) as conditioned by the elements; such is the established order of departure described.

And since this [process] is the same for all living beings, he says: "And it is the same for those who have not practiced austerity. He raises a doubt regarding the statement "seyaṃ" (this very one) based on the non-specific scriptural texts: "Of a person departing, speech is merged in the mind," and "Through knowledge, one attains immortality."

The meaning is "of those who have doubts regarding the objects [of knowledge]. In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the specific distinction of the departure (*utkrānti*)—namely, its lack of connection with one who knows Brahman with attributes—is established. Consequently, the result is that the meditator, without departing, attains liberation.
In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, there is a difference in the result: one who has departed [from the body] becomes a partaker of the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*).
Having raised an objection against the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he resolves it with the words "But [as for the claim] that through knowledge... and so forth.
The scriptural statement "through knowledge, immortality" refers to the supreme [immortality] belonging to one who possesses the knowledge of the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) Brahman.
The prohibition that "his vital breaths do not depart" also refers to that same subject.
Therefore, he establishes the conclusion—that even for one who knows [the qualified Brahman], there is indeed departure, as in the case of the ignorant—by saying "thus.
The path (sṛti) is the way; its commencement is the reaching of the light (arciḥ), and the departure prior to that is the same for both.
Therefore, the distinction is that the lay practitioner (upāsaka) attains the path beginning with light through the door of the *mūrdhan* channel, and no other does; this is the specific point.

As for the immortality (*amṛtatva*) heard in the case of the meditator on the "small space" (*dahara-upāsaka*)—namely, "Going upwards from there, he attains immortality"—that is merely relative and not absolute, because of the scriptural mention of enjoyment: "Whatever desire he desires, that arises for him by his mere volition. Thus [the author] says: "And this [immortality] is without having burned away [impurities]."
This is a form derived from the verbal root *uṣ* meaning "to burn. //7//

Topic 5: The Designation of Saṃsāra (Sūtras 8–11) START BsCom_4,2.5.8 5 saṃsāravyapadeśa adhikaraṇam // sū. 8-11 [The opponent argues: Since the individual soul (jīva) is designated as being subject to transmigration (saṃsāra), it must be distinct from Brahman. For the scripture declares that transmigratory existence consists of birth, death, and so forth; and since the individual soul is said to undergo these states, it follows that it is different from the immutable Brahman. Furthermore, the scripture speaks of the soul’s departure from the body, its ascent, and its descent, which would be impossible if it were identical with the omnipresent Brahman. Therefore, the individual soul is a separate entity. [The Sūtrakāra replies: This is not so. Even though the individual soul is designated as being in a state of transmigration, it is not essentially different from Brahman. Just as the ether within a jar is not different from the universal ether, so too the individual soul, though appearing to be in a state of transmigration due to its association with the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the intellect (buddhi), is in reality none other than Brahman. The scriptural texts concerning birth and death refer only to the soul's association with a new body and its separation from an old one, not to any change in its essential nature. The designations of "going" and "coming" likewise pertain to the soul's movement through the subtle body (liṅga-deha) under the influence of karma, and do not imply any spatial displacement of the omnipresent Self. Thus, the designation of saṃsāra does not prove the difference of the individual soul from Brahman. [The opponent objects: But if the soul is non-different from Brahman, then why does the scripture speak of its bondage and liberation? If they are one, there can be no distinction between the bound and the liberated. [The Sūtrakāra replies: This objection is resolved by the fact that the distinctions of bondage and liberation are merely apparent, arising from the limiting adjuncts. When the adjuncts are present, the soul appears to be bound; when they are removed through knowledge, it appears to be liberated. The reality remains one. As the scripture says: "Thou art That. Therefore, the designation of saṃsāra is consistent with the non-difference of the individual soul from Brahman. END BsCom_4,2.5.8 5 saṃsāravyapadeśa adhikaraṇam // sū. 8-11
"Until then [there is] the designation of transmigratory existence. (BBs 4.2.8) Regarding the passage,
"The light [merges] into the highest deity" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.6),

by the force of the context, that aforementioned light— along with the presiding overseer, along with the vital breath, along with the aggregate of the senses, and accompanied by the other elements— [merges] into the highest deity for the person who is departing.
"It is accomplished"—this is what has been stated. Now, it is considered what kind of accomplishment this might be.
In that regard, it follows first of all that it must be the absolute dissolution of its own nature.

Because that [state] is established as the primordial nature (*prakṛti*). For it has been established that the supreme deity is the primordial nature of the entire multitude of things subject to birth;
therefore, this attainment of non-distinction is absolute.

This being the case, we reply: that subtle element consisting of fire and the other elements, which serves as the substratum for the instruments such as the ear, persists until final dissolution—that is, until liberation from saṃsāra through the cause of perfect knowledge. As it is said: "Some embodied beings enter a womb for the sake of a body;
others go toward a stationary object, according to their karma and according to their learning" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.7).
This is because of such designations as "saṃsāra" (wandering).
For otherwise, everyone would attain absolute union with Brahman at the very moment of death due to the cessation of limiting adjuncts;
in that case, both the scripture of injunctions and the scripture of knowledge would be rendered purposeless.
Furthermore, bondage, which is caused by false knowledge, cannot be loosened without right knowledge.
Therefore, even though it has [prakṛti] as its material cause, this merging remains in the state of a seed, like deep sleep or cosmic dissolution. Thus ends the eighth [section].
"Until then" (tadāpīteḥ).

Having explained the remainder of the previously cited passage concerning departure, he states a doubt—arising because dissolution is seen to occur in both ways regarding whether the five elements, which serve as the substratum for the subtle body (liṅga), undergo absolute dissolution in Brahman or non-absolute dissolution: "But of what nature is this [dissolution]?"

The connection [of this section] arises from the objection that what was stated previously—that immortality is relative—is incorrect. The distinction is as follows: in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), liberation is established for one who has merely died;

however, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is established through the authority of the scriptures on ritual action (*karma*) and knowledge (*vidyā*) that dissolution is with remainder (*sāvaśeṣalaya*). //8//
And that fire, accompanied by the other elements, must be subtle both in its essential nature and in its dimension, serving as the substratum for the living being departing from this body.
For its subtlety is perceived from such [scriptural] indications as the departure through the channels;
therein, because of its thinness, movement is possible.
And because of its translucence, its non-obstruction is established;
for this very reason, it is not perceived by those standing nearby as it emerges from the body. // 9 //

Now, one might ask: how can light, which consists of *liṅga* (the subtle body), pass through the extremely subtle channels? Why is there no obstruction by any material object? And why is it not perceived? To this, he says: "Subtle" (*sūkṣmam*).
"Not by destruction" (BBs 4.2.10).
Precisely because of its subtlety, the other subtle body does not arise through the destruction of this gross body by means of burning or similar causes. // 10 //

The meaning is that because of the subtlety of its dimension, there is no perception of its movement; and because of its transparency—defined by the possession of unmanifest touch and color—there is no perception of its resistance. //10//
And from this very same reasoning, there is warmth. (BBs 4.2.11)
And this heat belongs to this very subtle body, which they perceive as warmth through touch within this physical body.

For indeed, in the state of death, although the body remains and its qualities such as form and so forth persist, no heat is perceived; whereas it is perceived only during the state of life. Therefore, heat is not among the qualities of the body.
However, it is perceived only in the state of being alive; therefore, it is established that this heat has its basis solely in something distinct from the well-known body.
And thus says the Śruti: "He who is warm shall live; he who is cold shall die. // 11 //
And regarding the existence of the probans (*liṅga*), he states the inference characterized by the probans of heat (*auṣṇya-liṅgaka*): "And of this very [fire]... (sūtra 11).
END BsCom_4,2.6.11 START BsCom_4,2.6.12 6.
The Section on Prohibition (Pratiṣedha-adhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 12–14.
If it be argued that [there is no departure] because of a prohibition, we say no, because of the [mention of] the embodied self.
From the qualification, "and immortality without having burned away [the body]," it is accepted that in the case of absolute immortality, there is an absence of both movement and departure.
Even there, however, having raised the suspicion of departure for some reason, the text prohibits it: "Now, he who is without desire, who is free from desire... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6).
"If he is free from desire, having attained all desires and desiring only the Self, his vital breaths do not depart; being Brahman, he merges into Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6).
