If it is argued that, because of this prohibition concerning the subject of higher knowledge (paravidyā), there is no departure of the vital breaths from the body for one who knows the supreme Brahman, we reply: "No. [This is followed by the refutation: For it is stated: "But as to those who depart, departing with the light, the day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the sun's northern course, they reach the Brahma-world" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.5); and "He, however, who departs through this [northern] door, attains immortality" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.6). Furthermore, the text "His vital breaths do not depart" must be understood as referring to the knower of the lower Brahman (aparabrahmavid), since the context concerns the meditation on the person within the eye (cakṣuṣ-puruṣa). Moreover, the statement "Being Brahman, he merges into Brahman" is intended to show that for him there is no further rebirth, not that there is no departure of the vital breaths. Therefore, the vital breaths of the knower of the supreme Brahman do indeed depart. However, upon reaching the world of Brahman, they do not return again to this mortal world. Thus, there is a distinction between the two cases. This is the conclusion.
For this prohibition of the departure of the vital breaths (prāṇas) refers to the embodied self (śārīra ātmā), not to the body.
How is this known? From the use of the ablative case in another recension: "From him the prāṇas do not depart.
Indeed, the genitive case, which denotes a general relationship, is restricted to a specific relationship by the ablative case found in that other recension.

And because of its predominance, by the word "therefore," it is the embodied soul (dehin) who is entitled to both worldly prosperity and the supreme good that is connected [with the departure], not the body. No; the meaning is that from the living self (jīva) which desires to depart, the vital breaths (prāṇas) depart along with it. // 12 //
If it be argued that [the soul's departure] is denied, we say no, because [this denial refers only to the soul] as embodied.

By the phrase "without having burned away" in the preceding section, the absence of departure and so forth for one who possesses knowledge of the attributeless (nirguṇa) and whose afflictions are entirely consumed was indicated. Since this point is raised here as an objection and then resolved, its connection with the distant [preceding topic] is established; thus he says: "And immortality... and so on.

The word "atha" (now) serves to introduce the section on liberation for one who is free from desire, following the description of *saṃsāra* for one who possesses desire. Because he desires the Self—meaning because he knows the Self as full bliss—he is one whose desires are fulfilled (*āptakāma*), having attained supreme bliss;
therefore, he is free from desire (*niṣkāma*), being devoid of internal latent impressions (*vāsanā*) in the form of unmanifested desire;
and thus, he is without desire (*akāma*), being free from manifest external desire.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "of such a one who was desireless.

Since there is doubt—arising from the fifth and sixth [chapter] Śruti texts—as to whether or not there is departure (*utkrānti*) for the knower (*jñānin*), the author sets forth the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) after first refuting the doubts of the proponent of the final conclusion (*siddhāntin*), beginning with the words "No" (*na*). //12//
And for one who departs while still possessing vital breath, there is an "exit" from the body. This being the position reached, it is replied:
For it is clear to some:
It is not the case that what was said—that even for one who knows the supreme Brahman there is an exit from the body because the prohibition of exit has the body as its basis—is correct.
For the prohibition of exit is clearly perceived by some reciters as having the body alone as its basis.

For instance, in the question of Ārtabhāga—"When this person dies, do the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) depart from him, or not? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.11)—Yājñavalkya, having adopted the position that they do not depart, saying "No," [the opponent objects]: "In that case, he does not die while the vital breaths have not departed. To this [objection, Yājñavalkya replies]:...

In response to this doubt, having first asserted the dissolution of the vital breaths in the passage, "Right here they are merged," the text— in order to establish that— declares for the very subject under discussion, which is referred to by the word "he" and serves as the point of departure from transmigration, the processes of swelling and so forth in the words: "He swells, he is inflated, and dead he lies" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.11).
And these [attributes] belong to the body, not to the embodied soul.

Because of that similarity, in the passage "The vital breaths do not depart from there; they are merged right here," the prohibition of departure likewise refers only to departure having the body as its point of origin, by means of a figurative identification.
Even if it were to be explained that "the embodied one" (*dehin*) is the primary referent for those who read the genitive case (*pañcamī*),

for those who read the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), the departure (*utkrānti*) belonging to the wise person is what is prohibited; thus, since this passage has the purpose of prohibiting departure, that departure is prohibited only with respect to the body as its substratum.

"The departure from the body has been established, but not for the embodied soul [who knows]. Moreover, after showing in detail—referring to the subject of the ignorant—the departure and the journey through transmigratory existence with the words: "As he departs, whether from the eye, or from the head, or from other parts of the body, the vital breath (prāṇa) departs after him; as the vital breath departs, all the vital breaths depart after it" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad), [the text continues]: "Thus indeed is he who desires" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6)."

Having thus concluded the discourse concerning the ignorant with the words, "Now, as for the one who does not desire" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6), if it were the case that even in the context of the knower, departure [from the body] had already been attained, then this designation would indeed be inconsistent.

Therefore, the departure and the exit [of the breaths] which apply to the case of the ignorant must be understood as being negated in the case of the knower; only in this way can the purpose of the designation be rendered meaningful.

Furthermore, for the knower of Brahman—who has become the all-pervading Self of Brahman and whose desires and karma have been exhausted—neither departure nor movement is possible due to the absence of a cause.
Scriptural passages such as "here he attains Brahman" likewise indicate the non-existence of both movement and departure. (13)
And it is also recorded in tradition;

furthermore, the absence of both a destination and a departure is recorded in the *Mahābhārata*: "Even the gods are bewildered regarding the path of one who has become the self of all beings, who perceives all beings correctly, and who is trackless while seekers look for his tracks."

Is it not recorded in the Smṛti that for one who knows Brahman—who has become the Self of Brahman which is omnipresent—there is "going"? For instance, it is said that Śuka, the son of Vyāsa, desiring liberation, set out toward the solar orb; and having been followed by his father and called out, he responded, "Bho! No;
this should be understood as the casting off of the body by one who was still embodied, preceded by the attainment of a specific location through the power of yoga.
This is because of the mention of being visible to all beings and so forth;
for indeed, all beings would not be able to see one who is bodiless while moving.
And thus it is concluded in that very same place: "But Śuka, having attained a swift motion through the power of the wind, traveled through the intermediate space."
"Having displayed his own power, he became one who has gone to all beings.
Therefore, for the knower of the Supreme Brahman, there is no departure [of the soul] nor any destination at death.
As for the subject matter of the scriptural texts concerning "going," we shall explain them later. // 14 //

In the *Kāṇva* recension, the pronoun "his" (*tasya*) refers back to the aforementioned knower, expressing a general relationship; however, in the *Mādhyandina* branch, the ablative case "from him" (*tasmāt*) expresses a specific relationship—that of departure. Thus, it appears that the negation of the departure of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) is from the individual soul (*jīva*), not from the body, since the word for the body is not mentioned by that pronoun. Consequently, the result of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there is indeed a departure even for the knower, which renders knowledge useless.
In the Siddhānta, he states its purpose with the words "For it is clear" (*spaṣṭo hi*).

Here, the body alone, which is denoted by the word *puruṣa*, is stated to be the limit of departure (*utkrānti*); the meaning is that the *puruṣa* under discussion—referred to by the word "that" (*sa*) and characterized by qualities such as swelling—is incapable of being the living soul (*jīva*).
It "swells" (*ucchvayati*) because it expands due to being filled with external air; it "inflates" (*ādhmāyati*), meaning it makes a sound like a moist drum.

For those who read the fifth case (*pañcamī*), although the embodied soul (*dehin*) is the primary subject, nevertheless, because of the non-difference between the body and the embodied soul, the word "from that" (*tasmāt*) refers back to the body; thus, the prohibition of departure (*utkrānti*) applies precisely to the bringing about of that [state] of the body.
It should be explained [as follows]:
the construction is that because this recension has the same meaning as the scriptural statement spoken in reference to that generality.
Now, he states the conformity with the Kāṇva recension: "But for those whose reading is in the genitive case..."

When there is an expectancy for a specific relation, that which is mentioned in the preceding scripture—namely, the enjoyer of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) and the specific nature of the vital breaths as instruments of enjoyment in the passages "consisting of breath" (*prāṇamaya*) and "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*)—is what must be accepted here.

One should not accept the status of being the point of departure (*apādāna*) found in another branch of the Veda, because it is impossible to negate the departure from the individual soul (*jīva*) when such departure has not yet been established.

Therefore, when there is an expectancy for the point of departure regarding the vital breaths associated with the knower, only those regions of the body already mentioned, such as "from the eye or from the head," are to be accepted.
And thus the meaning is this: for that wise one, the vital breaths (prāṇas), which constitute the instruments of experience, do not depart from the regions of the body.
In this way, it is entirely consistent that the purpose of the sentence is to negate the departure that might otherwise be presumed.
Furthermore, the word "api ca" (moreover) is for the sake of clarity.

For one who perceives all beings as his own self, for the trackless one who is devoid of any goal to be reached, even the gods are bewildered regarding the path; they do not know the path because such a path does not exist—this is the construction of the Smṛti passage.
Anticipating the contradiction with another Smṛti text, he raises the objection: "But is there not also a journey?
He resolves this by stating: "This journey belongs to one who still possesses a body," [meaning it occurs through the power of knowledge associated with qualities].

[Objection: "In that case, what is the status of such scriptural passages as 'Going upwards by that, one attains immortality' and 'He alone leads them to Brahman'? To this, he says: 'The two paths... (13) // (14) //14//
Section on the Dissolution of Speech and the Other [Organs] Sūtra 15:
The Dissolution of Speech and the Others.
Regarding those, it is said by another [author]:
"Furthermore, those elements and senses denoted by the word 'vital breath' (prāṇa) dissolve into that very same Supreme Self for one who knows the Supreme Brahman.
Why?"

For thus says the Śruti: "In this very way, these sixteen parts of this observer, which have the Puruṣa as their goal, reach the Puruṣa and go to their rest" (Praśna Upaniṣad 6.5). Now, one might object: another Śruti, concerning the subject of the knower, states that the dissolution of the parts occurs elsewhere than in the Supreme Self, saying, "The fifteen parts have gone to their respective foundations" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.7). No; [this is not so].
That [dissolution] indeed depends on conventional usage,
according to which the constituent parts such as earth and so forth dissolve back into their own respective primal sources, earth and so forth.
The other, however, depends on the realization of the wise.
For one who knows the Supreme Brahman, the entire collection of parts becomes Brahman itself;
therefore, there is no fault. // 15 //
Regarding those [elements], the other [teacher] says as follows:

Since the dissolution of the subtle parts (kalās) of the knower—namely the sense of smell and so forth—was stated in the preceding section by means of the negation of their respective courses, one must entertain a doubt based on that point, given the observation of two scriptural passages: does he [the knower] dissolve into the respective primordial natures (prakṛtis) of those elements, such as earth and so forth, or rather into the Supreme Self?

In this context, while about to state the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) based on the scriptural statement, "The elements (kalās) have gone," which is supported by the principle that "the modification dissolves directly into its material cause" (prakṛti), he first states the established conclusion (siddhānta): "Those [elements]...

The meaning is as follows: just as rivers dissolve upon reaching the ocean, even so, for one who perceives Brahman everywhere, these elements—beginning with breath and faith—which have the Puruṣa as their goal and are superposed upon the Puruṣa, go to dissolution upon reaching the Puruṣa alone, who is the object of knowledge.
By the unification of the mind (*manas*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), there is the state of fifteen digits (*kalā*).
"Pratiṣṭhā" is the accusative plural.
The meaning is "one's own primordial natures," such as earth and the other elements.

From the standpoint of reality and from the perspective of the wise, even though the Supreme Self is the abode of dissolution (*kalālaya*), the statement regarding dissolution into the *pratiṣṭhās* is not contradictory from the perspective of worldly convention.
Thus, the purport of the two scriptural passages is that the *kalās*, having been dissolved into their own respective primal natures (*prakṛtis*), dissolve into the *puruṣa* along with them. //15//
Topic 8: Non-Differentiation. Sūtra 16.
"Non-distinction [results] from the scriptural statement.
(BBs 4.2.16) Furthermore, regarding this dissolution of the parts for the wise one (*viduṣ*), does it occur with a remainder, as in the case of others, or rather without a remainder?
Since there is a possibility that a potentiality (*śakti*) remains due to the commonality of the term "dissolution," he says: "It is indeed the attainment of non-distinction."
Why? Because of the scriptural statement.
For, after describing the dissolution of the *kalās*, the text says: "Their names and forms are destroyed; he is called simply 'the Person'; he becomes partless and immortal" (Praśna Upaniṣad 6.5).
Furthermore, it is not logical that the *kalās*, which have ignorance as their cause, should remain with a residue when their dissolution is caused by knowledge.
Therefore, it is indeed non-distinct. // 16 //
"Non-differentiation, because of the scriptural statement.
Having relied upon the dissolution (laya) previously mentioned, he states the doubt—arising from the observation that dissolution occurs in two ways—with the words "That, moreover...
The result in both cases is the non-attainment of liberation or the attainment thereof.
Remainder (*avaśeṣa*) is the persistence [of the effect] in its primary cause in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*);
that is to say, it is the fitness for rebirth.
The subject under dispute, the substrate of *kalā*, possesses a remainder.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that [the world] is dissolved [into Brahman] because it is a substrate of parts (*kalālayatvāt*), as in the case of deep sleep (*suṣuptivat*). The author establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) through scripture supported by reasoning: "He says"—that the object of dispute is dissolved without remainder, because it is produced by ignorance (*vidyākṛtatvāt*), just as a snake is dissolved by the rope-ignorance (*rajjvā vidyayā sarpalayavat*).
The meaning is that name-and-form, although consisting of potentiality, are nonetheless distinct. //16//
The Topic of the Abode (tadoka-adhikaraṇa). Sūtra 17.

Then, the flame at the top of the heart blazes up; its door being illuminated by that [flame], [the soul] departs through the hundred-and-first artery, aided by the heart and by the application of mindfulness to the path which is the remainder of that knowledge, through the power of the Vidyā.
The incidental reflection concerning the higher knowledge (paravidyā) is now concluded;
however, he now resumes the reflection specifically concerning the sphere of the lower knowledge (aparavidyā).
It has been stated that the departure of both the knower and the ignorant is the same from the commencement of the ascent; now, he shows that [departure] which begins with the presence of Brahman.

For that self of consciousness (vijñānātman), who desires to depart after having withdrawn the aggregate of speech and the other organs, the heart is the abode (oka) or seat; for the scripture says: "Taking these particles of light (tejomātrāḥ) unto himself, he descends into the heart alone."

The departure [of the self] preceded by the blazing of its tip and having the eyes and other locations as its point of exit is heard in scripture: "At the tip of this very heart it blazes forth; by that light this Self departs, either through the eye, or through the crown of the head, or through other parts of the body" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2).

In response to the doubt— whether this [exit] occurs without any restriction for both the knower and the non-knower, or whether there is some specific restriction for the knower— it is declared that, although the illumination of the tip of the heart and the opening of the door revealed by it are the same for both the knower and the non-knower, the knower departs specifically from the location of the crown of the head.
But from other locations, the others [depart].
Why? Because of the power of knowledge (*vidyā*).
For if even a knower were to depart from just any part of the body like the others, he would not attain the exalted world.
In that case, the knowledge would be purposeless.

Therefore, because of the connection with the recollection of the remaining path, one should practice the movement connected to the central channel (anāḍī) at the crown of the head, which constitutes a remainder of the knowledge and is prescribed for specific types of knowledge; it is logical that by practicing this, one becomes established in that very [knowledge].

Therefore, favored by Brahman well-worshipped in his abode in the heart and having attained that state, the wise man departs by the hundred-and-first artery—that which exceeds the hundred—whereas others depart by the other channels.
For thus, with reference to the knowledge of the Heart (Hārdavidyā), they recite: "There are a hundred and one arteries of the heart; of these, one extends to the crown of the head."
"Going upwards by that [path], one attains immortality; the others depart in various directions by the other route" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.6). // 17 //
Then follows the blazing up of the topmost part.

To explain the commencement of the path of departure—the regulation of entry into the channels—he states the subject matter of the section (*adhikaraṇa*) by way of commenting on a portion of the Sūtra, beginning with "Of that" (*tasya*).
That one who is about to die [consists of] the subtle elements of light (*tejomātrā*), which are the sense organs.
The tip of that heart is the opening of the channel; its "flaming" is the throbbing of the impending fruit, known as the "radiance.

Because of the scriptural statement that there is no fixed rule regarding the eye (*cakṣuṣo vā*), and because of the specific scriptural statement that [the soul] goes upward through those two, a doubt arises: does the meditator also depart through whichever door he pleases, like one who is not a meditator, or only through the channel at the crown of the head (*mūrdhanyanāḍī*)?
In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the excellence produced by knowledge (*vidyā*) would not be established.
The distinction is that its accomplishment occurs according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

When the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—based on the scriptural statement—is reached that there is no fixed rule [regarding the path], as in the case of the "undivided" (*avibhāga*), the author establishes the conclusion with the words "He explains":

even for one who has departed by any path whatsoever, if the attainment of the world of Brahman were to occur, then the injunction to remember the path as a subordinate element of the knowledge (*vidyā*) would result in having a purely transcendental purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*); therefore, it must be by the very path remembered daily that [the goal is reached].
The sense is that going [through the heart] is logical.
"Hārda" refers to the Brahman within the heart.
"Viṣvaṅ" means other various kinds of channels belonging to others.

The channel named Suṣumṇā, having emerged from the heart, reaches the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) by way of the right eye, the palate, the throat, the interior of the neck, the breasts, and the middle of the nose; it becomes unified with the rays of the sun and serves as the path to the world of Brahmā for the practitioner—this is established. //17//
Topic: The Rays. Sūtra 18. The rays [of the sun] are the means of ascent. (Sūtra 18)
"Following the rays":
there is the knowledge of the heart (*hārdavidyā*), which is established beginning with the passage, "Now, that which is within this city of Brahman, a small lotus-palace" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.1).

In that context, having begun with "Now, as for these channels of the heart" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.1) and having explained in detail the connection between the channels and the rays of light, it is stated: "Then, when he departs from this body, he ascends upwards by means of these very rays" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.5).
Furthermore, it is said: "Going upwards by that [path], he attains immortality" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.6).
Therefore, it is understood that departing through the hundred-and-first artery, one departs following the rays.

Now, when a doubt arises as to whether this following of the rays applies without distinction to one dying either by day or by night, or only during the day—since there is scriptural mention without distinction, for the time being, it must apply without distinction.
It is asserted that [the cognition] follows the ray of light. // 18 //
"Following the rays.
Having first purified the context, he states the subject of the disciple following the rays with the words beginning "It exists," and so forth.
The meaning is that when this departure occurs at the end of the prārabdha karma, then one departs by means of these very rays connected to the channels (nāḍīs).
Regarding this, since no specific time for the connection [of the rays] is heard in the scripture and because the rays are absent at night, he states the doubt: "What then?
The connection [of the discussion] is due to the fact that the rays connected with the channels mentioned previously must be relied upon here.
In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is a waiting for sunrise by one who dies at night in order to reach the rays.
Thinking that [the objection] does not exist in the established doctrine (siddhānta), he asserts the established doctrine: "Without distinction" (aviśeṣeṇa) //18//

If it is argued that [the soul] does not go at night, we say no; for the connection [of the soul with its subtle body] persists as long as the body exists, and scripture also demonstrates this. (BS 4.2.19)

If it is argued that because there is a connection between the channels (*nāḍī*) and the rays [of the sun] during the day, one who dies by day would follow the rays, but for a deceased person at night this would not occur due to the severance of the connection between the channels and the rays— [we reply: no,
because the connection between the channels and the rays persists as long as the body exists.
For as long as the body exists, there is indeed contact with the rays through the channels;
and scripture demonstrates this point: "From that sun they spread out and enter into these channels; from these channels they spread out and enter into that sun" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.2).
Furthermore, even during the nights of the summer season, the persistence of the rays is perceived, as evidenced by the observation of effects such as heat.
However, because the persistence [of the rays] is slight, they are difficult to perceive during the nights of other seasons, just as on cloudy days in the winter.
And the statement, "He places this very [light] in the night," demonstrates this very point.
Furthermore, if one who has departed at night were to ascend upwards even without following the rays, then the instruction to follow the rays would be rendered purposeless.
For this is not specifically taught: that he who dies by day ascends upwards depending upon the rays, whereas he who dies at night does so without depending on them.
Moreover, if even a knower were not to ascend upwards merely due to the fault of dying at night, then knowledge would have only an occasional result, and there would be no engagement in it at all;
for the time of death is not fixed.
Moreover, even if he were to die at night, he would await the arrival of day;
for even upon the arrival of day, his body might sometimes be unfit for connection with the rays [of the sun] due to contact with fire or other elements.
As it is said: "He goes to the sun in as much time as it takes to move the mind" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.5).
And thus the Śruti shows that there is no initiation [into the state of being a ray];
therefore, this following of the rays day and night applies without distinction. 19.
Having set forth the seed of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), he refutes it with the words beginning "niśi" (at night).
"Śirāḥ" refers to the channels (*nāḍyaḥ*); they are "pratāyante," meaning they expand or become widespread; "sṛptāḥ" means interconnected.
He provides the reasoning for the existence of the connection mentioned in the scripture during the night with the word "nidāgha" (in the heat of summer).
In that case, one might argue that heat would be perceived during the nights of winter and so forth; to this he says: "slight" (*stoka*).
The statement that "the sun bestows day even during the night" is intended to mean only the persistence of a few rays.

Furthermore, if one who dies at night were to attain the upward path even without contact with the rays, then the scriptural mention of the rays would have to be restricted to those who die during the day; and if there were no upward path [at all], there would be no engagement in the pursuit of knowledge (*vidyā*).
It might be argued that there is no waiting for the upward journey; however, this cannot be said,

because if the body were consumed by fire before the emergence of the rays, it would follow that waiting for the sun is futile, and furthermore, it would contradict the scriptural text concerning the absence of waiting.
Therefore, whenever one has died, there is an immediate attainment of the world of Brahman through reaching the rays. //19//

Section on the Southern Solstice (Dakṣiṇāyana-adhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 20–21 11. [The section concerning] the southern course of the sun. Sūtra 20: [The deceased] departs during the southern solstice. Sūtra 21: [This is so] because of the scriptural statement regarding the path of the fathers.

And for this reason, [the fruit is attained] even during the southern course. Because waiting is not possible, because the fruit of knowledge is non-exclusive, and because death is not restricted to a specific time, the wise man attains the fruit of knowledge even when dying during the southern course. This is because there is no established excellence in dying during the northern course, and because we observe Bhīṣma’s waiting [for the right time], as stated in Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.5: "From the bright fortnight, he goes to those six months during which the sun moves northward."

And with this sūtra, he dispels the doubt raised by the scriptural passage, "The northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa) is to be awaited," [by showing that] the well-known praise [of the northern solstice] refers to those who lack knowledge;
as for Bhīṣma's waiting, it was for the purpose of maintaining proper conduct and for the purpose of demonstrating that he possessed the power of voluntary death obtained through his father's grace.
But the meaning of the scripture will be stated [later] in the sūtra: "The [deities] are conductors, because of the indicative mark thereof" (Brahma-sūtra 4.3.4). // 20 //

Thus, regarding the doubt as to whether a wise person who dies during the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana) attains the fruit of knowledge or not—given that the scripture declares the fruit of knowledge as constant and there are scriptural passages praising the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa)—the author extends the previously stated reasons [to this case]: "And therefore, even in the southern solstice... Having raised the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), he refutes it with the words beginning "nor by the northern solstice," and so forth.

If the death of the ignorant occurs during the northern course (uttarāyaṇa) by chance, it is praiseworthy; Bhīṣma’s waiting was for the purpose of maintaining the established custom consisting of the words of those who possess higher knowledge.
As for the Vedic statement regarding "six months," it will be explained that it refers to the deities presiding over the northern course.
Thus, since the deity is ever-present, there is no contradiction in attaining that [state] through knowledge even during the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana); this is the intended meaning. //20//

"Those who depart go to that fruit; I shall declare it, O bull of the Bharatas" (Gītā 8.23). Having thus commenced with an emphasis on time, specific times such as the day and so forth are prescribed in the Smṛti for the sake of non-return. How then could one who departs at night or during the southern solstice attain non-return? To this it is replied:
And these two are recorded in Smṛti for the sake of yogins; and these two, Yoga and Sāṃkhya, are based on Smṛti, not on Śruti.
Furthermore, this application of time beginning with the day is recorded in Smṛti for the sake of yogins as leading to non-return.
And these two, Yoga and Sāṃkhya, are based on Smṛti, not on Śruti.

Therefore, due to the difference in subject matter and because it is not a distinct means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), this application of time belonging to the Smṛti has no application to the Śruti-based cognitions.
Now, [one might object]: "Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, and the six months of the northern course;
smoke, night, likewise the dark fortnight, and the six months of the southern course" (Gītā 8.24, 25).
Thus, these two paths—the path of the gods and the path of the ancestors—are recognized as being mentioned in the Śruti as well as in the Smṛti.
It is replied: since the Smṛti makes a promise regarding time in the words, "I shall declare that time" (Gītā 8.23), an objection based on contradiction was raised and then resolved.
But when, even in the case of Smṛti, the deities such as Agni and others are understood to be the conducting deities (ativāhikyaḥ), then there is no contradiction whatsoever. // 21 //
He raises an objection regarding the predominance of time by saying, "But surely...

He states that there is no contradiction by saying, "The yogins," meaning that while we have stated that those who meditate on the *dahara* (the small ether) and so forth as taught in the Śruti do not depend on time, the dependence on time for practitioners of yoga according to the Smṛti is indeed mentioned in the Smṛti.

One might ask: why could the yogi not be the very same person who worships the "small" [space] and so forth as taught in the Smṛti? To this he says: "And that which is taught in the Smṛti. Action performed with the intention of propitiating the Blessed Lord is Yoga, according to the Smṛti: "He who performs the duty that must be done without depending on the fruit of action—he is both a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) and a yogi."
The experience of non-agency preceded by *dhāraṇā* (steadfast concentration) is Sāṃkhya, according to the Smṛti: "Holding [the thought] that 'the senses operate upon the objects of the senses'.

One might object: "Is it not improper for the Śruti and Smṛti to have different meanings, as this would contradict recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)? Thus he raises the doubt with the words: "But [it is like] fire... and so on.
It was stated that there is a difference in meaning regarding the one who seizes [the time] at the end of the day.
However, if the word "time" (kāla) refers to the deity by means of the recognition of the Vedic sense, then there is indeed identity of meaning; this is the purpose of the resolution.
Therefore, it is established that through the power of the knowledge (vidyā), the practitioner who has departed for the highest state (diṣṭa) attains the fruit at all times. //21//

Thus ends the second quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā*, a commentary on the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsā* composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Govindānanda.

The Third Quarter of the Fourth Chapter.
START BsCom_4,3.1.1: The third quarter (pāda) of the fourth chapter (adhyāya).
In this quarter, the northern path for one who possesses knowledge of the qualified Brahman (saguṇavidyā) after death is described.
1. The Section on the Path Beginning with Light (Arcirādy-adhikaraṇa).
Sūtra 1: [The soul proceeds] by way of light and so forth, because that is well-known.
It has been stated that the departure is the same for all until the commencement of the journey.
The path, however, is heard of in various ways in different Vedic texts.
In one way, it is described through the connection of the channels (*nāḍī*) and rays (*raśmi*), as in: "Then, by these very rays, he ascends upwards" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.5).
In another way, it begins with light (*arcis*), as in: "They reach the light; from the light, they go to the day" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.15).
"Having reached this path of the gods, he comes to the world of Agni" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 1.3);

"When a person departs from this world, he comes to Vāyu" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.10.1); and "Free from passion, they depart through the gate of the sun" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.11). These are other [scriptural passages].
And there is another [passage] as well.
Regarding this, a doubt arises: are these paths mutually distinct, or is it rather one single path with multiple qualifications?
On this point, the initial position is that these paths are indeed distinct.

Because they belong to different contexts, and because they are distinct insofar as they are subordinate to different meditations (*upāsanā*). Moreover, [it says]: "Now, by these very rays... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.5).

Thus, the restriction [implied by the word "only"] would be contradicted if there were dependence on the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*), and the statement regarding speed— "As quickly as one might direct the mind, so quickly he goes to the sun" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.5)— would also be undermined. Therefore, these paths are indeed distinct from one another.
This being the case, we reply: "By the way beginning with light. We maintain that every seeker of Brahman proceeds by the very path beginning with light.
Why? Because of its renown. For this path is well-known to all the wise.

For instance, in the section concerning the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*), the scripture declares that even for those devoted to other forms of knowledge— namely, "those who, in the forest, worship faith as the truth" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.15)—
the path beginning with light (*arcirādi*) is taught. This might be so.

Regarding those Vidyās in which no specific path is mentioned, let this path beginning with light (arcir-ādi) apply; but as for those in which another path is heard, why should the path beginning with light be adopted?
To this it is replied: This would indeed be so if these paths were absolutely distinct.
However, we maintain that there is only one single path leading to the world of Brahman (brahmaloka), which possesses many attributes and is characterized in various places by different attributes.
Because there is recognition of a single part everywhere, the relationship of mutual qualifier and qualified is established.
For even when there is a difference in context, if the knowledge (*vidyā*) is one, there is a combination of the qualifiers of the path, just as there is a combination of mutual qualifiers;
likewise, even if the knowledge differs, because there is recognition of a single part of the path and because the destination is non-different, the path itself is indeed non-different.

For thus it is said: "In those worlds of Brahman they dwell, supreme beyond the supreme" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.15); "In that [world] they dwell for eternal years" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.10.1);
"Whatever victory and whatever splendor belong to Brahman, that victory he wins, that splendor he attains" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 1.4).

Furthermore, in various places such as Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.4.3, "Those who find this world of Brahman through celibacy," that very same single fruit characterized by the attainment of the world of Brahman is demonstrated.
As for the restriction "by these alone," it would not apply if one were to rely on the path beginning with light (arcirādi).
This is not a fault,
because this [passage] has the reaching of rays as its primary purpose;
for a single word cannot both cause one to reach the rays and exclude the *arciḥ* (flames) and so forth.
Therefore, it should be understood that this [process] is determined to be simply a connection with the rays.

However, the mention of speed is not contradicted even when there is a dependence on the path beginning with light (*arcis*), because its purpose is to indicate swiftness in relation to other destinations to be reached,
just as one might say, "He arrives here in the mere twinkling of an eye."

Moreover, by stating that those who have fallen away from either of these two paths have a "terrible third place" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 5.10.8), the text proclaims a single Devayāna path— distinct from the Pitṛyāṇa— consisting of the stages beginning with light (*arcis*). Furthermore,
the stages of the path in the sequence beginning with light are numerous, whereas they are few elsewhere.

Furthermore, it is logical that the few should be led in accordance with the many; for this reason also, it has been stated that "it is well-known through the path beginning with light" (*arcirādi*). // 1 //

Having thus described the departure (utkrānti), he begins the [fourth] quarter to describe the path to be traversed and the goal to be reached: "By the path beginning with light, because that is well-known" (sūtra 4.3.1).
Stating the subject matter of the first section (adhikaraṇa) by way of a summary of what has preceded, he describes the path: "As far as the world of Brahman" (sūtra 4.3.7).
"Viraja" means free from passion; that is to say, devoid of sin.
Doubt arises from the conflicting nature of the scriptural texts.

The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) holds that since it was previously stated that even one who has died at some time may obtain the fruit, there is an option (vikalpa) that the departure occurs by any path whatsoever;
whereas the established conclusion (siddhānta) distinguishes that there is a single uniform path.
Due to the difference in modes of worship (*upāsanā*), there is a difference in the paths (*mārga*) to be meditated upon as subordinate to them,
as indicated by the word "only" (*eva*). Furthermore,
the meaning is that since there is a plurality of paths, it is logical that this particular path leads to the goal with speed, which would not be the case if there were only one single path.

He establishes the final conclusion—that although there is a difference in the modes of worship (*upāsanā*), there is no contradiction in the unity of the path, just as there is unity in the Brahman that is worshipped—by the word "evam" (thus).
The meaning of the reason is "because that path is well-known.

He raises the objection regarding a difference in paths by means of the phrase "ye ca" (and those who), suggesting that the scriptural statement without qualification refers to the knowledge of those whose departure [from the body] has not been mentioned. This is expressed as: "It might be thus."

The meaning of the resolution is that since it is stated that there are many qualifiers, such as "fire" and so forth, for one and the same path, there is no difference in the path due to parsimony (*lāghava*), and because of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*). He explains the unity of the destination with the words "For thus... (*tathā hi*).

The meaning is that they dwell for "distant" [periods], meaning long-lived; for "long" years, meaning many *saṃvatsaras*, in the presence of Hiraṇyagarbha; and they obtain "conquest," which is victory everywhere, and "manifestation," which is pervasion—this is the sense.

Thus, since the identity of the path is determined through recognition (pratyabhijñā) based on the identity of the destination, it has been stated that the difference in context (*prakaraṇabheda*) is irrelevant. Now, he explains the function of the particle *eva* ("only") and the word expressing speed (*tvarā*), beginning with the words "As for what... (*yattu*).

Because there is an absence of distinct rays at night, the word "only" (eva) is used to exclude the possibility that even a knower might fail to attain union with the rays; it does not serve to exclude others [from the path].
The meaning is that just as there is delay on the worldly path, there is none on the path beginning with light (arcis), and thus the statement regarding speed is appropriate.
He states an indicative mark for the unity of the path: "Moreover" (api ca).

The sense is that if there were a multiplicity of auspicious paths, there would be no mention of "the third station. Even though the subsequent path is one, as to why the qualification "by the path of light, etc. (arcirādi) is used, he says: "Because they are many" (bhūyāṃsi). //1//

[Objection: But how can this be reconciled with the statement that the soul goes to light? [Reply: That statement refers to the case where the soul departs through the head, as the scripture says: "Those who depart through the head go to light" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.5). "From the year [he goes] to air by means of both the non-specific and the specific.
But by what distinction of arrangement do these various stages of motion stand in a relationship of mutual qualifier and qualified? Being a friend, the Teacher strings them together for us:

"Having entered upon this path of the gods, he comes to the world of fire, then to the world of air, then to the world of Indra, then to the world of Prajāpati, and then to the world of Brahman" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 1.3).
Thus, the path of the gods (devayāna) is recited among the Kauṣītakins.

In that context, since the terms *arcis* and *agniloka* have the same meaning—both denoting "flame"—no sequence of their arrangement needs to be sought here. However, as for *vāyu*, it is not mentioned on the path beginning with *arcis*; at what point, then, should it be inserted?

It is said: "They go to the light itself; from the light to the day; from the day to the waxing fortnight; from the waxing fortnight to those six months when the sun moves northward; from the months to the year; from the year to the sun.
(Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.1, 2).
Here, they go to Vāyu, who is beyond the year and prior to the sun.
Why?
Because of both non-distinction and distinction.
For it is said: "He [goes] to the world of Vāyu" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 1.3).

Thus, regarding the wind taught here without specification, a specific teaching is seen in another scriptural passage: "When a person departs from this world, he goes to the wind; for him, the wind parts there as the hole of a chariot wheel, and through that he ascends upwards; he reaches the sun" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.10.1).
Because of this specific distinction—the observation that Vāyu comes before Āditya—Vāyu must be placed in the interval between the year (abda) and Āditya.
But why, on account of the specific distinction that he is observed to come after Agni, is Vāyu not placed immediately after Arcis?
We reply that there is no such distinction here.
But has not the Śruti been cited: "Having entered upon this path of the gods, he goes to the world of Agni, then to the world of Vāyu, then to the world of Varuṇa" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 1.3)?
It is replied: here there is merely a sequential arrangement of the reading; there is no word here that expresses a sequence [of stages].

For here, there is merely the pointing out of the objects: "He comes to this and that"; whereas in the other case, the sequence is understood as: "Having ascended upwards through an opening the size of a chariot wheel provided by Vāyu, he reaches the sun.
Therefore, it is well said: "By way of the general and the particular."
The Vājasaneyins, however, record: "From the months to the world of the gods, from the world of the gods to the sun" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.15).
In that case, before reaching the sun, they would attain Vāyu from the world of the gods.
The statement "from the year to the air" is made with reference to the Chāndogya Śruti.

However, in the Chāndogya and Vājasaneyaka [Upaniṣads], the world of the gods (devaloka) is not found in one place, while the year is not found in the other. Therefore, based on the authority of both Śrutis, both [stages] must be combined in both places.
In that case as well, because of the connection with the month, it should be distinguished that the year comes first and the world of the gods comes later. // 2 //
Having stated that the unity of the path is presupposed, he now explains the sequence of stages (*parvakrama*).

Having stated the purport of the section—that the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified is expressed by the sequence "from this [fire], this [wind] is next among those beginning with light" (*arcirādi*)—he states the subject matter (*viṣaya*) with the words "He reaches this...
(*sa etam*). Here, the subject matter is the wind, which is mentioned immediately after fire.

Regarding the doubt—whether he [the soul] goes immediately after the fire consisting of light or after the year—due to the textual sequence and the specific details about to be mentioned, the author begins with the established conclusion: "It is said. The meaning of the scripture is as follows:

the person, that is, the worshiper, departs from this world, that is, from the body; for that person who has departed, that wind (vāyu) relaxes within itself—that is, it creates an opening—and through that door provided by the wind, which is like the hole of a chariot wheel, he goes upward to the sun.
Now he states the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa): "But why [is it so]?
The meaning is that, by the force of the textual reading, air follows immediately after light;
this is merely the reading of the Kauṣītakins.
There is no word whatsoever that expresses a specific sequence;

however, for the Kāṇvas, because the sequence is determined by the two words "tena" (by that) and "ūrdhvam" (upwards), there is a sublation of the textual order—this is the meaning of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Let it be that in the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*) found in the Chāndogya, Vāyu follows after the year (*abdāt*) due to the mention of the year.

But since the word "year" (saṃvatsara) is not heard in the passage concerning the "Vājins," how can it be said that Vāyu is beyond the year? To this he says: "The word 'Vāja' [is used]. If that were so, the Sūtra would have been "from the world of the gods to Vāyu"; to this he says: "But [the Sūtra says] 'from the year to Vāyu'.

Since the year has months as its constituent parts, there is immediate succession from the month; thus, the sequence established by the two scriptural passages is: the world of the gods is beyond the year, Vāyu is beyond that, and Āditya is beyond Vāyu.
The word "tena" (by that) indicates, through the direct hearing of the instrumental case, that Vāyu is preceded by Āditya;
however, it is established that in the Sūtra, the term "Vāyu" refers to the Vāyu who is preceded by the world of the gods. //2//

Varuṇa is superior to lightning because of their connection; for it is said,
"From the sun to the moon, from the moon to lightning" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.5),
and since it is stated that "beyond this lightning is the world of Varuṇa," this Varuṇa is thus connected [to the path].
For there is indeed a connection between lightning and Varuṇa.
When vast, intense flashes of lightning with thundering sounds dance within the bellies of the clouds, then the waters fall.
"It lightens, it thunders, or it will rain" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.11.1).
And so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Furthermore, it is well known from the Śruti and Smṛti that Varuṇa is the lord of the waters.
Indra and Prajāpati follow Varuṇa because there is no other place for them and due to the force of their position in the text.
Because Varuṇa and the others have no further destination, their placement is indeed at the end, as there is no specific place for them; and lightning is at the end of the path beginning with light.

Having thus stated the position of Vāyu, who is recited by the Kauṣītakins immediately after Agni, he now states the position of Varuṇa, who is recited after Vāyu, within the path beginning with light (*arcis*). Regarding the doubt as to whether Varuṇa and the others, who are recited [in the text], are connected as stages of the path or not—[the answer is] "Varuṇa is above lightning," because of their connection. This is because the sequence beginning with light and ending with Varuṇa is connected as stages of the path by means of the ablative case in "from light to day" (*arciṣo 'har*), and so forth.

Since Varuṇa and the others have no specific location mentioned for them—unlike wind, which is bound by the sequence of the path and the mountains—they do not connect [with the stages] as they have not obtained a location; this being the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), the author states the established conclusion (siddhānta): "From the sun.
He provides the proof for the connection of water with lightning on the grounds that it is an effect of lightning: "It lightens."

The meaning is that because Varuṇa is connected to lightning through the medium of the waters, and according to the maxim "that which is adventitious is placed at the end," Indra and Prajāpati follow immediately after lightning; thus, their sequence is as stated in the text. //3//

Topic 4: The Conveying Deity (Ātivāhika Adhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 4–6. END BsCom_4,3.3.3 START BsCom_4,3.4.4 4 ātivāhika adhikaraṇam / sū. 4-6The term *ātivāhika* refers to the deities who convey the soul along the path of the gods (*devayāna*). Regarding this, the following doubt arises: Do these deities merely assist the soul by way of providing instruction and the like, or do they actually carry it? On this point, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Since the word "conveying" (*vaha*) is used in the sense of carrying, and since there is no distinction made between the two meanings of "carrying"—namely, carrying on one's own shoulders versus carrying by means of an instrument—it is understood that the deities themselves carry the soul. This is because the scripture states, "Light leads him," and so forth. To this, we reply: It is not so. For the word *ātivāhika* is derived from the root *vah* preceded by the prefix *ati*, and it denotes those who convey beyond [the limits of the world]. Furthermore, the suffix *-ika* here signifies "belonging to" (*tadadhīna*), meaning "those who are dependent upon them. Therefore, the deities are called *ātivāhika* because they convey the souls belonging to them—that is, those who have attained the state of being fit for the path—along the path of the gods. Moreover, the word *ātivāhika* is well-known in common usage to mean "one who conveys beyond"; for example, when it is said, "He is the *ātivāhika* of this caravan. Thus, the deities are *ātivāhikas* because they convey the souls beyond [the worlds] by way of their own specific functions. Furthermore, the statement "Light leads him" (*jyotir evainam upanayati*) does not mean that light carries him; rather, it means that light leads him to the deities of wind and the rest. For it is observed in common usage that the act of leading (*upanayana*) is distinct from the act of carrying (*vahana*). Therefore, the deities do not carry the soul; rather, they lead it. This is established. [End of Topic 4] Topic 5: The Nature of the Path (Arcir-ādi Adhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 7–14. Now, the following doubt arises: Are the deities such as Light (*jyotis*) and the rest the very nature of the path itself, or are they merely the leaders of the path? On this point, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Since the word "path" (*adhvan*) is used in the neuter gender, and since the deities are feminine, it is understood that the deities are not the path itself. Furthermore, the scripture speaks of the path as consisting of light, smoke, and so forth, whereas it speaks of the deities as Agni, Vāyu, and so forth. Therefore, the deities are merely the leaders of the path. To this, we reply: The deities are indeed the path. Why? Because they are designated as such. For the scripture designates the deities as the path: "By this path, those who know Brahman go to the sun" (*etena pratipadyamānā imaṃ mānavam avartam nāvartante*), and "They reach the world of Agni" (*te 'rciṣam abhisambhavanti... agnilokam*). Moreover, the word "path" is used in the masculine gender in other passages, such as "the northern path" (*udag adhvānaḥ*). Furthermore, the designation of the deities as the path is logical, because they are the ones who convey the souls along the path. And the fact that the deities are feminine does not contradict their being the path, because the word "path" is also used in the feminine gender in the phrase "the southern path" (*dakṣiṇaḥ panthāḥ*). Therefore, the deities are the path itself. [End of Topic 5] Topic 6: The Lightning Deity (Vaidyuta Adhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 15. Now, the following doubt arises: Does the soul proceed from the deity of lightning to the world of Varuṇa immediately after leaving the deity of lightning, or does it wait for the command of the deity of lightning before proceeding? On this point, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Since the scripture says, "From there, they reach the world of Varuṇa" (*ato vai khalu durniṣprapataram*), it implies that the soul proceeds immediately after reaching the deity of lightning. To this, we reply: It is not so. For the scripture states, "When he reaches the deity of lightning, the deity of lightning, having recognized him, leads him to the worlds of Varuṇa" (*sa etaṃ devayānaṃ panthānam āpadyāgnilokam āgacchati... sa vāyulokam āgacchati... sa varuṇalokam āgacchati*). Here, the use of the locative case (*varuṇaloke*) indicates that the soul waits for the command of the deity of lightning before proceeding to the world of Varuṇa. Moreover, the deity of lightning is a female deity, and it is logical that she should wait for the command of her husband, the deity of Varuṇa, before leading the soul further. Therefore, the soul proceeds to the world of Varuṇa only after receiving the command of the deity of lightning. [End of Topic 6] Topic 7: The World of Varuṇa (Vāruṇa Adhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 16. Now, the following doubt arises: Does the soul proceed from the world of Varuṇa directly to the world of Indra, or does it proceed through the world of Prajāpati? On this point, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Since the scripture mentions the world of Indra immediately after the world of Varuṇa, it is understood that the soul proceeds directly from the world of Varuṇa to the world of Indra. To this, we reply: It is not so. For the scripture mentions the world of Prajāpati between the world of Varuṇa and the world of Indra: "From there, they reach the world of Prajāpati" (*te prajāpatilokam āgacchanti*). Therefore, the soul proceeds from the world of Varuṇa to the world of Prajāpati, and from the world of Prajāpati to the world of Indra. [End of Topic 7] Topic 8: The World of Prajāpati (Prajāpati Adhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 17. Now, the following doubt arises: Does the soul proceed from the world of Prajāpati to the world of Brahmā, or does it proceed to the world of Hiraṇyagarbha? On this point, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Since the scripture uses the term "world of Brahmā" (*brahmaloka*), it is understood that the soul proceeds to the world of Hiraṇyagarbha. To this, we reply: It is not so. For the term "world of Brahmā" refers to the world of the supreme Brahmā (*parabrahman*), because the scripture describes the attainment of immortality and liberation in that context. Furthermore, the scripture speaks of the soul reaching the "fourth state" (*turīya*) after passing through the worlds of Prajāpati and others. Therefore, the soul proceeds from the world of Prajāpati to the world of the supreme Brahmā. [End of Topic 8] Topic 9: The Attainment of the World of Brahmā (Brahmaloka-prāpti Adhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 18. Now, the following doubt arises: Is the world of Brahmā reached by all who follow the path of the gods, or only by those who possess knowledge? On this point, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Since the scripture says, "Those who know Brahman go by this path," it is understood that the world of Brahmā is reached by all who follow the path of the gods. To this, we reply: It is not so. For the scripture
"They are conducting deities because of the indicative mark.
Regarding those very [stages] beginning with light, there is a doubt: are these signs of the path, or places of enjoyment, or rather leaders of those who go?
On this point, the initial position reached is that light and the others are signs of the path.
This is because the instruction has that very nature as its essence.
For just as in the world, someone intending to set out for a village or a city is instructed:
"As you go, you will reach this mountain, then the banyan tree, then the river, then the village, or then the city"—in this manner.
In this context as well, he says, "From here, by the rays, during the day, during the waxing fortnight," and so forth.

Alternatively, it follows that these are "lands of enjoyment" (*bhogabhūmi*), for indeed, he connects the word "world" (*loka*) with Agni and the others, as in: "He comes to the world of Agni" (*Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad* 1.3), and so on.
Furthermore, the word *loka* is used to denote the abodes of experience for living beings, as in: "the world of men, the world of the fathers, the world of the gods" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.16).
Likewise, a Brāhmaṇa text states: "They become attached to those worlds, namely the days and nights," and so forth.
Therefore, the light (*arcis*) and the others are not conductors.
Furthermore, because they are insentient, it is untenable for them to be conducting deities (*ātivāhika*).
For in the world, it is sentient persons appointed by a king who conduct those to be conducted along difficult paths.
This being the case, we reply: these [fires] must indeed be conducting deities.
Why? Because of that indicative mark (*liṅga*).

For it is established that [the text] shows the state of being a conductor in the passage: "From the moon to lightning; there a person who is not human leads them to Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.5).
If it is argued that those words are exhausted by referring only to that specific subject [the path], we say no;
for the qualification is intended to exclude the state of being human (*mānavatva*) which has been reached.

If those persons who lead [the soul] through the path of light and so forth are understood to be human (*mānava*), then it is appropriate to qualify them as "non-human" (*amānava*) in order to exclude that [human nature]. 4.
Having thus determined the sequence of the light and the other stages, he now determines their essential nature: "They are conducting deities (ātivāhika), because of the indicative mark.
A doubt arises due to the similarity in the mention of signs, the use of the word "world" (loka), and the indicative mark of being a leader.
The first two positions constitute the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).

He establishes the final position with the words beginning "Thus," [arguing] that the light and the others, ending with lightning, are conscious conductors because they are mentioned together with the superhuman person as the conductor.

He raises an objection with the words "That statement," suggesting that according to the literal text, the status of conductor belongs to the superhuman person alone and not to the light and the others.

[The response is that] if the passage were intended to convey both the superhuman nature and the status of conductor for the person, there would be a syntactical split (vākya-bheda); therefore, by the words "light" and so on, the conductors [are indicated].

Thus, it must be stated that, by the force of the context, since a "human" (mānava) is obtained immediately after the lightning as the leader, the text merely teaches the single quality of being non-human (amānavatva) by way of restating the leadership already established by the context. To this effect, he says: "No. For if the context of the leader were not accepted, the sentence "a non-human person leads them" would be split, because leadership—just like the state of being non-human—would not have been previously established [by the context]. This is the intended meaning.
He takes up the sūtra which provides the supporting reasoning for the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mention of leadership (*netṛtva*): "But surely... (nanu). //4//
Objection: But surely that mere indicative mark is not a means of knowledge, because there is no logical necessity (*nyāya*).
This is not a fault, because that [attainment] is established through the delusion regarding both.

For those who follow the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*) have their collection of faculties (*karaṇagrāma*) condensed due to separation from the body; thus, they are not independent [of the guides] such as light.

Furthermore, because they are insentient, they lack independence; therefore, it is understood that specific conscious deities who preside over the light (*arcis*) and so forth are appointed to the journey beyond.
For even in the world, those who are intoxicated or in a swoon, whose faculties are withdrawn, proceed along paths directed by others.
Furthermore, because the rays and so forth are not constant, it is not logical for them to constitute the characteristics of the path;
for it is not possible for one who has died at night to encounter the nature of the day,
and it has already been stated previously that there is no waiting.

However, because the deities are eternal, this fault does not apply. Furthermore, their designation by terms such as "light" (*arcis*) and so forth is appropriate because they identify with light and the rest; thus, the scriptural instruction beginning with "from light to day" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 4.15.5, 5.10.1) is not contradicted even if they are conducting deities (*ativāhika*), for one reaches the day by means of light as the cause.
"By day, by means of that cause, [one reaches] the waxing fortnight.
And likewise, even among those well-known in the world who are of a transporting nature (*ativāhika*), such instructions are observed:
"Go from here to Balavarman, then to Jayasiṃha, then to Kṛṣṇagupta."
Moreover, at the beginning [of the passage], it is stated merely that "they reach the light" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.15),
without specifying any particular nature of that connection;
however, in the conclusion, it says, "He leads them to Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.6).
Thus, the specific relationship characterized by being "carriers" (*ativāhika*) has been stated; by this, it is determined that the same applies at the beginning as well.
Furthermore, because their sensory organs (*karaṇa*) are withdrawn into a mass, there is no possibility of experience for those travelers there.
However, the word "world" (*loka*) can still be applied even to those travelers who are not experiencing anything.

Because those other worlds are lands of enjoyment for their inhabitants, one should apply the principle accordingly: having reached the world whose master is fire, one is carried away by fire; having reached the world whose master is wind, one is carried away by wind. // 5 //
If the light and the other [stages] were indeed non-intelligent and lacked a leader, then, due to the delusion and ignorance of both the path and its traveler, there would be no upward movement;

therefore, being itself devoid of effort, it must be led by another intelligent being. Thus, the meaning of the Sūtra is that the aforementioned indicative mark (liṅga) is established by the support of worldly logic, thereby establishing the existence of a leader.
He refutes the two preceding positions with the words "because of instability," and so forth.

Since it has been stated that because the light, day, and other stages are unstable, there is no waiting for one who dies during the night or at other such times, they cannot be signs of the path nor objects of enjoyment;
however, if they are deities, the defect of instability does not apply—this is the meaning.
As for the claim that the state of being a sign appears from the natural force of the instruction itself, he says in response: "From the light to the day.
Furthermore, because there is a doubt as to whether [the light] is a sign or a guide, he states that the determination is made by means of the remainder of the passage: "Moreover."

Regarding what was stated—that there is the state of being an object of enjoyment (bhogyatva) from the word "world" (loka)—he says "no," beginning with the words "saṃpiṇḍita. He introduces another aphorism with the words "kathaṃ punar" (But how?). //5//
But how, moreover, is that [conducive nature] possible in the case of Varuṇa and the others under the view that they are "conveying" deities?

For Varuṇa and the others have indeed been mentioned as starting from lightning; however, it is heard in scripture that immediately after lightning, until the attainment of Brahman, the agency of leading belongs exclusively to the non-human person (puruṣa).
Therefore, he recites the following [sūtra]: "By the one belonging to lightning alone, because of the scriptural statement to that effect. (BBs 4.3.6)

Therefore, it should be understood that after reaching the lightning, those [souls] are led by the non-human person (puruṣa) who exists immediately following the lightning through the worlds of Varuṇa and so forth to the world of Brahman;

for this is understood from the scriptural statement of that very person's role as the guide: "A non-human person [comes] from the lightning, and having approached, he leads them to the world of Brahman.

As for Varuṇa and the others, they should be understood as being merely assistants to that same person, either by not creating obstacles or by providing some form of assistance through their own activity.
Therefore, it has been well said that the deities beginning with light (arcis) are conducting souls. // 6 //
The meaning is that the non-human [being] has come from the world of lightning; thus, it is by means of the one belonging to lightning (vaidyuta).
In the Śruti, the meaning is "from the world of lightning.
The intention is that although Varuṇa and the others do not act as direct leaders according to the Śruti, they are included within the path by virtue of being supportive. //6//
END BsCom_4,3.4.6 START BsCom_4,3.5.7 5.
The Section Concerning the Effect (Kāryādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 7–14.
Bādari [holds that the conductor] leads him to the effected [Brahman], because that is logically consistent with his movement.
Regarding the passage, "He leads them to Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.5), a doubt arises: does he lead them to the effected, lower Brahman, or rather to the supreme, unmodified, primary Brahman?
Whence arises this doubt?
From the use of the word "Brahman" and from the scriptural mention of a "path.
Regarding this, the teacher Bādari maintains that it is the effected, lower Brahman with qualities that leads them [the souls], by means of a non-human person.
Why? Because its movement is logically possible.
For this effected Brahman (kāryabrahman), the state of being a destination is logically possible;
for it is logically possible that this effected Brahman is a destination because it possesses spatial extension.
But in the case of the supreme Brahman, neither the state of being a goer, nor the state of being the goal, nor the act of going is possible;
for [Brahman] is omnipresent and is the inner self of all goers. // 7 //
Having thus ascertained the path, he considers the destination: "The effected [Brahman] (kārya) is the goal, because its movement is logically possible" (Bādarī).

While the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) holds that the Supreme Brahman (*paraṃ brahma*) is the destination, and thus the path serves the purpose of liberation, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) maintains that the effected Brahman is the goal, and thus it serves the purpose of enjoyment. Keeping this in mind, he first states the established conclusion: "In that case, it is indeed the effected [Brahman].
Even though [Brahman] is all-pervading, space can be a destination by virtue of being distinguished by a different location.
The meaning is that, because Brahman is the very Self (pratyak), it cannot be reached by any means whatsoever. //7//
And because it has been specified. (BBs 4.3.8)

Furthermore, because it is specified in another scriptural passage—"He leads them to the worlds of Brahman; in those worlds of Brahman they dwell for the highest of high distances" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.15)—it is understood that the journey has as its object only the effected (kārya) Brahman. Indeed, a specification by means of the plural number is not appropriate in the case of the supreme (para) Brahman.
However, in the case of the effect, the plural number is possible because of the occurrence of different states.
Furthermore, common worldly usage and scriptural tradition apply directly only to that sphere of experience characterized by specific arrangements within the realm of transformations;
elsewhere, however, such usage is figurative, as in passages like, "This world, O Emperor, is Brahman itself."
Furthermore, even the designation of the subject to be governed would not be direct with respect to the supreme Brahman;
therefore, this leading [of the soul] has as its object only the effected [Brahman]. // 8 //

By means of the locative case-ending in the word *brahmalokeṣu* (in the worlds of Brahman), which expresses plurality and serves as the locus for the term "worlds," and because that which is to be reached is distinguished from the Supreme, he states that the Supreme is not the destination—this is based on the phrase "and because of being specified.
The meaning is that the scriptural usage of the word "world" (*loka*) with respect to the Supreme Brahman is figurative, since it is metaphorically treated as an object of enjoyment.

By the neuter word *brahma*, which denotes the cause, the effect is indicated in order to harmonize with multiple scriptural passages such as the plural number and others, which are supported by the logic of being a destination.
Nor can the Supreme be the destination on the basis of the mark of non-return;
for the meaning is that the mark is otherwise established by means of gradual liberation (kramamukti). //8//

Objection: But even with respect to an effect, the word "Brahman" is not appropriate, for it has been established in the *Samanvaya* [Sūtra] that Brahman is the cause of the origin and so forth of the entire universe.
To this it is replied: "But that designation [of the self] is due to proximity.
The word "but" (tu) is for the purpose of setting aside the objection.
Because of its proximity to the Supreme Brahman, the application of the word "Brahman" to the lower Brahman is not contradictory;

for it is established that the Supreme Brahman itself, when connected with pure limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and taught for the purpose of meditation by certain [teachers] through certain modified attributes such as "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*), is designated as the "lower" Brahman.
But surely, if the state of being an effect were attained, the scriptural teaching of non-return would not be possible;
for they do not conceive of eternity anywhere other than in the supreme Brahman. Moreover, scripture demonstrates that those who have set out upon the path of the gods do not return.

If it be argued that there is no return for them here, as stated in "Those proceeding by this path do not return to this human whirlpool" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.6) and "Going upwards from those two, one attains immortality" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.6; Kaṭha Upaniṣad 6.16),
we reply as follows:
"Because of the statement that they go from here along with their presider when the dissolution of the effect occurs.

(BBs 4.3.10) When the dissolution of the world of the effected Brahman is present, those who have produced right vision right there, being together with Hiraṇyagarbha— the presider over that— proceed from here to the beyond, the supremely pure, highest station of Viṣṇu.
Gradual liberation must be accepted on the basis of scriptural declarations such as "not returning" and so forth;
for it has been established that the attainment of the Supreme cannot occur directly without being preceded by a journey. // 10 //
And because of Smṛti:
Smṛti also authorizes this meaning: "When the dissolution has arrived, at the end of the highest [Brahmā], all those who have perfected themselves enter the supreme state together with Brahmā."
Therefore, the established conclusion is that the scriptural teaching regarding the journey concerns the effected Brahman (kāryabrahman). // 11 //

Furthermore, what prior position (*pūrvapakṣa*) was anticipated such that this established conclusion (*siddhānta*) was set forth by [the Sūtra] beginning with "Bādari [holds that the soul goes] for the sake of the task" (BS 4.3.7)?
That [position] is now demonstrated by the Sūtras themselves:

"But Jaimini [holds it to be] the Supreme, because of its being primary. The teacher Jaimini, however, maintains that in the passage, "He leads them to Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.6), it is the Supreme Brahman alone that he causes them to attain.
Why? Because of its primary sense. For the Supreme Brahman is the primary referent of the word "Brahman," while the lower [Brahman] is secondary.
And when there is a connection between the primary and the secondary, the cognition occurs with respect to the primary. // 12 //
The *pratisaṃcara* is the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*).

When that occurs, at the end of the Supreme One, Hiraṇyagarbha—specifically at the conclusion of the modifications consisting of the collective subtle body (*samaṣṭi-liṅga-śarīra*)—all those residing in the world of Brahmā who have realized the Self, whose intellects are purified, and in whom right knowledge has arisen, are liberated along with Brahmā as he is being released. They proceed to the Supreme.
The construction is: "they enter the state.
Having thus stated the established conclusion (siddhānta), he states the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) refuted by it, beginning with the words "But which... [verses 9–12].
And because it is observed [in scripture]. (BBs 4.3.13)
And the passage, "Going upwards by that, one attains immortality" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.6; Kaṭha Upaniṣad 6.16), shows that immortality is preceded by a journey.
Furthermore, immortality is possible only in the supreme Brahman, not in the effected [Brahman].
Because the effect is perishable;
for there is a scriptural teaching: "Now, that wherein one sees something else—that is the finite, that is mortal" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1).
Moreover, this very destination is taught in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad as pertaining exclusively to the Supreme;
for there is no introduction to any other knowledge therein, since it is the Supreme Brahman alone that has been introduced with the words, "Other than dharma, other than adharma" (Ka. 2.14).
In the Dahara-vidyā, in the Kaṭhavallīs, and in the context of the Supreme Brahman, the departure [of the soul] is shown by the words, "Going upwards from there... (KaU 2.6.15). //13//
And there is no intention to realize the goal within the effect itself. BBs_4,3.14.

Moreover, the intention expressed in "I enter the assembly hall and the dwelling of Prajāpati" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14.1) does not concern the effected [Brahman], because what is under discussion is the supreme Brahman itself, which is distinct from the effected, as stated in: "The one who carries forth name and form— that within which they are, that is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14.1).
And because it begins by identifying [the Self] as the Self of all in the passage, "I am the glory of the brahmins" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14.1), and [continues with],
"There is no likeness of him... (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1).
Furthermore, because it is well known that the name and fame belong to the Supreme Brahman alone— as seen in the passage, "He whose name is great fame" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.19)—
this attainment of the abode mentioned in the Hārdavidyā is preceded by a journey, as stated there: "That unconquered city of Brahman, the golden hall built by the Lord" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.5.3).
Furthermore, since the root *pad* also has the meaning of "going," it is determined that there is an expectation of a path;
