therefore, there is another position that the scriptural texts concerning "going" have as their object the supreme Brahman.
These two positions were set forth by the Teacher [Bādarāyaṇa] in the Sūtras through arguments such as the possibility of going (*gati-upapatti*).
One [set of categories] consists of "primacy" and so forth, while the other consists of "destiny," "rebirth," and so forth.

In this regard, destiny, rebirth, and the rest are capable of making primacy and the rest appear as if they were present, but primacy and the rest cannot make destiny, rebirth, and the rest appear so; thus, the first alone is explained as the established doctrine (siddhānta), while the second is the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).
For there exists no authority that mandates the adoption of the primary meaning alone even when its occurrence is impossible.

Furthermore, even within the context of the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*), the mention of the path based on other forms of knowledge is appropriate for the purpose of praise, just as in the passages: "The others go in various directions at the time of departure" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.6) and "I enter the assembly hall, the abode of Prajāpati" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14.1).
Thus, by breaking off the preceding statement, there is no contradiction in the intention to convey that [the soul] undergoes a transformation even into an effect.

Furthermore, even in the case of Brahman with attributes (saguṇa), the proclamation of its being the self of all is appropriate, as in such passages as "possessing all works, possessing all desires," and so forth.
Therefore, the scriptural texts concerning the journey have as their object only the lower [Brahman].

Furthermore, some, adhering to the rule that the preceding [sūtras] are prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the subsequent ones are established conclusions (*siddhānta*), maintain that the scriptural passages concerning "going" refer exclusively to another realm; however, that is untenable because it is impossible for Brahman to be a destination to be gone to.

That which is all-pervading, internal to all, and the self of all— the Supreme Brahman— of whom it is said: "All-pervading and eternal like space" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.1), "The Brahman that is immediate and direct" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.1), "The Self that is within all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.1),
and "This whole world is indeed the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2).
"‘This entire universe is indeed Brahman, the most excellent’" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.11)—
for one whose specific nature has been thus determined by such scriptural passages, its being an object to be reached is never logically possible;
for that which has already been reached cannot itself be the goal of a journey.
For it is well known in the world that one thing goes to another.
But is it not observed in the world that even for one who has already gone, there remains a state of being "to-be-gone-to," characterized by another location?
For example, one who is already standing on the earth goes to the earth itself by way of another location.
Likewise, even if there were non-difference [between the Self and Brahman], one might argue that because Brahman is endowed with all powers, it could somehow be an object of going;
but this is not so, because all distinctions have been denied of Brahman:
"It is partless, actionless, tranquil, irreproachable, and stainless" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.19).
"It is neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8);
"For it is without interior or exterior, indeed unborn" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2);
"Verily, this great unborn Self is undecaying, immortal, deathless, fearless Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.25).

From such scriptural passages as "This Self is 'not this, not this'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26), as well as from Smṛti and reasoning, it is impossible to conceive of any connection with distinctions such as space or time in the Supreme Self;
by virtue of which [distinction] it could be subject to the logic of being a destination, analogous to a region of the earth or a stage of life.
If it is argued that, because of its connection with specific attributes such as location and state, the earth and ether can possess a destination characterized by space and time—
given that Brahman possesses manifold powers according to the scriptural testimony regarding its being the cause of the origin, sustenance, and dissolution of the world— we say no;
for there are scriptural passages that negate all distinctions, and they serve no other purpose.
If it is argued that the scriptures concerning origination and so forth are likewise identical in having no other purpose [than establishing non-duality], we say no;
for they are intent upon demonstrating unity.

Since the scripture, through examples such as clay and the like, demonstrates that the one existent Brahman alone is real and that its modification is illusory, it cannot be intended to teach origination and the rest.
But why is it that the scriptural passages concerning origination and so forth are subordinate to the [passages concerning the Self], and not the other way around?
It is said: because the scriptural passages that negate distinctions have a meaning that leaves no further expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣārthatvāt*).

For once the oneness, eternity, purity, and so forth of the Self have been understood, no further expectancy arises, since the realization of the completion of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is thereby established.
"In that state, what delusion and what sorrow can there be for one who perceives oneness? (Īśā Upaniṣad 7);
"O Janaka, you have indeed attained fearlessness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.2.4);
"The knower does not fear anything from any quarter."
This is indeed confirmed by such scriptural passages as: "It does not afflict him [who knows this]: 'Why did I not do what is good? Why did I do what is evil?
(Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.9.1), and likewise by the observation of contentment, experience, and so forth among those who possess such knowledge.
Furthermore, because of the censure of those who have a false intention regarding modifications, it is said: "He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were diversity.
Therefore, it cannot be understood that the scriptural texts denying distinctions are subordinate to other passages.
Such is not the case for the scriptural texts concerning origination and so forth, for they possess the capacity to establish their own meanings independently, without requiring anything else.
However, their purpose as being for something else is clearly perceived;

for, having introduced the passage, "Know this, my dear, that this sprout has sprung up; it cannot be without a root" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.3), the text shows at the conclusion that the single Existent alone is to be known as the root of the world.
"From which indeed these beings are born; by which, once born, they live; into which they enter when they depart—that you should seek to understand."
And [it says], "That is Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1.1).
Thus, since the scriptural texts concerning origination and so forth have as their ultimate purport the realization of the oneness of the Self, Brahman cannot possess manifold powers;
and consequently, it is impossible for it to be a destination to be reached.
And the passage, "His vital breaths do not depart; being Brahman, he merges into Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6), precludes any movement toward the supreme Brahman.
This has been explained under the Sūtra, "For it is clear for some" (Brahma-sūtra 4.2.13).
Furthermore, if one conceives of movement, the living soul (*jīva*) as the mover would have to be either a part or a modification of the Brahman that is the goal of movement;
for movement is impossible if there is absolute identity.
If this were so, what would follow?
It is said:

if it were a part (*ekadeśa*), then because that part would be eternally attained by the possessor of the parts (*ekadeśin*), a further journey to Brahman would not be possible. Furthermore, the conceptualization of Brahman as having parts is untenable, since its partlessness (*niravayavatva*) is well-established.
Even in the case of modification (*vikāra*), this [objection] remains unequal, because the modifier is eternally connected with its modification;
for a jar does not exist having abandoned its nature as clay, or else, if it were so abandoned, it would result in non-existence.

Furthermore, in the cases of modification and [the view of] parts (*avayava*), since that which possesses them is stable, the transition of Brahman into the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is likewise untenable.
Now, if the individual soul (jīva) were indeed different from Brahman,
it would have to be either atomic, all-pervading, or of intermediate size.
If it were all-pervading, its movement would be impossible.
Furthermore, if it were of intermediate size, there would be the undesirable consequence of impermanence;
if it were minute, the experience of sensation throughout the entire body would be impossible.
Moreover, both minuteness and intermediate size have already been refuted in detail previously.

Furthermore, if the individual soul were different from the Supreme, there would be the undesirable consequence of contradicting such scriptural texts as "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7). This same defect applies equally to the views that the soul is either a modification or a part [of the Supreme].
If it is argued that there is no fault because the modification and its constituent parts are non-different from their possessor, we say no;
for primary oneness is untenable. In all these positions, the consequence is the impossibility of liberation.
Because transmigratory selfhood has not been ceased;
or, if it were ceased, there would be the consequence of the destruction of one's own nature;
and because the identity with Brahman is not admitted.
As for what is prattled by some— that obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites are performed to prevent the arising of sin,

that optional (*kāmya*) and prohibited (*pratiṣiddha*) acts are avoided to prevent the attainment of heaven or hell, and that actions to be experienced in the present body are exhausted through experience alone; therefore, after the fall of the current body, there will be no further connection with another body.

[Objection: "Because of the absence of any cause, liberation—characterized by abiding in one's own essential nature—will be accomplished for one who has lived in this manner even without [realizing] the identity with Brahman.
[Reply: That is incorrect, because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
For this has not been established by any scripture that one seeking liberation should act in such a manner;
rather, this is merely conjectured by one's own intellect on the grounds that since transmigratory existence is caused by karma, it will cease to exist due to the absence of its cause.
Yet even this cannot be logically established, because the absence of a cause is difficult to ascertain.
For indeed, many karmas accumulated over various previous births—having desirable and undesirable ripenings—are possible for every single living being.

Since it is impossible to experience those [karmas] of contradictory results simultaneously, some of them, having found their opportunity, fashion this present birth; however, others remain non-existent, awaiting specific place, time, and causal conditions. Therefore, regarding those remaining [karmas]:

Since exhaustion [of karma] is impossible through enjoyment in the present life alone, it cannot be ascertained that even for one whose conduct has been as described, there is an absence of the cause for another body upon the fall of the current body;
for the existence of a remainder of karma is established by such scriptural and traditional texts as, "Those here whose conduct was pleasant, by that remainder... and so forth.
It might be argued:
"The obligatory and occasional rites will serve as their expiations.
That is not so.
Because there is no contradiction.
For the relationship of the sublated and the sublator exists only when a contradiction is present;
and there is no contradiction between meritorious deeds accumulated in other lifetimes and the obligatory (nitya) or occasional (naimittika) rites.
Because pure form is non-distinct [from the Self],
whereas evil deeds consist of impure form, their destruction may indeed occur when there is a contradiction; however, that alone does not establish the absence of a cause for another body,
since it is logical that such a cause could be good karma (*sukṛta*).
Furthermore, there is no realization of the complete eradication of even misdeeds [through mere non-performance].

Nor is there any authoritative evidence for the claim that the performance of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites results merely in the non-occurrence of demerit (*pratyavāya*), and not in the production of some other fruit; for it is possible that another fruit arises as a byproduct.
Indeed, Āpastamba records: "Just as when a mango tree is the cause for seeking fruit, shade and fragrance arise as well, so too when dharma is practiced, worldly benefits arise as byproducts."

Moreover, in the absence of right vision (*samyak-darśana*), it is impossible for anyone to assert that there is a total avoidance of both desired and prohibited actions during the interval between birth and death;
for even the most skillful perceive subtle transgressions.
Although one might thus remain in doubt, even so, the impossibility of such a state remains difficult to ascertain due to the difficulty of perceiving the absence of causes [for transgression].

Furthermore, if the identity of Brahman and the Self as knowable through wisdom is not accepted, it is impossible to desire the absolute isolation (*kaivalya*) of a Self whose very nature is that of an agent and an enjoyer;
for such a nature, like the heat of fire, is unavoidable. This might be argued:

Agency and enjoyership are the effect, which is the misfortune; it is not their potentiality (*śakti*). Therefore, even when the potentiality remains, liberation is possible through the cessation of the effect.
But that is not so, because as long as the potentiality exists, the production of the effect is unavoidable.
Now, it might be argued that a causal capacity does not initiate an effect without depending on other auxiliary conditions;
therefore, even though it remains solitary, it is not at fault.
But that is not so.

Because even the signs are eternally connected by way of a relationship characterized by their inherent power (*śakti*), therefore, as long as the nature of being an agent and an enjoyer persists—provided that another reality, the state of being Brahman as the Self accessible through knowledge, does not exist—there can be no hope for liberation whatsoever.
And the Śruti says: "There is no other path for going" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8).
Thus, [the scripture] precludes any path to liberation other than knowledge.

If it is argued that even if the individual soul (*jīva*) were non-different from the Supreme, all worldly transactions would necessarily cease because the means of valid cognition such as perception would not function, we say: no.
Because that [worldly activity] is possible prior to awakening, just like the conduct of a dream;

and because the scripture, after describing the operation of perception and other means of knowledge regarding the unawakened state in such passages as, "For where there is duality, as it were, there one sees another" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14; 4.5.15), further states regarding the awakened state: "But where for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14).
By these and other such statements, he demonstrates its non-existence.
Thus, because for one who knows the supreme Brahman the cognition of a destination and so forth has been sublated, a departure can in no way be established.
But what, then, is the subject matter of the scriptural texts concerning departure?
It is said: they will pertain to knowledge with attributes (*saguṇavidyā*).

For instance, in some places, the journey is described in connection with the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*), such as "Breath is Brahman, Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.10.5), and "Now, that which is within this city of Brahman, the small lotus-palace" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.1).

And thus, even in that case, since it is the Brahman with attributes alone that is to be meditated upon through qualities such as "the dwarf-like" (*vāmanī*) and "having true desires" (*satyakāma*), the going [of the soul] is possible;

for nowhere is a going directed toward the Supreme Brahman heard of in scripture, as is the case where the negation of going is proclaimed: "His vital breaths do not depart" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.4.6).
[In contrast, regarding the Supreme Brahman: "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.1.1).
In passages such as these, however, although the root *āp* has the sense of "going," because reaching another location is impossible according to the reasoning already described,

this is stated— namely, "being Brahman, he attains Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.7)— as the realization of one's own true nature with reference to the dissolution of name and form superimposed by ignorance.
It should be understood as being like the aforementioned examples.
Furthermore, when the journey to the supreme realm (*paraviṣaya*) is explained, it must be for the sake of either generating enthusiasm (*prarocanā*) or for the sake of contemplation (*anucintanā*).
Of these, first, as for generating enthusiasm:
For those who know Brahman, no destination is established by verbal description,
because that [attainment] is accomplished through a state of well-being that is self-evident, immediate, and conferred by knowledge itself. Furthermore,
for a cognition that reveals eternally established liberation— a fruit that is not something yet to be achieved— no dependence on the contemplation of a destination is logically possible.
Therefore, the state of being situated in the lower Brahman [occurs].

In that regard, due to a lack of discernment between the higher and lower Brahman, scriptural passages concerning the state of being situated in the lower Brahman are superimposed upon the higher Brahman.
Are there two Brahmans, a higher and a lower?
"Certainly; for there is the vision [of scripture] stating: 'Verily, O Satyakāma, this syllable Om is both the higher and the lower Brahman' (Praśna Upaniṣad 5.2), and so forth.
But what, then, is the higher Brahman, and what is the lower?"
It is said:

where Brahman is taught by means of words such as "not gross" (*asthūla*) through the negation of specific distinctions such as name and form (*nāmarūpa*) created by ignorance (*avidyā*), that is the higher [Brahman].

That very same [Brahman], however, where it is taught for the purpose of meditation (*upāsana*) as qualified by some specific distinction of name, form, and so forth—such as "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*), "having breath as its body" (*prāṇaśarīra*), and "having light as its form" (*bhārūpa*) [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.2]—[is the lower Brahman].
By such words as these, that [Brahman] is shown to be non-different.

Now, one might object: "In this case, would not the scriptural teaching of non-duality (*advaita*) be contradicted? No; for this has been resolved by the fact that [the distinctions] are merely limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of name and form created by ignorance (*avidyā*).

And for that meditation on the lower Brahman, the fruit— which is heard in its proximity as "If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.2.1) and so forth— is characterized by sovereignty over the world and belongs exclusively to the sphere of saṃsāra,
because ignorance has not been dispelled.
And because that [knowledge] is bound to a specific location, its movement for the purpose of reaching that location is not contradictory.

Furthermore, even though the self is all-pervading like space, we have already stated in the commentary on *Brahmasūtra* 2.3.29 (*tadguṇasāratvāt*) that the conventional designation of "movement" occurs when the limiting adjuncts, such as the intellect (*buddhi*), move, just as there is movement when jars and other objects move within space.
Therefore, this very position— that "Bādari [holds that the soul becomes] an effect" (Brahma Sūtra 4.3.7)— is established;
whereas "Jaimini [holds it to be] the Supreme [Self]" (Brahma Sūtra 4.3.12).
However, it should be understood that this is merely a demonstration of alternative positions for the purpose of expanding one's wisdom. // 14 //

Thus, it has been stated that the journey concerns the Supreme Being (paraviṣaya) on account of the indications of Brahman, immortality, and the context; now, he dispels the doubt that there is no destination higher than the effected (kārya) realm—based on the scriptural statement of the meditator's resolve at the time of death, "May I reach the assembly hall and the palace of Prajāpati"—by stating: "Nor [is it] the effected."

Since the subject under discussion is the Supreme Being, and because the word *yaśas* (glory) is well-known as a name for the Supreme Self, the Self is expressed by the word *yaśas*. [Thus it is said:
"I become the glory that is the Self of the Brahmins."

Likewise, because there are signs of universal identity in such expressions as "the glory of kings" and "the glory of the Vaiśyas," the meaning is that this is indeed an intention for the attainment of the Supreme.
Even if it be granted that the desire to reach the house has the Supreme Brahman as its object, one might ask how that could be preceded by a journey; to this, he says:
"And that... [referring to the city] which is unassailable (*aparājitā*) and situated in front of Brahmā Hiraṇyagarbha in that world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*), by him alone...
In the Dahara-vidyā, it is stated that the attainment of the house is preceded by a journey, as it says: "There is a golden mansion built by the Lords; the knower enters it.

Therefore, the meaning is that even in the case of the Supreme Brahman, its attainment is established as being preceded by a journey, due to the commonality of the term "attainment of a house" (veśmapratipatti).
Furthermore, since the root *pad* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha with the meaning "to go," the expectation of a path is apparent in the phrase "I enter the house"; thus he says, "of *pad* also.
He concludes the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words, "therefore.
He then proceeds to conclude by reinforcing that the first [position] alone is the established conclusion (*siddhāntapakṣa*), using the words, "those two."
He clarifies the fallacious nature of the reasons—such as the primary meaning of the word "Brahman" and so forth—with the words "Not indeed" (*na hi*).

The meaning is that because the state of being a destination, the use of the plural "in the worlds of Brahman," and the scriptural statement regarding the attainment of divine enjoyments such as fragrance through mere volition are impossible in the case of the Supreme Brahman, the primary sense [of the word] must be abandoned.
Even though the word "Brahman" occurs in scriptural passages such as "This, O Satyakāma, is indeed the higher and the lower Brahman," where the usage is identical;

Although [the term "Brahman"] is primary in both senses due to its conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), it should be understood that it is accepted as being non-primary with respect to the lower Brahman (*apara-brahman*) because, in the case of the full [higher Brahman], the etymological meaning (*avayavārtha*)— namely, unsurpassed greatness— is obtained.
As it has been stated in the *Kaṭhavallīs*, by the force of the context, the "going" (*gati*) refers to the higher [Brahman].
To this he replies with the word "pare" (the higher).

Just as there is a mention of other channels not connected with it for the purpose of praising the Suṣumnā which is connected with knowledge (*vidyā*), so too, even in the context of the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*), there is a mention of the path based on lower knowledge (*aparavidyā*) for the purpose of praising that [higher knowledge]. For even without the path, the higher knowledge possesses a fruit of unsurpassed excellence; however, in that [context], the fruit of lower knowledge—which is accomplished by means of the path—is included within it. Thus, the meaning is that [the mention of the path] serves to provide praise.
As for what was said— that even the intention regarding attainment refers to the subject under discussion, namely the Supreme (Brahman)— he says "no," citing the passage beginning with "of Prajāpati.
The context is set aside by the scriptural mentions of the hall and palace of Prajāpati, as well as by the statement that [the Self] consists of those very aggregates.
The meaning is that the identification with all things (*sārvātmya*) expressed as "I am glory" is employed for the sake of meditation upon the lower Brahman (*apara-brahman*).
Having stated his own position, he refutes the opposing view with the words beginning "some say":

[he argues that] even though Brahman is omnipresent and constitutes one's very self, it might still be something to be reached by going from one place to another place or from one time to another time that is distinct from the former—this being illustrated by the two examples of the earth and age.
He raises an objection with "nanu" (but surely):
non-difference is already established even without effort, because the state and that which possesses the state are non-distinct, being of the very nature of one's own self.

Now, it may be argued that even though earth and age have already been attained, they can still be objects of going because they are qualified by different locations and times, and because they are distinct from the goer; however, how can Brahman, which is non-different from the goer, be an object of going? To this he says: "Omnipotent" (sarvaśakti).

That earth which has already been attained cannot be an object of going, and as for that other location which is to be gone to, it is not yet attained; how then can there be an object of going for what is already attained? As for age, it is merely a manifestation at another time.
The actual nature of reality is that there is no state of being "to be gone to.

Having provisionally accepted that the specific locations and times [of the world] are places to be traversed, he states with the words beginning with "no" that the Supreme Brahman cannot be reached in any way whatsoever, because it lacks any spatial or temporal qualification.

The scriptural authority is the Smṛti passage beginning with "the beginningless, supreme Brahman," and the logical principle is that the Self, which is pure Consciousness, is devoid of distinctions because all perceived particulars are superimposed upon that Consciousness.

One might raise the objection that Brahman with attributes alone is the supreme goal to be reached in relation to the *sūtrātmā*, while Brahman without attributes does not exist at all— this is expressed in the phrase "jagadutpatti" (the origin of the world).

Is the non-existence of the attributeless [Brahman] due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or due to its contradiction with scriptural texts concerning Brahman with attributes?
He says "no" to the first [objection], stating "not so.
He raises the second doubt: "arising and so forth.

He says "no" to this as well, explaining that there is no contradiction because the scriptural passages concerning the qualified [Brahman] are supplementary to the scriptural passages concerning the unqualified [Brahman].

He asks "Why? [in response to the question]: why should it not be that the scriptures concerning the featureless (nirviśeṣa) are themselves subordinate to the scriptures concerning the qualified (saviśeṣa)? He answers with the words beginning "It is said": because those [scriptures concerning the featureless] are complete in themselves, having attained their fruit in their own meaning, they have no further expectancy; whereas the scriptures concerning the qualified, being themselves fruitless, are subordinate by way of providing the specific objects to be negated and so forth, according to the maxim: "In the proximity of that which has a fruit, that which is fruitless is its subsidiary. Thus he says.
He states "But [it is] directly perceived" to show that the status of being a subordinate element (śeṣatā) is established not only by logic but also by direct scriptural statement (śruti).

In that regard, having begun in the *Chāndogya* with the statement, "From that root-cause, Brahman, this sprout consisting of the world as its effect has arisen," and concluding with, "Seek the root by means of that sprout," it is stated that Being alone is the object of knowledge.

Likewise, even in the Taittirīyaka, by restating the origin of the world and so forth, it is shown that Brahman alone is the object of knowledge; therefore, the meaning is that the scriptures concerning creation themselves clearly indicate their status as being supplementary to the cognition of the attributeless [Brahman].
Having thus established that there is no place to go because Brahman is attributeless, he states the conclusion: "In this way.
Furthermore, he states that the Supreme cannot be a destination because of explicit prohibitions: "Not of Him," and so on.

Having thus refuted motion by means of the analysis of the "to-be-traversed" (*gantavya*), he refutes it by means of the analysis of the "goer" (*gantr*) as well, with the words beginning "And in the conceptualization of motion," and so forth.
There are two conceptualizations based on difference and non-difference; the third conceptualization is that of absolute difference.
[Objection: Why is the conceptualization of absolute non-difference not mentioned?
Regarding this, he says "absolutely" (*atyantam*). He asks what the fault is in the three alternatives with the words "if it were so" (*yady evam*).
He states another defect in both of the two remaining alternatives with the words "and in the two positions of modification and part" (*vikārāvayavapakṣayoś ca*).

If Brahman were qualified by the individual souls (*jīva*), which are of the nature of modifications (*vikāra*) or parts (*avayava*), then because Brahman is eternal, there could be no going or coming for those souls.
The point is that there is no movement in the case of two frogs or fragments of stone residing within a massive, immovable boulder.
For us, however, the delusion of going and coming arises through limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) imagined due to ignorance; this is the intended meaning.
Having restated the third alternative and having analyzed it, he refutes it with the words beginning "Now" (*atha*).

The proponent of both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda-vādin*) says—referring to the phrase "of the modification and the part"—that "I have no fault in the form of contradiction with the scriptural texts on non-difference.
[The author] replies, "No," because the primary non-difference of two things that are distinct is not logical due to their mutual contradiction.

Furthermore, all three positions are untenable; for if the state of being a transmigrator—which is the transmigrator's real status as a living soul (jīva)—were destroyed, it would follow that the real nature of the living soul itself must be destroyed.

Nor has the identity with Brahman been accepted by you as the real form of the living soul in such a way that it would not perish even upon the destruction of transmigration, as we do; thus he says: "In all... [etc.].
Now, what is the use of this identity with Brahman?

Having set forth the view of those dull-witted by nature—that liberation (mokṣa) is indeed the absence of saṃsāra, and that this will be accomplished merely through the absence of karma—the author refutes it with the words beginning "yattu" (but as for that).
"Tat" (that) means:
there is a lack of valid evidence (pramāṇa) for the claim that such conduct is the cause of liberation.
To the objection that reasoning alone is the means of knowledge, he says: "And this cannot even be reasoned. Now, one might object:

"Even for you, this is merely a matter of reasoning, since it is impossible to experience in a single lifetime the fruits of various contradictory karmas; therefore, there must remain residual karma which serves as the cause for another birth. Anticipating this doubt, he states the proof for that [residual karma]: "And the establishment of the existence of residual karma."

One might raise the objection: "Since merit and demerit whose fruits have not yet begun are destroyed by the performance of obligatory rites (*nitya*) and so forth, there will be no future birth. To this he says, "It might be so. Merit is not destroyed by merit because they are not mutually contradictory; otherwise, there would be an over-extension of the principle. Furthermore, there is no evidence that demerit is entirely destroyed by merit. Therefore, he states with the words "That is not so" and so forth, that a future birth resulting from accumulated merit and demerit is unavoidable.

He says "nor by the obligatory [rites]" (na ca nitya) because birth could also result from the performance of obligatory rites and so forth, since there is an undifferentiated scriptural statement that "by action one attains the world of the ancestors" (karmaṇā pitṛlokaḥ), as well as supporting Smṛti texts.

This is an illustration regarding the point that when one is engaged in the performance of obligatory rites (*nitya*) and so forth for the purpose of averting transgression (*pratyavāya*), another result subsequently arises.
"Just as" (*tadyathā*) means:
when something has been constructed or superimposed.
Nevertheless, since there is no certainty regarding the existence of karma such as that performed for specific desires, he says, "But it must be doubted.
The sense is that, because one cannot attain the certainty that liberation occurs upon the fall of the body without [perfect] knowledge, there is a flaw in your position.
Furthermore, he says, "Nor... because even the hope for liberation is not tenable for a *jīva* who is distinct from Brahman and whose nature consists of agency and so forth.
He raises the objection that the effect, such as agency and so forth, is not the [inherent] nature [of the self], but rather its power (*śakti*), by saying "it might be thus" (*syādetat*).

Since it is illogical for a power— whose existence is inferred from its effect— to exist when the effect is absolutely non-produced, if that power were to exist, then because the effect which is its object,
as well as the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), time, place, and other causal conditions, would be eternally connected to the self through that power, liberation (*mokṣa*) would be impossible.
He refutes [the objection] with the words "And that," etc.

Having raised the doubt that if the individual soul (*jīva*) is accepted as being Brahman for the sake of establishing liberation, then transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) would be untenable, he reminds us of what has been stated more than once—that its occurrence is possible due to ignorance—with the words "From the Supreme," etc.
Having resolved this incidental point, he concludes the primary subject at hand with the words "Thus, therefore."

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that even in the context of higher knowledge (*paravidyā*), movement is heard of through the word 'attains'? To this he says: "The knower of Brahman attains [Brahman]. Furthermore, because movement would be purposeless, it cannot have the higher [Brahman] as its object; thus he says: "Moreover... He refutes the position that it refers to meditative reflection (*anucintana*) by saying: "And because it is eternally established."
Anticipating the objection, "How then is it that some have stated that the movement [of the soul] has another realm as its object?", he says, "In that regard, the higher and the lower...
He states that the movement is purposeful with respect to the lower Brahman, explaining the distinction between the higher and lower Brahman by means of a question beginning with, "Are there two?
To the question, "How can there be movement for a soul that is all-pervading?", he replies, "Even though it is omnipresent... (14).
END BsCom_4,3.5.14 START BsCom_4,3.6.15 6.
The Section Concerning Non-Symbolic Meditative Objects (Apratīkālambanādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 15–16.
"Bādarāyaṇa [holds] that he leads those who have not meditated on symbols, because there is a fault in both cases, and because of the nature of their resolve (tatkratu).
It has been established that this journey has the effected Brahman as its object, and not the highest Brahman.
Now, this is being deliberated: does the non-human person lead all those who have meditated upon the various effects without distinction to the world of Brahman, or only some of them?
What, then, is the prima facie position? It is that for all these knowers, there must be a departure [to the world of Brahman] other than the supreme Brahman.
For it has been introduced without distinction in the various meditations [of the Upaniṣads] under the Sūtra: "There is no restriction regarding all [the meditations]" (Brahma-sūtra 3.3.31).
This being the case, he replies: "Excepting those that have a symbol as their object.
The teacher Bādarāyaṇa maintains that, setting aside those whose objects are symbols, all others whose objects are modifications lead [the soul] to the world of Brahman;
for it is not the case that both [types of meditation] lead [to that result].
There is no fault in accepting non-existence,

because the principle of non-restriction applies even to meditations other than those involving a specific counter-entity; and the scriptural statement "he becomes according to his resolve" (tatkratu) should be seen as the supporting reason for this twofold state of affairs.

For it is connected [to the idea] that "he who has Brahman as his resolve (brahmakratu) shall attain the sovereignty of Brahman," according to the scriptural text: "In whatever way they meditate upon it, that very thing they become. However, in the case of symbols (pratīka), there is no "resolve on Brahman" because the meditation is primarily focused on the symbol.
But is it not heard in scripture—even one whose resolve is not on Brahman goes to Brahman—as in the Pañcāgnividyā: "He leads them to Brahman"? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.5)

Let it be so where such an explicit statement is found; however, in its absence, by the general rule (*autsargika*) and according to the principle of "that-which-is-intended" (*tat-kratu-nyāya*), it is understood that the attainment of Brahman belongs only to those whose sacrifice is Brahman (*brahma-kratu*), and not to others.
Having thus determined the goal to be reached, he identifies the travelers [to that goal] with the words "not on symbols" (*apratīka*).
This is because of the scriptural statement without qualification, "He alone leads them to Brahman," and also because of the *tat-kratu-nyāya*.
He states the doubt with the words "this" (*idam*).
In the section concerning non-restriction (*aniyamādhikaraṇa*), it was stated that for those who know reality (*tattvavid*) and for all other worshippers (*upāsaka*), there is a convergence of paths.

Now, if it were said that the path belongs only to those who worship the subordinate parts (*apatīka*) and not to all worshippers of the transformations (*vikāra*), there would be a contradiction with what was previously stated, as this would imply two different states of affairs.
Therefore, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the attainment of the higher path belongs to one who is merely a lay follower (*upāsaka*);
however, in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is established that it exists in both ways.
The phrase "because there is no fault" (*adoṣāt*) constitutes a separate section in the Sūtra.
The meaning is "because there is no contradiction.
The intention is that in the sūtra, "There is no restriction for all," the word "all" refers to those other than the meditators on symbols (*pratīka*).

Although it must be said that for those who meditate on symbols, the path beginning with light (*arcirādi*) applies—since they do not enter either the path of the fathers (*pitṛyāṇa*) or the third station—nevertheless, let their journey extend only as far as lightning; there is no attainment of Brahman, because they lack the meditation on Brahman (*brahmakratutva*).
For according to the principle that "whatever one meditates upon, that one attains," which is rooted in scripture,
there can be no meditation on Brahman in the case of symbols such as names and so forth, because Brahman is merely an attribute of those objects of meditation.
And the meaning of the Sūtra and Bhāṣya is that for this principle, a sublation is accepted because of a direct statement in the Pañcāgnividyā, which is an explicit declaration. //15//
And it demonstrates a distinction: BBs_4,3.16.

Regarding the meditations on symbols such as Name and so forth, [the scripture] shows that for each successive meditation there is a specific excellence of fruit compared to the preceding one: "As far as Name extends, over that he has freedom of movement" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.5);
"Speech, indeed, is greater than Name" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.2.1).
"Wherever speech reaches, there he has freedom of movement as he desires" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.2.2),
and "Mind, indeed, is greater than speech" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.3.1), and so forth.
And this distinction of results is appropriate because meditations on symbols (*pratīka*) are dependent upon those symbols.
However, if they were dependent upon Brahman, since Brahman is without distinction, how could there be a distinction of results?
Therefore, meditations that have symbols as their support do not possess the same results as the others. // 16 //

Furthermore, because scripture declares a gradation of fruits corresponding to the gradation of symbols, those who meditate on symbols do not attain Brahman; thus he says, "And [there is] a distinction.
Therefore, in the absence of a specific scriptural statement to the contrary, it is established that only those who meditate on Brahman go to Brahman. //16//
Thus ends the third quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Śrīmacchārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya* composed by the venerable Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda, the disciple of the venerable Govindabhagavatpūjyapāda. // 3 //
Thus ends the third quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā*, composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Govindānanda Bhagavat.

Thus ends the third quarter (pāda) of the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Northern Path for One Who Possesses Knowledge with Attributes and Has Died. The Fourth Quarter of the Fourth Chapter. START BsCom_4,4.1.1: The Soul's Departure from the Body. Now, therefore, we shall explain the departure of the soul from the body. It has been stated that the soul, accompanied by the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the sense organs, and the mind, proceeds upward along the path of the gods. Regarding this, a doubt arises as to whether this departure occurs for all souls or only for those who possess knowledge (*vidyā*). On this point, the opponent maintains the following view: The departure of the soul from the body occurs for all souls alike. Why? Because there is no specification; the scripture speaks of the departure of the soul without making any distinction. Furthermore, the scripture mentions the departure of the soul even in connection with those who lack knowledge, as in the passage: "When a person departs from this world, he goes forth together with his consciousness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2). Moreover, the fact that the soul departs from the body is established by the necessity of its seeking another body; for it is impossible for the soul to enter another body without first departing from the one it currently occupies. Therefore, the departure of the soul is common to all. To this, we reply: This departure of the soul from the body occurs only for those who possess knowledge. Why? Because of the scriptural statement concerning the two paths. For the scripture declares two distinct paths for those who possess knowledge: the path of the gods (*devayāna*) and the path of the fathers (*pitṛyāna*). Since these two paths are specified for those who possess knowledge, it follows that the departure of the soul must also pertain to them. Furthermore, the scripture describes the departure of the soul through the arteries (*nāḍī*) in the context of knowledge, stating: "When a person departs from this body, he goes out through the hundred-and-first artery" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.6). Also, the scripture speaks of the departure of the soul in connection with the meditation on the "small ether" (*dahara-vidyā*): "When he departs, his speech merges into his mind" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.5). And again: "He goes out through the gate of the sun" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.5). These and other such passages indicate that the departure of the soul is associated with knowledge. Moreover, the scripture teaches that for those who do not possess knowledge, there is a different destiny: "Those who live in villages and perform sacrifices, works of public utility, and alms-giving—they pass into smoke" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.3–5). This implies that for those who lack knowledge, there is no journey along the path of the gods. Thus, since the two paths are taught specifically for those who possess knowledge, and since the departure of the soul is a prerequisite for traveling those paths, we conclude that the departure of the soul from the body belongs only to those who possess knowledge. As for the argument that the scripture mentions the departure of the soul even in the absence of a specific qualification, we reply that such statements are made in reference to the general process of death, which applies to all beings, or they may be intended to show that the soul of the knower does not depart in the same manner as that of the ignorant. Furthermore, the necessity of the soul seeking another body does not prove that every soul must depart; for the scripture teaches that the soul of the knower, having attained liberation, does not enter another body at all. Therefore, the departure of the soul from the body is restricted to those who possess knowledge. Thus ends the discussion of the soul's departure. Now, we shall consider the nature of the soul's departure. Does the soul depart from the heart through the arteries, or does it simply exit the body through the upper opening? On this point, some hold the view that the soul departs through the upper opening, because the scripture says: "He goes out through the gate of the sun" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.5), and because the head is the most prominent part of the body. However, this is not correct. The soul departs from the heart through the arteries. Why? Because the scripture states: "These hundred-and-one arteries of the heart... through one of them he goes out" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.20). Also, the scripture says: "When a person departs from this body, he goes out through the hundred-and-first artery" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.6). Furthermore, the scripture describes the soul as residing in the heart during the state of deep sleep: "When a person sleeps here, he becomes united with the True" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1). Therefore, it is logical that the soul departs from the heart through the arteries. Regarding the mention of the "gate of the sun," that refers to the point of exit from the head, not the point of origin. The head is the highest part of the body, and the soul's exit through the head is consistent with its ascent toward the divine realm. Thus, the soul departs from the heart through the arteries and exits the body through the upper opening. Now, we shall consider the size of the soul as it departs. Is the soul atomic (*aṇu*), or does it pervade the entire body? On this point, the opponent maintains that the soul is atomic, because the scripture speaks of its movement: "It moves about, according to its pleasure, within its own body" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7). If the soul were all-pervading, such movement would be impossible. Furthermore, the scripture speaks of the soul entering the body: "Just as a razor placed in a razor-case, so does this subtle essence enter this body" (Praśna Upaniṣad 4.8). If the soul were all-pervading, it could not be said to "enter" the body. Therefore, the soul is atomic. To this, we reply: The soul is all-pervading. Why? Because the scripture attributes omnipresence to it: "He is indeed this great, unborn Self, who is this consciousness, all-pervading" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22). Also, the scripture says: "This Self is indeed Brahman, the experiencer of all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19). If the soul were atomic, it could not experience sensations throughout the entire body. Moreover, the scripture speaks of the soul's identity with the all-pervading Brahman: "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7). Therefore, the soul is all-pervading. However, although the soul is all-pervading, it is spoken of as moving or entering the body because it is associated with the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*). Just as the light of a lamp, though pervasive, appears to move when the lamp is moved, so too the soul, though all-pervading, appears to move due to its association with the subtle body. Thus, the scriptural descriptions of the soul's movement and entry are metaphorical, referring to the movement of the subtle body. Now, we shall consider the nature of the soul's departure in relation to the senses. Does the soul depart taking the senses with it, or do the senses remain in the body? On this point, the opponent maintains that the senses remain in the body, because the scripture says: "When he departs, his speech merges into his mind" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.5). This suggests that the senses merge into the mind rather than departing with the soul. To this, we reply: The soul departs taking the senses with it. Why? Because the scripture says: "When a person departs from this world, he goes forth together with his consciousness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2). Here, "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to the mind and the senses, as they are the instruments of consciousness. Furthermore, the scripture speaks of the soul's departure from the body as being accompanied by the vital breath (*prāṇa*): "When he departs, his speech merges into his mind, his mind into his breath, his breath into heat, and heat into the Supreme Deity" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.6). Since the vital breath is the leader of the senses, and since the
The Fourth Chapter, Fourth Quarter. [In this quarter, there is an investigation into the attainment of Brahman and the state of existence in the world of Brahman. 1.
The Section on Manifestation upon Attainment (Sūtras 1–3).
"Manifestation with its own [form], because of the scriptural word.
(BBs 4.4.1) Thus it is heard in scripture: "This serene being (saṃprasāda), having risen from this body and having reached the highest light, manifests in its own form.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: does it manifest by means of some adventitious attribute, as in the case of places of enjoyment such as the world of the gods, or rather by the self alone?
What, then, is the position reached?
It would be a manifestation in some adventitious form, as in other locations,
since liberation is also established as being a fruit.

And because "is manifested" (*abhiniṣpadyate*) is a synonym for "arising," if manifestation were merely by way of its own nature (*svarūpamātra*), it would have been perceived even in previous states, since its own nature does not depart; therefore,
it is manifested by means of some particular distinction.
This being the case, we reply: he manifests by means of the Self alone, and not by means of any other attribute.
Why? Because of the word "own" in the phrase "he is perfected in his own form.
For otherwise, the qualification "by the word 'own'" would be inappropriate.
[Objection: But surely the word *sva* (own) will have the intended meaning of "belonging to oneself" (*ātmīya*). [Reply: No, because that is inexpressible.
For in whatever form something is produced, it is logically possible for that very thing to belong to itself; therefore, the qualification "by oneself" (*svena*) would be purposeless.
But in the case of its being spoken of as "self," it is meaningful in that it is manifested solely through its own nature, and not through any adventitious or other form. // 1 //
In the preceding section, the attainment of the effected Brahman (kāryabrahma) by those who meditate on Brahman was stated;

now, intending to elaborate upon their specific lordly powers pertaining to the world of Brahman (brāhmalaukika) in the latter half of this section, [the author] first describes the state of being the undifferentiated Brahman attainable through the most venerable higher knowledge (paravidyā): "Upon attaining [Brahman], there is manifestation [of one's true nature], because of the word 'own'. (Sūtra 4.4.1).

Having cited the scriptural passage concerning the fruit of knowledge that is devoid of qualities (nirguṇavidyā), he states the doubt— using the word "thus" (evam)— regarding whether the term "own" (sva) denotes one's own adventitious form or one's own essential nature.
The result is that, according to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), liberation would be no different from heaven, whereas according to the established conclusion (siddhānta), there is a distinction.

In this regard, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by means of the scriptural passage concerning "attainment" (*abhiniṣpatti*), which is supported by the logic that "liberation there is adventitious because it is an effect, like heaven": "What [is it]? and so forth.

Considering that the logical argument is sublated by the direct hearing of the word "own" (*sva-śabda*), and that "attainment" refers to the modification of the mental faculty (*vṛtti*) consisting of direct realization, while the arising of the destruction of bondage is merely figurative, he establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "Thus... (*evam*).

The word "own" (sva) is used for the purpose of negating the idea that liberation is something newly acquired as a result; for if it were to mean "belonging to oneself," it would be a redundant restatement of what is already established—this is the meaning. //1//
But what is the distinction between the previous states and this one, given that there is equality in the non-deprivation of its own nature? To this, he says:
[The soul is] liberated according to its own declaration (BBs 4.4.2).
That which was described here as "attaining [the state]" remains established in its very pure self, completely released from all bonds.

However, in the previous state, it was said that "it becomes blind," "as if it weeps," and "it has gone to utter destruction"; thus, the distinction lies in the fact that in those cases, the self was defiled by these three conditions.

But how is it understood that "this one is now liberated"? [The author] says: "Because of the formal proposition (*pratijñā*). For instance, having proposed the Self—devoid of the defects of the three states—as the subject to be explained with the words, "I shall explain this very same thing to you further" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.9.3; 8.10.4; 8.11.3), [the text continues]: "Verily, when one is bodiless, pleasure and pain do not touch him" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.1).
Having introduced the subject in this way, he concludes with the words: "He attains his own true form; he is the Supreme Person" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3).
Likewise, at the beginning of the narrative itself, it says: "The Self which is free from evil... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1).
Thus, the aforementioned declaration refers exclusively to the liberated self.
Furthermore, the well-known status of liberation as a "fruit" depends merely upon the cessation of bondage, not upon the production of something previously non-existent.
As for the statement that one "attains" (*abhiniṣpadyate*), which is a synonym for arising, that too is relative to a prior state, just as when a disease is cured, one is said to "attain health."
Therefore, there is no fault. // 2 //
He cites another Sūtra: "Who, moreover...

For in the waking state, one possesses bodily attributes such as blindness; however, in a dream, one is actually killed by someone. Furthermore, due to the loss of a son or other loved ones, one even seems to weep.
The meaning is that there is a great difference: in deep sleep, [the self] is as if destroyed due to the absence of specific cognition;
during the state of bondage, it remains with a defiled nature; but in liberation, it abides as one whose all suffering has dissolved and who exists as a self of full bliss shining forth on all sides.
The Self [is meant] because of the context.
But how, then, is it said that he is "released," given that [the scripture says], "having attained the highest light" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3)?
Thus, he makes it known that this [word] has as its scope only the realm of effects (*kārya*),
because the word "light" (*jyotis*) is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of elemental light (*bhautika-jyotis*).
And no one who has not transcended the sphere of modifications (*vikāra*) can possibly be liberated.
[Objection: Because it is well known that a modification (*vikāra*) is subject to suffering (*ārtatva*).

[Reply: This is not a fault, because by virtue of the context, what is indicated by the word "light" (*jyotis*) is the Self described as "the Self which is free from evil, free from old age, and free from death" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1).
For thus, since the Supreme Self is the subject under discussion, it is not possible to understand the word "light" as referring to material light;
for that would entail abandoning the subject at hand and introducing a topic not under discussion.
Moreover, the word "light" is seen to be applied even to the Self, as in: "The gods [meditate] on that light which is the light of lights" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.16).
And this has been explained at [Brahma-sūtra 1.3.40]. // 3 //
"Within the sphere of activity" means that the light has been attained as an effect.
To the question, "Even if one has attained the effect, would one not be liberated?", he says: "And not having transcended [it]. //3//
