[The soul
Because it is seen as non-differentiated.
Regarding the one who, having attained the supreme light, manifests in his own true form: does he remain distinct from the Supreme Self, or does he abide in a state of non-differentiation?
In this regard, [the text says]: "There he moves around" (8.12.3).

To instruct one who holds the view that the liberated soul remains in a state of distinction—on account of the mention of the locus and the subject to be located in the phrase "having reached the Light" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3), and on account of the mention of agent and object—it is explained that the liberated soul remains as non-distinct from the Supreme Self.
Why? Because it is so seen [in scripture].
For instance: "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7),
"I am Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10),
and "where one sees nothing else" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1).
"But there is not a second thing existing, other than that, distinct from it, which one might see" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23).
Passages such as these show the supreme Self as indeed non-distinct.
And it is logical that the fruit corresponds exactly to the vision, according to the principle of "as one intends, so one becomes."
And such statements as, "Just as pure water poured into pure water becomes exactly like that,
so does the self of the sage who understands become, O Gautama" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 4.15), which are intended to define the nature of the liberated one, demonstrate non-differentiation alone.
There are also illustrations such as the river and the ocean;
however, a description of differentiation is employed even where there is no actual difference, as in:
"In what, O Blessed One, is he established? In his own majesty" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1).
Thus, it is because of such scriptural observations as, "He who delights in the Self, who plays with the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2). // 4 //
Because it is seen as non-distinct.

Since there is doubt regarding the difference or non-difference of Brahman—arising from the disputes of various theorists concerning whether liberation consists in abiding in one's own nature—he states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) that there is absolute difference, and then declares the established conclusion (siddhānta) with the words "Of whom... (yasya). //4//
END BsCom_4,4.2.4 START BsCom_4,4.3.5 3. Section concerning the Brahmin (Brāhma-adhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 5–7.
"Jaimini [holds that the soul manifests] in its Brahmanic form, on account of the introductory statements and so forth. (BS 4.4.5).
It has been established that in the passage, "by his own nature" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.4), the soul manifests in the form of the Self alone, and not in some adventitious, other form.

Now, however, in response to the desire to know its specific nature, it is stated that his own form is the Brahman-nature, beginning with freedom from sin and ending with the power of true resolve, as well as omniscience and omnipotence; the teacher Jaimini maintains that he becomes manifest in that very form.
Why? Because its being so is understood from the introductory statements and other such passages; for instance:
"That Self which is free from evil" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1), and so forth, ending with "whose desires are true, whose resolves are true" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1).
Thus, by this introductory statement, he makes known the nature of the Self;
likewise, with the words, "There he moves about, laughing, playing, and rejoicing" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3), he reveals its form as sovereign power.
And [it is said]: "He has freedom of movement in all worlds" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2).
Furthermore, designations such as "the omniscient one" and "the lord of all" will thus be appropriately established. // 5 //

Jaimini has stated that regarding the nature of Brahman as taught by Bādarāyaṇa, there is a disagreement among sages as to whether it remains endowed with attributes such as omniscience through its true existence; or whether, because those attributes are absolutely non-existent like the horn of a hare, it remains as pure consciousness alone; or whether, although in reality it is pure consciousness, it possesses attributed omniscience and so forth from the perspective of the empirical dealings of other individual souls.
Since there is doubt, he states the initial prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words beginning "now" (*adhunā*).
It should be understood that the very establishment of each respective position is the result.

The meaning of the injunction "he is to be sought" (*so 'nveṣṭavyaḥ*) is the subject matter (*uddeśa*), while the formulation beginning with "that which is the Self" (*ya ātmā*) constitutes the meaning of the formal presentation (*upanyāsa*).
By the phrase "and so forth" (*ādipadāt*), the mention of "injunction" (*vidhi*) is included.
Among these, an injunction is that which makes known what was previously unknown; he states this with the words "thus, there... (*tathā sa tatra*).

However, the designation "omniscient" and so forth is indeed not a mere reference (*uddeśa*); because there is no injunction, it is not an injunction either, since it is stated as an established fact (*siddhavat*). This is the meaning. //5//
"By means of the subtle element of consciousness alone, because he consists of that," so says Auḍulomi. (BBs 4.4.6)
Although attributes such as freedom from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*) are indeed indicated as distinct qualities, nevertheless, these are merely born of verbal conceptualization (*śabdavikalpa*).
For in that context, only the cessation of evil and so forth is understood;
however, consciousness alone is the true nature (*svarūpa*) of this Self. Therefore, it is logical that its manifestation occurs solely through that essential nature.
And thus the Śruti will be supported by such passages as: "Verily, my dear, this Self is without interior and without exterior, entirely a mass of consciousness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.13).

As for [qualities] such as having true desires (*satyakāmatva*), although they are stated as attributes of the essential nature of the reality itself—as in "his desires are true"—[they are nevertheless figurative].
Nevertheless, because they are dependent on their connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), their own nature cannot exist as pure consciousness;
for multiplicity of form has been denied.
Indeed, the multiplicity of forms in Brahman has been refuted in the sūtra: "The Supreme does not possess both characteristics even from the standpoint of location" (Brahma-sūtra 3.2.11).

For this very reason, even the mention of eating and so forth is intended merely to signify the absence of suffering for the sake of praise, just like the passage beginning with "delighting in the Self" (ātmarati).
Indeed, primary forms of delight, play, and sexual union cannot be attributed to the Self, because they require a second object.

Therefore, the teacher Auḍulomi maintains that one becomes manifest as the nature of pure consciousness—tranquil, indefinable, and from which the entire phenomenal world has been entirely dispelled. // 6 //
Refuting the reality of properties such as "truth" (satyatva) and so forth, he states the position of their absolute non-existence with the words "by mere consciousness" (cititanmātreṇa).
"Consciousness" (citi) is sentience (caitanya);

those [properties] which arise from conceptual constructions (vikalpa)—such as verbal cognition and the like—which are unreal cognitions, are "absolutely non-existent," that is to say, they do not exist at all.

Anticipating the objection that while non-existent entities (abhāva-dharma) may lack existence, existent entities (bhāva-dharma) must possess it, he states "satyakāma" etc., asserting that even those are non-existent because they are merely adventitious (aupādhika). To the question of how scriptural passages concerning eating and so forth apply to the liberated one who is pure consciousness (cinmātra), he says "ata eva ca," meaning: precisely because of the negation of all attributes (dharma). //6//
Even so, because of the introductory statement and because of its prior existence, Bādarāyaṇa maintains that there is no contradiction. (BS 4.4.7)

Even though the ultimate nature is thus admitted to be pure consciousness alone, the teacher Bādarāyaṇa considers there to be no contradiction, because from the perspective of empirical usage (vyavahāra), the Brahmanic form of sovereignty— previously understood through such means as scriptural declarations— is not denied. //7//

The two positions—that phenomena are real or that they are absolutely non-existent—are untenable; for this would result in the sublation of the scriptural texts on non-duality (*advaita*) as well as the scriptural texts concerning omniscience and other attributes, along with their conventional usage. Therefore, he establishes the third position as superior with the words "even so" (*evamapi*).

Here, some are deluded, thinking: "Since there is an absence of ignorance for one liberated through the knowledge of undivided pure consciousness (*akhaṇḍacinmātra*), how can there be a connection with phenomena born of ignorance?"
They should be informed as follows:
those very attributes of the Lord are designated by other liberated souls as belonging to the conscious self (cidātman).
Nor should it be argued that because there is only one root-ignorance (mūlāvidyā), once that is destroyed, how could there be another liberated soul?
We do not say that upon its destruction there is the activity of another soul;

rather, we say that when a portion of it is destroyed, those souls who were previously characterized by the conceit of the two internal bodies composed of that portion become, through the limiting adjuncts of other portions, the agents of activity in liberation.
If it is asked: "In that case, why is the position of manifold ignorance (*anekavidyā*) not preferred, since the distinction between souls is necessary?"—we reply: No.

The view that there is a plurality of primordial natures (*prakṛti*) and a differentiation of the phenomenal world for each individual soul is rejected because it involves the burden of numerous meanings not supported by authoritative scripture. Therefore, the position of a single ignorance (*ekāvidyā*), which is accepted by all the elders, is superior;
and the distinction between bondage and liberation is established through the differentiation of parts (*aṃśabheda*). This is the summary. //7//
Section on Volition (Saṃkalpa-adhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 8–9 4. [The section concerning] volition. Sūtras 8–9.
"But [the attainment of objects] is from mere volition alone, because of the scriptural statement. (BBs 4.4.8).
In the *Hārdavidyā*, it is heard: "If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers, by his mere volition the fathers arise for him" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.2.1), and so forth.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: is volition alone the cause for the arising of the fathers and others, or is it accompanied by some other instrumental cause?
In this regard, even though there is the scriptural hearing that [the creation occurs] "from mere volition" (*saṃkalpād eva*), it is logical that other causes are required, just as in the world.
Just as in the world, for people like us, the attainment of fathers and so forth occurs through volition as well as causes such as going [to them], so too it may be for the liberated one.
In this way, nothing contrary to what is observed will be postulated.

The statement "by mere volition alone" is said with reference to the ease with which the collection of auxiliary means for accomplishing the desired object is obtained—just as in the case of a king. Furthermore, fathers and others who arise from mere volition would not be capable of providing abundant enjoyment, because they would be as unstable as the manifestations of a daydream.
This being the position, we reply: the arising of fathers and others occurs indeed from volition alone.
Why? Because of the scriptural statement.
For the scripture stating, "By his mere volition alone, his fathers arise" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.2.1), would be contradicted if there were a dependence on any other instrumental cause.

Furthermore, even if another cause were to conform to volition, let it be so; however, it is not accepted that this other cause is to be produced by a separate effort, because prior to its production, there would be the undesirable consequence of volition being fruitless. Moreover, the inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*)—namely, "as in the world"—does not apply to a matter that is to be understood through scripture.

Moreover, by the power of their resolve alone, these [objects] possess stability for as long as they are required; this is because the resolve of one who is liberated is distinct from ordinary resolve. // 8 //

Thus, the fruit of higher knowledge (*paravidyā*) has been stated; now, the fruit of lower knowledge (*aparavidyā*) is being elaborated: "But [it is] from mere volition (*saṃkalpa*) alone, because of the scriptural statement.
Since the particle *eva* (alone) is common to both the exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*) and the exclusion of connection with something else (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*), a doubt arises:
does the volition of the worshipper who has gone to the world of Brahman depend upon some other effort?

The meaning of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: [The fulfillment of desires occurs] because it is a conceptualization of the collection of enjoyments (*bhogasāmagrī*), just like the conceptualization of ourselves and others. Nor is there a contradiction with the particle *eva* (only), because by means of the conceptualization, it excludes the impossibility of the collection [of conditions], and thus has the sense of ease; furthermore, if effort were not admitted, the nourishment of enjoyment would not be established.
In this regard, the result is the conformity with worldly conduct;
however, according to the Siddhānta, the Veda teaches that by the power of knowledge (*vidyā*), the mere volition (*saṃkalpa*) itself accomplishes the nourishment of enjoyment.
Furthermore, if even after the volition for enjoyment there were a dependence upon external causes to be accomplished through further effort, then [the attainment of those causes]—

Since there would be a failure of a previously formed resolve due to a delay in enjoyment, the scripture stating that his resolves are true implies no dependence on other efforts; thus he says: "But even another cause... (8).
And for this very reason, it has no other sovereign. BBs_4,4.9.
And for this very reason, because his resolve is never in vain, the wise man becomes one who has no other lord; the meaning is that no other person becomes his master.
For even an ordinary person, when forming a resolve, does not conceive of himself as being under the dominion of another if a way [to avoid it] exists.
And the Śruti shows this: "Now, those who depart from here having discovered the Self and these true desires—for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.6). 9.
Now, one might ask: how can the accomplishment of enjoyment through mere volition occur for the knower who is dependent upon Īśvara? To this he says: "For this very reason.
The sense is that since the attributes of Īśvara themselves have become manifest in the knower, there is no failure of his volition. //9//
END BsCom_4,4.4.9 START BsCom_4,4.5.10-11 Section on Non-existence (Abhāva-adhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 10–14.

Bādari says there is non-existence [of external objects], for it is so stated [in scripture]. Since the scriptural passage, "By his mere volition (*saṃkalpa*), the fathers arise" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.2.1), and others, establish that the mind is the instrument of volition, it is proven that the mind alone exists.
Furthermore, it is examined whether the body and senses exist or do not exist for the wise one who has attained lordship.
In this regard, the teacher Bādari maintains that there is an absence of both body and senses for the wise one who is being magnified.
Why?

For thus says the sacred tradition: "Beholding these desires with the mind, he rejoices" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.5), and "those which are in the world of Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.13.1). [This would be impossible] if, at liberation, the body and the senses were separated from the mind. // 10 //
"Jaimini [holds] that there is existence, because of the mention of manifoldness.
(BBs 4.4.11) But the teacher Jaimini considers that for the liberated one, there is existence of the body along with its sense organs, just as there is of the mind;
for it is said: "He becomes singlefold, he becomes threefold" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.2).
By such passages, they teach the manifold conceptualization of non-existence.
For this manifold nature could not be direct without a difference in the underlying substratum (*śarīra*).
Even though this manifold conceptualization of non-existence is recited in the context of the knowledge of the earth (*bhūmavidyā*), which is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), nevertheless...

This very sovereignty, which exists even in the state of possessing qualities (saguṇa), is proclaimed for the purpose of praising the knowledge of the Infinite (bhūmavidyā); therefore, it presents itself as the fruit of the saguṇa-vidyā. // 11 //

By means of the qualification "with a mind possessing the word *eva*," which excludes connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there is an absence of the body and so forth; for Bādari says, "He [the soul] is non-existent, for thus it is stated.
Here too, because of the dispute among disputants, there is doubt;
therein, the two positions—that the body and so forth do not exist at all, and that they always exist—are the prima facie view.
The established position (siddhāntapakṣa) should be understood as follows: they exist or do not exist according to the distinction of time and one's desire;
however, the distinction is that the fruit [of this view] is the preeminence of those respective scriptural statements. // 10 // // 11 //
[End of BsCom_4,4.5.10] [End of BsCom_4,4.5.11] [Start of BsCom_4,4.5.12–14]
It is said:
"Bādarāyaṇa [holds it to be] twofold, like the twelve-day sacrifice;
therefore. Master Bādarāyaṇa, moreover, because he observes scriptural indications of both kinds, considers the twofold nature to be correct: when he wills embodiedness, then he becomes embodied.
But when there is bodilessness, then one is "bodiless," because of the truthfulness of one's resolve and because of the variety of that resolve.
It is like the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).

Just as the twelve-day sacrifice is both a sacrificial session (*sattra*) and a non-session (*ahīna*), because both characteristics are seen in the scriptural texts, so too is this [the *jyotiṣṭoma*]. 12.
In the absence of the body, [the objects of desire] are possible as in the state of the intermediate realm (saṃdhyavat).

When there is an absence of the body together with the senses, then, just as in the intermediate state (saṃdhye sthāne), even though the body, senses, and objects do not exist, the desires for fathers and so forth consist of mere perception; likewise, they would be so in liberation as well. Thus.
For this is indeed logical. // 13 //
In the case of existence, it is like being awake.
Furthermore, just as in the waking state the desires for a father and so forth exist while the body is present, so too is this possible for the liberated one. (4.14)

"Like the twelve-day sacrifice": the status of the twelve-day sacrifice as a *satra* is established because it is understood from the injunctive text "those who, knowing thus, enter upon the *satra*" (*ya evaṃvidvāṃsaḥ satram upayanti*), and because its characteristic as a *satra* consists in being enjoined by the terms "they sit" (*āsate*) or "they enter upon" (*upayanti*). This is the settled rule.

Likewise, because the injunction "one should cause one desiring offspring to sacrifice with the twelve-day rite" (dvādaśāhena) is seen as a *yajati*-codanā (a prescription for a sacrifice), and because it is understood that its performance is restricted to specific officiants, it possesses the character of an *ahīna* (a non-soma-less sacrifice), just like the *dvirātra* and other such rites; this is the meaning. // 12 // // 13 // // 14 //
Topic 6: The Lamp (Pradīpa) Sūtras 15–16 END BsCom_4,4.5.12-14 START BsCom_4,4.5.15 6 pradīpa adhikaraṇam / sū. 15-16: The Topic of the Lamp. Sūtras 15–16.
"The entry [of the soul] is like that of a lamp; for thus the scripture shows:
'Jaimini [maintains] the existence [of a body], because of the mention of meditative reflection on various forms' (Brahma-sūtra 4.4.11).
Herein, the state of possessing a body for the liberated one is stated.

In that regard, concerning the threefold manifestation and so forth, when there is the production of multiple bodies, a doubt arises as to whether those bodies are produced without a self (*nirātmaka*), like wooden automata, or with a self (*sātmaka*), like our own bodies.
Since a distinction between the self and the mind is untenable because [the mind] is conjoined with only one body, it follows that the other bodies are without a self.
This being the position reached, the author replies: "The entry [of the self] is like a lamp."

Just as a single lamp attains the state of many lamps through its connection with the power of transformation (*vikāra-śakti*), so too the wise one, though being one, attains manifold states through his connection with sovereign power (*aiśvarya*) and enters all bodies. Why? Because the scripture demonstrates the manifoldness of the one, stating: "He becomes one-fold, he becomes three-fold, five-fold, seven-fold, nine-fold" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.2), and so forth.
This [explanation] is not tenable either under the assumption that [the body] is like a wooden machine, nor under the theory of the entry of another soul.
Furthermore, the activity of bodies devoid of a self is impossible.
As for the claim that the connection with multiple bodies is impossible because a distinction between the self and the mind cannot be established—
This is not a fault;
for, by virtue of his power of true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpatva*), he will create other bodies that possess minds following after his single mind.
And once those have been created, his status as the presiding controller will be appropriate through the distinction of the self [in each] due to the difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
And this very [power] is the yogins' performance of the application of multiple bodies in the Yoga treatises. (15)
The entry [of the self] is like that of a lamp.
Because one observes both [the presence and absence of experience] in the case of assuming created bodies through mere volition, he states a doubt: "bhāvam" (existence).

The prima facie conclusion (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that since the beginningless subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) exists in only one single body, the experience of enjoyment in the many created bodies is not established.
Considering that this is established in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), he explains the Sūtra with the words beginning "Just as" (*yathā*).
By such scriptural passages as "He becomes one-fold, three-fold, five-fold," etc., it is stated that the transformation into multiple forms belongs only to the knower (*vidvas*).
However, the knower is neither the body nor pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).
However, the self is conditioned by the subtle body (liṅga),
and its multiplicity is not possible without a difference in that subtle body.
Therefore, on the strength of scripture, one must accept that this single, beginningless subtle body undergoes differentiation by entering into multiple bodies.

Although there is an absolute difference between the original lamp and the lamps produced in other wicks, the difference in the subtle body (*liṅga*) is not intrinsic but caused by the difference in bodies; for if the subtle body were different in itself, the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) conditioned by it would differ, making recollection impossible.
Furthermore, the creation of multiple adventitious subtle bodies would result in the fallacy of *asatkāryavāda* (the theory that the effect is non-existent prior to its production).

Nevertheless, because the identity of the individual instances is superimposed upon them through the unity of the universal *pradīpatva* (lamp-ness), the similarity between the example and the thing exemplified (*dārṣṭāntika*) should be understood.

Thus, just as a lamp enters into many wicks, so too, by the power of the yoga of knowledge (*vidyā-yoga*), there is a simultaneous entry into multiple bodies due to the pervasiveness of the body of the knower (*vidval-liṅga*); such is the meaning of the Sūtra. He says "This is not so" to show that the scriptural teaching of the knower’s manifold state would otherwise be untenable.
For this reason as well, he states that there is a self (sātmakatva), saying: "And not of those that are soulless" (*na ca nirātmakānām*).

That mind which has been present in a single body since beginningless time continues to follow [the self] even when residing in other bodies, because it is possible for those minds situated in those [new] bodies to be governed by it.
Regarding this, he cites the consensus of the Yogaśāstra, saying: "This very... (*eṣaiva*).
"From mere *asmitā* (ego-sense), the minds of emanation proceed; one mind is the motivator for many"—thus was it aphorized by the Blessed Patañjali.
The meaning is that through the mere conceit of the yogin, minds of emanation arise within the bodies of emanation, and the primordial mind (*anādicitta*) is their regulator. //15//

But how can the sovereignty of the liberated one— characterized by the entry into multiple bodies and so forth— be admitted, given that [the scripture] says, "Then by what means, and whom, would he know? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15)?

"But there is not a second thing existing, other than that, distinct from it, which he might cognize" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.30), and "He becomes one with the waters, a seer without duality" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.32)—
since such scriptural passages preclude specific cognition, the author reads the following reply:
For it is declared that [the state of being unmanifest] depends on either deep sleep (*svāpyaya*) or liberation (*saṃpatti*);

"deep sleep" (*svāpyaya*) is the state of profound slumber, according to the Śruti: "He has gone to his own self (*svam apīto bhavati*), therefore they say of him 'he sleeps' (*svapiti')" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1).
"Liberation" (*saṃpatti*) is absolute isolation (*kaivalya*).
This is because of the Vedic scripture: "Being Brahman itself, he attains Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6).
This statement regarding the absence of specific designations refers to either one of those two states;
in some cases it is spoken with reference to the state of deep sleep (suṣupta), and in others with reference to the state of absolute liberation (kaivalya).

How is this understood? Because it has been explicitly revealed in that very context by virtue of the subject matter: "Arising from these elements, one perishes after them; there is no consciousness after death" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad);
and "But where everything has become the Self alone for him" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14);
and "Where, being asleep, he desires no desire and sees no dream" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.19; Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 5).
This is because of such scriptural passages as these.
However, this state of abiding in the ripening of knowledge with attributes (saguṇavidyā) is merely another state, like heaven and so forth, wherein this lordly power (aiśvarya) is described.
Therefore, there is no fault. // 16 //
He states the doubt to be dispelled by the subsequent sūtra with the words, "But how?
[The term] *salila* means like water; that is to say, clear.

However, the statement "there is no second thing there" is spoken in some places with reference to deep sleep (*suṣupti*), as in "by what means could one see whom? and so forth, while in other places it is spoken with reference to liberation (*mukti*). Thus, he says "svāpyaya" (in deep sleep), meaning that such statements regarding the absence of specific cognition depend on either deep sleep or liberation; they are not contradicted by the description of the enjoyment of one who meditates on the Saguna Brahman, because their subject matters are distinct. This is due to the force of that very Śruti's context, and by virtue of the sections concerning deep sleep and so forth.
The meaning is that since the fact that spoken words depend upon one or the other has been revealed, it is understood from that [source].
Here, the distinction is that the passage beginning with "samutthāna" concerns liberation (mukti), while the passage beginning with "yatra suptāḥ" concerns deep sleep (supti). //16//

The Section Concerning the Activity of the World (Jagadvyāpārādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 17–22.
"Except for the activity of the world, because of the context and because [the Lord] is not present [to them].

(BBs 4.4.17) There arises a doubt: do those who, through meditation on the Brahman with attributes, attain union (*sāyujya*) with the Lord together with their mind, possess unlimited sovereignty or limited sovereignty?
What, then, is the prima facie position?
Their sovereignty must indeed be absolute and unrestrained, as evidenced by such scriptural passages as:

"He attains self-rule" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.6.2), "All the gods bring him tribute" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.5.3), and "For them there is freedom of movement in all worlds" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2; 8.1.6).
"From such scriptural passages as these," so it was argued.
To this, the author of the Sūtras replies: "Excluding the activity of the world.

Excluding the activity of the world—namely, its creation and so forth—the other sovereignty consisting of *aṇimā* and the rest may belong to the liberated souls; however, the activity of the world belongs only to the eternally established Lord (*īśvara*).
Why? Because He is the subject under discussion there, whereas the others are not proximate;
for the Supreme Lord alone is authorized over the activity of the world, since the teaching regarding origination and so forth is given with reference to Him alone.

And because [the Lord] is the basis for the term "eternal," whereas the other [beings'] sovereignty, such as *aṇimā* and so forth, is heard in scripture as being preceded by seeking and desiring to know;
therefore, they are not present in the activity of the world.

Furthermore, precisely because these [subordinate beings] possess minds, there might occasionally arise a contradiction due to their lack of unanimity—such that one intends stability while another intends destruction.

If, however, the absence of contradiction were maintained by asserting that the intention of one follows the intention of another, then it would be established that the others are entirely dependent upon the will of the Supreme Lord. (Sūtra 17:
"Except for the activity of the world."

The connection [of this section] arises because there is a rebuttal here of the sovereignty described in passages such as "by mere volition" (*saṃkalpād eva*), by showing that its scope is distinct from the creation of the world and so forth.
Doubt arises because both possibilities are observed.
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) results in the plurality of Lords.

In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, because those possessed of knowledge (*vidyā-yogins*) are subject to the governance of the Lord, it is established that the agency of the world belongs solely to the one eternally perfected Lord; this is the distinction. At the time of creation following dissolution, the creative agency preceded by reflection (*īkṣaṇa*) which is introduced in the Scripture belongs to Him alone, and the cosmic activity of the world—such as its governance and so forth—is His alone. For such reflection is not possible for those who meditate upon [the Lord] without a body.
Furthermore, since God is eternally established and is accessible through scripture alone, his status as the creator of the world is logical;
however, this is not the case for individual souls (jīvas) whose attainments are obtained through His grace. Thus he says: "And because [the status of the creator] is based on the eternal word.
Moreover, if all the knowers were of equal authority, there would be mutual contradiction among them.
If others were subordinate to one [of them], then there would be only one Lord; thus he says: "Because of possessing a mind" (samanaskatvāt) //17//
If it is argued that [the Lord's form] is directly taught [in scripture], we say no; for what is stated refers to those situated in the spheres of authority.

Now, as for what was stated— that because of the direct instruction in passages such as "He attains self-sovereignty" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.6.2), it is logical that those who possess knowledge should have unimpeded lordship— that must be refuted.
To this, it is said:
This is not a fault,

because it refers to one who resides within the [divine] sphere of authority (*ādhikārika-maṇḍala*). That which is called the attainment of self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) is said to be dependent precisely upon that Supreme Lord (*para īśvara*), who is the special authority established in the abodes such as the solar orb (*savitṛmaṇḍala*).
For this reason, the text immediately following says, "He attains the Lord of the Mind" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.6.2).
What is meant by this is that he attains that Lord who is the master of all minds and is already established from before.
And in accordance with that very point, the text further says, "He becomes the Lord of Speech, the Lord of Sight, the Lord of Hearing, and the Lord of Discernment" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.6.2).
In the same way, elsewhere as well, sovereignty should be applied to others as being entirely dependent upon the eternally established Lord, according to the possibility of each case. // 18 //

The term "adhikārika" means that he appoints [beings] such as Āditya to their respective offices; furthermore, it refers to the one residing in the solar orb (maṇḍala), because He is said to be the goal to be attained.
The Lord of the Mind is the Supreme Self (paramātman) dwelling within the solar orb, as expressed in the mantra: "We meditate upon that most excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ."

According to the Vedic scripture, "May He impel our intellects," it follows that if independent sovereignty (*svārājya*) had been previously described as absolute and unrestricted, one would not have stated that it is to be attained only in the presence of the Lord.
Therefore, the intended meaning is that independent sovereignty pertains to enjoyment, but not to the creation and other functions of the world.
He states that even such qualities as eloquence and the like are dependent on the Lord of Lords by saying, "in accordance with that.
He extends the aforementioned principle to passages concerning the freedom to act as one wishes and so forth by saying, "thus. //18//
And it does not abide in modifications, for thus it declares its state. (BBs 4.4.19)

Moreover, the supreme form of the Lord, which is eternally liberated, is not subject to transformation alone; the substratum, such as the solar orb and so forth, is not merely within the sphere of modification.
For thus the sacred tradition (Āmnāya) declares its twofold state: "Such is His greatness, and yet the Puruṣa is greater than that;
all beings constitute but one quarter of Him."
"Three quarters of Him are the immortal in heaven" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.6),
and so forth.
Nor can it be said that those who have other supports attain that changeless form, because they do not possess that specific resolve.

Therefore, it should be understood that just as [devotees] remain established in the qualified form alone without attaining the qualityless form of the Supreme Lord who possesses two forms, so too those in the qualified state remain established with limited power alone without attaining unbounded sovereignty. // 19 //

Having raised the objection that the activity of the world is attainable by the worshiper because it resides in the object of worship—just like the fulfillment of one's will and so forth—the author states the following sūtra to point out an instance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the attributeless nature (*nirguṇasvarūpa*) residing in the object of worship: "And [the Lord] does not abide in modifications" (Sūtra 1.2.19).
And perception and inference likewise demonstrate this. (BBs 4.4.20)
Moreover, both Śruti and Smṛti demonstrate that the supreme light is not subject to modification:
"There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire" (Kaṭha 5.15;
Śvetāśvatara 6.14; Muṇḍaka 2.2.10).
And [as it is said]: "Neither the sun, nor the moon, nor fire illumines that" (Gītā 15.6).
Thus, the intention is that the quality of being beyond the cycle of modifications is well-established for the supreme light. // 20 //
He states the authoritative proof for the nature of the one devoid of qualities (nirguṇasvarūpa) with the words "and because [the two gods] show" (darśayataśca).

Just as the state of being devoid of qualities is not attained due to the absence of knowledge, so too the status of being the creator of the world and so forth is not attained due to the absence of meditation (dhyāna). And the absence of meditation is due to the absence of an injunction; this is the intended meaning. //20//
And because there is a mark indicating equality in respect to enjoyment alone. (BS 4.4.21)

Furthermore, the sovereignty of those who rely on transformations is not absolute, because it is heard in scripture that their mere enjoyment is equal to that of the eternally established Lord: "They say, 'Verily, this world is measured by water';
as all beings protect this deity, so do all beings protect one who knows thus; therefore, for her..."
This is because of indicative marks of difference found in such passages as, "He wins union with and residence in the same world as that deity" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.23). // 21 //

To that lay follower who has gone to the world of Brahmā, Hiraṇyagarbha says: "Indeed, these waters, which are of the nature of nectar, are measured out and enjoyed by me; the meaning is that that world of yours also is characterized by water that is nectar. He cites another scriptural passage: "Just as... The meaning of "just as" is that it is an illustration regarding the equality of enjoyment.
The word *api* (also) has the sense of "even" (*ittham*).
The syntactical connection is: "even [attaining] co-residence (*salokatām api*).
*Sāyujyam* means having a common body, or liberation attained through gradual stages. //21//

[Objection: But if this were so, then because their sovereignty possesses degrees of excellence, it would be finite; consequently, the recurrence of these [liberated souls] would follow as a logical consequence. To this, the venerable teacher Bādarāyaṇa recites the following reply.
"No return, on account of the word; no return, on account of the word.

Those who go by the path of the gods (*devayāna*), which is provided with channels and rays and has the stages beginning with light (*arcis*), to the world of Brahman characterized by the attributes mentioned in the scriptures—in that world of Brahman where, as it is said, "the two oceans Ara and Nyāra exist in the third heaven from here," and where there is the *aśvattha* tree—[for them there is no return].

Having reached that [world]— wherein the Soma-pressing takes place, wherein lies the unconquerable city, and wherein is the golden abode built by the Lord for Brahman— and which is described in manifold ways in various passages such as the Mantras and Arthavādas— they do not return after having experienced their enjoyment, as is the case with the world of the Moon and other such realms. Why is this?
"Going upwards by that, one attains immortality" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.6; Kaṭha Upaniṣad 6.16);
"For them there is no return" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.15);
"He reaches the world of Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.15.1).
This is known from such scriptural passages as "and he does not return again" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.15.1).

Furthermore, even though their sovereignty is finite, the manner in which there is no return has been described in the Brahmasūtra (4.3.10): "At the dissolution of the effect, [they go] with its presiding deity to that which is beyond this."
But for those whose darkness has been utterly destroyed by right vision (*samyak-darśana*) and who are intent upon eternally perfected *nirvāṇa*, non-return is indeed established;

for it is precisely by taking refuge in them that non-return is established for those intent upon eternally perfected *nirvāṇa*. Indeed, by taking refuge in them, the establishment of non-return is achieved even for those who have taken refuge in the one with qualities (*saguṇa*).
"Non-return, on account of the word; non-return, on account of the word"—this repetition of the sūtra indicates the completion of the treatise. // 22 //
Indicating the completion of the treatise, he honors the author of the Sūtras by calling him "Bhagavān.
His status as Bhagavān consists in his omniscience;
his status as Ācārya (Teacher) arises from establishing his disciples in right conduct through the medium of the Sūtras.

By the use of the term "Bādarāyaṇa," which indicates his residence at Badarikāśrama, he manifests the grace of Nārāyaṇa—the eternal omniscient Supreme Guru—and thereby demonstrates the faultlessness of the scripture composed by Him. Although knowledge of the qualified Brahman (saguṇavidyā) yields results that are subject to gradation, he states that from it follows non-return through the knowledge of the unqualified Brahman (nirguṇavidyā): "Non-return, on account of the scriptural statement; non-return, on account of the scriptural statement. The connection is as follows: those who go to the world of Brahman, having reached it, do not return.
He qualifies the world with the words "in which":

in that Brahma-world which is in the third heaven from here, from this earthly world; therein, the words *ara* and *ṇya* are equal to the syllables *ṛ* and *ṇ*, meaning they are like nectar and a heart (*sudhā-hṛda*). *Airam* means consisting of food (*anna-mayam*).
"My lake is intoxicating;
[I am] Soma-savana, the showerer of nectar.

Although there is no returning again to this human world for them, according to the Śrutis, the qualification "to this" (*imam*) suggests that those who have gone to the world of Brahmā in this *kalpa* may return in another *kalpa*.

Nevertheless, for those who have gone [to the world of Brahman] by means of practices such as the Pañcāgni-vidyā, the Aśvamedha sacrifice, and firm celibacy (*brahmacarya*), there would be a return because of the absence of the rule of knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).

However, for those who have gone by means of the meditation on the Lord (*īśvara-upāsti*) within the small space (*dahara*) and so forth, liberation occurs through the knowledge of the Self obtained by the unimpeded grace of the Lord, even when the fruit of that qualified knowledge (*saguṇa-vidyā*) has exhausted; having this in mind, he says: "But even though there is finitude... (*antavattve 'pi tu...*) and so on.

Now, one might raise the objection: "In this context, the author of the Sūtras has described the sequence of non-return only for those who know the Saguna Brahman, not for those who know the Nirguna Brahman; what is the reason for that? Anticipating this doubt, he says "samyak" (perfectly), meaning "by resorting to that.
This implies that while the possibility of return might arise for those who know the Saguna Brahman, non-return is established precisely by resorting to perfect realization (*samyagdarśana*).
Therefore, the meaning is: what more need be said regarding the fact that for those who possess right vision (*samyagdarśin*), there is no possibility of returning?
Wherever the end of a chapter occurs, the repetition of only a word has been shown;
here, however, because of the repetition of the entire *sūtra* itself, the completion of the treatise is indicated. Thus he says: "Non-return [is established] from the Word" (*anāvṛttiḥ śabdāt*).

Thus, by means of the statement on systematic concordance (*samanvaya*), it has been determined that the identity of Brahman and the Self is established by the authority of the Vedāntas; all contradictions regarding the knowledge of the meaning of the sentences—such as those arising from Smṛti and reasoning—have been removed, and the perfection of the means [of knowledge] has been demonstrated.

Therefore, for one who is endowed with the means such as discrimination and whose entire obstructions have been dispelled through the repeated practice of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, there occurs the destruction of bondage along with its root through the realization of the indivisible Self.
Thus it is established that [liberation] consists in abiding as the self, which is truth, stainless, infinite, and of the nature of self-luminous consciousness-bliss. //22//

Thus ends the fourth quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Śrīmacchārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya*, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpūjyapāda— the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya.
This Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Brahma-sūtras is completed.
Having thoroughly examined various types of texts according to my own understanding, this commentary on the *Śārīrakabhāṣya* has been composed for the delight of the virtuous. (1)

The Inner Controller, the witness of the universe, the creator of all, and the scion of Raghu—therefore, no fault can be suspected here, for according to the scriptural teaching, "He alone indeed [is this]. (2)

Beholding upon his chest and eyes, on his two sides, and in the pair of his palms— the luster of the Kaustubha gem, compassion, Sītā, the consecration of the bow, and the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting— and seeing that the embrace of Rāma’s body would belong to her alone, this commentary named *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā*, having fixed its mind thus in her heart, desiring only the bliss of her own Self, has sought refuge at the pair of lotus feet of the best of the Raghus. 3.

Thus ends the fourth quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā*, a commentary on the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsā* (Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya), composed by the venerable Govindānanda Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Gopālasarasvatī, the worshipful teacher among the illustrious Paramahaṃsa Parivrājakas.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of Brahman and Abiding in the World of Brahman."
Thus ends the fourth chapter, named "Fruit" (*phala*), in the illustrious *Śaṅkara-bhāṣya* on the *Brahma-sūtras*.
Oṃ tat sat.
